questions.q: Who is credited with first introducing the term 'Biochemistry' in 1903?
questions.e: The term 'Biochemistry' was coined in 1903 by German chemist Carl Neuberg, from the Greek word 'bios' meaning life.

questions.q: The Greek word 'bios', from which part of the word 'biochemistry' derives, means:
questions.e: 'Bios' is Greek for 'life' — biochemistry is literally the chemistry of life.

questions.q: Biochemistry is best described as the science concerned with:
o: only the physics of subatomic particles
the chemical constituents of living cells and the reactions/processes they undergo
questions.e: Biochemistry studies the chemical basis of life — the chemical constituents of cells and the reactions they undergo.

questions.q:
The major macromolecules that are usually studied in biochemistry include:
I. Proteins
II. Nucleic Acids
III. Carbohydrates
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. All three — proteins, nucleic acids, and carbohydrates (plus lipids) — are the major classes of biomolecules central to biochemistry.

questions.q: According to the landmark discoveries table, who isolated ATP from muscle in 1926?
questions.e: Fiske and Subbarow isolated ATP from muscle in 1926.

questions.q: Which scientist first achieved the laboratory synthesis of urea, according to the historical timeline?
questions.e: Wöhler achieved the synthesis of urea in 1828 — a landmark showing organic compounds could be made from inorganic starting materials.

questions.q: Who is credited with first extracting enzymes in cell-free form, in 1897?
questions.e: Edward Buchner extracted enzymes in 1897.

questions.q: Hans Krebs' landmark 1937 discovery, listed in the timeline, was:
questions.e: Hans Krebs discovered the citric acid cycle in 1937.

questions.q: The double-helix structure of DNA was described in 1953 by:
questions.e: Watson and Crick described the structure of DNA in 1953.

questions.q: According to the conclusion of the notes, dysregulation of metabolism can contribute to which group of conditions?
questions.e: The notes explicitly state that metabolic dysregulation can lead to diabetes, obesity, and metabolic syndrome.

questions.q: Many enzymes function by ___ the activation energy of reactions:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Enzymes provide an alternative, lower-energy reaction pathway — lowering the activation energy needed.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed among the three major purposes requiring free energy?
o: Performance of mechanical work in cellular movements
Storage of genetic information in chromosomes
Synthesis of macromolecules from simple precursors
Active transport of molecules and ions across membranes
questions.e: The three listed purposes are mechanical work, biosynthesis, and active transport — storage of genetic information is not one of them.

questions.q: To survive, the notes state that humans must meet how many basic metabolic requirements?
questions.e: Humans must meet two basic requirements: synthesizing what isn't supplied by diet, and protecting the internal environment from toxins and changing conditions.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes one of the two basic metabolic requirements listed in the notes?
o: Protecting the internal environment from toxins and changing external conditions
Doubling the total cell count every 24 hours
questions.e: One basic requirement is protecting the internal environment from toxins and changing external conditions.

questions.q: How many basic types of pathways does the body use to metabolize dietary components, per the notes?
questions.e: The notes describe four types: fuel oxidative pathways, fuel storage & mobilization pathways, biosynthetic pathways, and detoxification/waste disposal pathways.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the four basic pathway types described in the notes?
questions.e: Fuel storage & mobilization pathways is one of the four types; the others are fuel oxidative, biosynthetic, and detoxification/waste disposal pathways.

questions.q: Metabolism is best defined, according to the notes, as:
o: exclusively anabolic reactions occurring in the liver
the sum of chemical changes that convert food nutrients into energy and complex cellular products
only the breakdown of glucose into pyruvate
questions.e: Metabolism is the sum of chemical changes converting food nutrients into energy and the complex products of cells.

questions.q: According to the notes, a striking feature of metabolism across very different species is:
o: the complete absence of any shared pathways
the exclusive use of anaerobic pathways in all organisms
the similarity of basic metabolic pathways and components, even between vastly different species
the total independence of metabolism from enzyme activity
questions.e: The notes highlight the striking similarity of core metabolic pathways and components across very different species.

questions.q: Metabolites are best described in the notes as:
o: large structural proteins that never change
small molecules that are intermediates in the degradation or biosynthesis of biopolymers
hormones secreted only by the pancreas
questions.e: Metabolites are the small-molecule intermediates involved in breaking down or building up biopolymers.

questions.q: Catabolism is best defined as:
o: a pathway found only in plant cells
the set of pathways that build complex molecules, requiring energy
a process with no associated energy change
the set of metabolic pathways that break down complex molecules into smaller units, releasing energy
questions.e: Catabolism breaks down complex molecules into smaller units and releases energy in the process.

questions.q: Many anabolic processes are powered mainly by:
questions.e: The notes state that many anabolic processes are powered by ATP.

questions.q: Glycogenesis is classified as:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Glycogenesis builds glycogen from glucose — an anabolic (synthetic) pathway.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly lists the three stages of anabolism, in the correct order?
o: Production of simple precursors → activation of precursors using ATP → assembly into complex molecules
Assembly into complex molecules → activation using ATP → production of simple precursors
Production of simple precursors → assembly into complex molecules → activation using ATP
Activation using ATP → assembly into complex molecules → production of simple precursors
questions.e: The correct order is: production of simple precursors, then activation using ATP, then assembly into complex molecules.

questions.q: During ___, the final product of a metabolic pathway turns off the first step of that pathway:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. This end-product shutting down an earlier step is the definition of negative feedback (feedback inhibition).

questions.q: The term describing pathways that act as links between anabolic and catabolic pathways is:
questions.e: Amphibolic pathways act as links between anabolic (building) and catabolic (breaking down) processes.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the 'common themes' organisms demonstrate, according to the notes?
o: Spontaneously generating entirely new genetic codes
Using cell membranes as a physical barrier separating cell components from the environment
Extracting energy from external sources to drive energy-consuming reactions
Maintaining specific internal concentrations of ions, metabolites, and enzymes
questions.e: The notes list maintaining internal concentrations, membrane barriers, and energy extraction as common themes — not spontaneous generation of new genetic codes.

questions.q: According to the notes, enzymes within a pathway may be organized in all of the following ways EXCEPT:
questions.e: The three organizational forms described are separate enzymes, multienzyme complexes, and membrane-bound systems — not a hormone cascade.

questions.q: The Citric acid cycle is organized as a:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Oxaloacetate is regenerated each turn — a true cycle.

questions.q: Which pathway shape best describes the biosynthesis of fatty acids, where the same set of enzymes is used repeatedly to lengthen the chain?
questions.e: Fatty acid biosynthesis is the classic example of a spiral pathway, reusing the same enzymes repeatedly to extend the chain.

questions.q: Most regulatory responses in metabolic pathways occur within what general timeframe, according to the notes?
questions.e: The notes state that most regulatory responses occur in millisecond time frames, allowing rapid adjustment to changing conditions.

questions.q: Under physiological conditions, most metabolic pathways are best described as:
questions.e: The notes state that most metabolic pathways are irreversible under physiological conditions.

questions.q: The minimum amount of energy needed for a process to occur is called the:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Activation energy is the energy barrier a reaction must clear to proceed; enzymes work by lowering this barrier.

questions.q: The general term used for the anaerobic degradation of glucose to obtain energy is:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Fermentation is the general term for anaerobic glucose breakdown for energy (e.g. lactic acid or alcoholic fermentation).

questions.q:
In predicting spontaneity of reactions, if ΔG is negative and large, the reaction is:
I. Exergonic
II. Spontaneous
III. Proceed in forward direction
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. A large negative ΔG means the reaction releases free energy (exergonic, I) and will proceed spontaneously (II). Statement III is considered not an automatic consequence purely of the sign/magnitude of ΔG in the way the other two are, hence it is excluded here.

questions.q: True or False: The three ways enzymes within a pathway may be organized are as separate enzymes, as a multienzyme complex, or as a membrane-bound system.
questions.e: True — these are exactly the three organizational forms described in the notes.

questions.q: True or False: According to the notes, most metabolic pathways are reversible under physiological conditions.
questions.e: False — the notes explicitly state that most metabolic pathways are irreversible under physiological conditions.

questions.q: Consider this reaction: A + B → C + D + energy.
o: An enzyme could still speed the reaction
A and B are reactants; C and D are products
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Releasing energy makes it exergonic; enzymes speed up both exergonic and endergonic reactions by lowering activation energy; and by definition A, B (reactants) become C, D (products) — all three statements hold.

questions.q: True or False: NADH and FADH2 are described in the notes as electron carriers important in energy production during cellular respiration.
questions.e: True — the notes describe NADH and FADH2 as electron carriers playing a crucial role in energy production during cellular respiration.

questions.q:
Which of the following are among the four basic pathway types used to metabolize dietary components?
I. Fuel oxidative pathways
II. Fuel storage & mobilization pathways
III. Photosynthetic carbon-fixation pathways
questions.e: I and II are correct — the four types are fuel oxidative, fuel storage & mobilization, biosynthetic, and detoxification/waste disposal pathways. Photosynthetic carbon-fixation (III) is not one of them.

questions.q:
Which of the following are considered energy currencies mentioned in the notes?
I. ATP
II. GTP
III. Insulin
questions.e: I and II are correct — ATP and GTP are energy currencies discussed in the notes. Insulin is a hormone, not an energy currency.

questions.q:
Regarding the stages of anabolism, which of the following statements are true?
I. Anabolism proceeds in three stages.
II. The FIRST stage involves activation of precursors using ATP.
III. The final stage involves assembling precursors into complex molecules.
questions.e: I and III are correct. Statement II is false — activation of precursors using ATP is the SECOND stage, not the first; the first stage is production of the simple precursor.

questions.q:
Which of the following scientists are correctly matched with a landmark discovery listed in the historical timeline?
I. Wöhler – synthesis of urea
II. Buchner – extracted enzymes
III. Mullis – structure of DNA
questions.e: I and II are correctly matched. Statement III is false — Kary Mullis developed PCR, not the structure of DNA (that was Watson & Crick).

questions.q: An uncatalysed reaction requires a:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Without a catalyst, the reaction must climb the full, higher activation-energy barrier on its own.

questions.q:
Which of the following are among the 'common themes' organisms demonstrate, according to the notes?
I. Cell membranes provide a physical barrier separating cell components from the environment.
II. Organisms extract energy from external sources to drive energy-consuming reactions.
III. Metabolic pathways are completely independent of an organism's genes.
questions.e: I and II are correct. Statement III is false — the notes state that metabolic pathways ARE specified by the genes in each organism, not independent of them.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The citric acid cycle is described as an amphibolic pathway.
Reason (R): It participates in both energy-yielding catabolic processes and biosynthetic anabolic processes.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are false
questions.e: Both statements are true, and R correctly explains why the citric acid cycle is amphibolic — it plays roles in both catabolism and anabolism.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: ATP releases a large amount of energy upon hydrolysis
REASON: ATP has low energy bonds.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The assertion is true — hydrolysis of ATP's terminal phosphate is highly exergonic. But the reason is false: ATP's phosphoanhydride bonds are described as HIGH-energy bonds, not low-energy ones.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Metabolic pathways are in equilibrium
REASON: metabolic pathways are in a steady state.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The assertion is false: living metabolic pathways are deliberately kept away from true chemical equilibrium (equilibrium would mean the reaction has stopped net flow). The reason is true — pathways operate at a steady state, where intermediates are maintained at fairly constant concentrations even as flux continues through the pathway.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Anabolism produces energy in living organisms
REASON: anabolism supplies energy for use in catabolic process in living organisms.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Both statements are false. Anabolism is the energy-CONSUMING (endergonic) arm of metabolism — it uses energy to build complex molecules from simpler ones. It is catabolism that breaks molecules down and releases energy, some of which is then used to drive anabolic reactions — the reverse of what is stated here.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Hans Krebs and Carl Neuberg are both credited with introducing the term 'biochemistry' in 1903.
Reason (R): Both scientists worked together on the discovery of the citric acid cycle in 1937.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are false
questions.e: Both statements are false. Only Carl Neuberg introduced the term 'biochemistry' (1903); Hans Krebs alone discovered the citric acid cycle (1937) — they were not collaborators on either.

questions.q: Vitamins are essential to the survival of organisms because vitamins usually function as:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Many vitamins (B-vitamins especially) are precursors to essential coenzymes — e.g. niacin→NAD⁺, riboflavin→FAD, thiamine→TPP.

questions.q: An inhibitor that changes the overall shape and chemistry of an enzyme is known as a(n):
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere on the enzyme (not the active site) and distort its overall conformation, indirectly disabling catalysis.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of enzymes?
o: They are permanently used up after catalyzing a single reaction
They remain chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction
questions.e: Enzymes are reusable catalysts — they are colloidal, thermolabile, and specific, but they are NOT consumed; they are released unchanged and ready to catalyze again.

questions.q: Which non-protein biomolecule can act as a biological catalyst, forming an exception to the 'enzymes are proteins' rule?
questions.e: The lecture specifically notes RNA acting as a ribozyme as the exception — most enzymes are protein, but some RNA molecules (like the RNA component of ribonuclease P) show true catalytic activity.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: The active site is directly involved in catalysis
REASON: the active site contains between 8 to 10 amino acid residues.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The assertion is true — the active site is where substrate binding and the catalytic chemistry occur. The reason is false: there is no fixed rule that active sites contain 8–10 residues; typically only a small number of residues make direct catalytic contact, and this varies from enzyme to enzyme.

questions.q: What happens to an enzyme's catalytic activity when it becomes denatured?
o: Activity is unaffected since only the primary structure matters
Activity is lost because the enzyme's three-dimensional shape is disrupted
The enzyme is converted directly into a coenzyme
Activity increases because more active sites are exposed
questions.e: Denaturation disrupts the folded 3D shape that creates the active site. Without the correct shape, the enzyme can no longer bind substrate effectively, so activity is lost.

questions.q: Which suffix is traditionally added to the name of a substrate to form the trivial (common) name of the enzyme that acts on it?
questions.e: The lecture gives examples like lipase (acts on lipids), nuclease (acts on nucleic acids), and lactase (acts on lactose) — all formed by adding '-ase' to the substrate name.

questions.q: Which body appointed the Enzyme Commission in 1961 to develop systematic rules for naming and classifying enzymes?
o: International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry acting alone
questions.e: Trivial names like pepsin and trypsin gave no information about function, so the IUB appointed an Enzyme Commission in 1961 to create a systematic naming and classification system.

questions.q: Enzymes that catalyze oxidation-reduction reactions belong to which IUB class?
questions.e: Oxidoreductases (EC 1) are specifically defined as enzymes involved in oxidation-reduction reactions — the very first of the six major IUB classes.

questions.q: An enzyme that catalyzes the joining of two molecules using energy from ATP belongs to which class?
questions.e: Ligases (from the Greek 'ligate' — to bind) catalyze synthetic reactions where two molecules are joined together, using ATP as the energy source.

questions.q: Which class of enzymes specializes in adding or removing water, ammonia, or carbon dioxide (without using hydrolysis)?
questions.e: Lyases (EC 4) specialize in the addition or removal of groups like water, ammonia, and CO2 without a hydrolytic step.

questions.q: Which antibiotic blocks the active site of an enzyme that many bacteria use to make cell walls?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Penicillin blocks the transpeptidase enzyme that cross-links peptidoglycan in bacterial cell walls. (Cephalosporins work similarly, but penicillin is the classic textbook answer here.)

questions.q: An inhibitor binds a site away from the active site and changes the enzyme’s overall shape. It is best described as:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Binding away from the active site and disabling the enzyme through a change in its overall shape is non-competitive inhibition, and because that second site is an allosteric site the same event is also described as allosteric inhibition — so both B and C apply.

questions.q: At high temperature the rate of enzyme action decreases because the increased heat:
o: Changes the pH of the system
Neutralizes acids and bases in the system
Alters the active site of the enzyme
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Excess heat disrupts the weak bonds holding the enzyme's 3D shape together, distorting (denaturing) the active site so substrate no longer fits well.

questions.q: The catalytic activity of an enzyme is restricted to its small portion called:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Catalysis happens specifically at the active site — the small pocket/region that binds substrate and carries out the reaction.

questions.q: When a molecule binds to an area of an enzyme that is not the active site, and changes the shape of the enzyme so it no longer works, this is called:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Binding away from the active site and disabling the enzyme via a shape change is the definition of non-competitive (allosteric) inhibition.

questions.q: Which one inactivates an enzyme by indirectly changing the shape of the active site of an enzyme?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and distort the enzyme's overall shape, which indirectly disrupts the active site too.

questions.q: The 'lock and key hypothesis' attempts to explain the mechanism of:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. It's a model for why each enzyme works on only its own specific substrate(s).

questions.q: In the Lock and Key model of enzyme action, the part of the enzyme that recognizes the substrate is known as the:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The active site is the specific region shaped to recognize and bind the substrate.

questions.q: The 'lock and key' model of enzymes suggested that ___ were rigid in nature:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Fischer's lock-and-key model pictured the enzyme's active site as a rigid, pre-shaped mould that only a perfectly complementary substrate could fit — later revised by Koshland's induced-fit model.

questions.q: The 'lock and key' model of enzyme action illustrates that a particular enzyme molecule:
o: Interacts with a specific type of substrate molecule
Reacts at identical rates under all conditions
May be destroyed and resynthesized several times
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The model's core point is specificity — a given enzyme's active site shape fits only a particular substrate, like a specific key fits a specific lock.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: The lock and key model of enzymes is accepted
REASON: the lock and key model was able to explain the kinetic behavior of enzymes.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Both statements are treated as true here (the lock-and-key model is a foundational, historically accepted model, and it does describe basic enzyme kinetics), but the second statement does not causally explain why the model is 'accepted' — they are independent facts, not explanation and assertion.

questions.q: Who proposed the 'lock and key' model to study enzyme-substrate interaction?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Emil Fischer proposed the lock-and-key model in 1894/1898, picturing the enzyme's active site as a rigid, pre-shaped mould.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Coenzymes are usually loosely bound to an enzyme
REASON: coenzymes usually attach themselves to enzymes through covalent bonding.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The assertion is true — coenzymes typically associate loosely/transiently (non-covalently) with enzymes, unlike prosthetic groups. The reason is false: covalent, tight binding describes prosthetic groups, not the loose association of coenzymes.

questions.q: Which term describes a cofactor tightly and stably bound to an enzyme by covalent or strong noncovalent forces?
questions.e: Prosthetic groups (e.g., FAD, biotin, metal ions like Zn or Cu) are distinguished from coenzymes by their tight, stable attachment to the enzyme's structure.

questions.q: The function of competitive inhibitors is defined by their ability to interact or bind to:
o: The active site of an enzyme
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate and compete directly for the active site.

questions.q: As temperature rises within an enzyme's optimal range, what generally happens to its activity, before denaturation sets in?
o: The enzyme instantly loses its 3D structure
Enzyme activity stays exactly the same regardless of temperature
Enzyme activity decreases steadily from the start
questions.e: Enzyme activity rises with temperature up to a point — beyond the optimum, the enzyme's folded structure starts to break down (denature) and activity falls sharply.

questions.q: Why can food be preserved for longer when kept in a refrigerator?
o: Refrigeration increases the concentration of spoilage enzymes
Cold permanently denatures every bacterial enzyme on contact
Cold destroys the substrates that would otherwise spoil
Low temperature reduces the activity of bacterial enzymes, slowing spoilage
questions.e: Just as jollof left in a cooler stays fresh longer at a chilly campus event, lower temperatures slow down the bacterial enzymes responsible for spoilage rather than destroying them outright.

questions.q: Koshland in 1959 proposed the:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Koshland's induced-fit model (1959) proposed that the active site's shape adjusts to better fit the substrate upon binding.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between pH and enzyme activity?
o: Activity keeps increasing indefinitely as pH rises
All enzymes in the body share exactly the same optimum pH
Enzyme activity is completely unaffected by pH
Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which its velocity is maximal, with activity dropping on either side
questions.e: Just as pepsin in the stomach works best in very acidic conditions while pancreatic enzymes prefer a more alkaline environment, every enzyme has its own optimum pH beyond which activity falls.

questions.q: The site where the enzyme-catalyzed reaction takes place is called:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Catalysis occurs at the active site.

questions.q: A student tests the efficiency of a certain enzyme. Which would probably NOT result in a change in the enzyme's efficiency?
o: All A, B, & C change the enzyme's efficiency
Adding more substrate but not enzyme
Adding an acidic solution to the setup
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. pH and temperature changes directly alter the enzyme's own conformation/activity. Adding more substrate (without more enzyme) just changes the rate of product formation up to saturation — it doesn't change how efficient each enzyme molecule is.

questions.q: It suggests that the binding of substrate to the enzyme alters the structure of the enzyme, placing some strain on the substrate and further facilitating the reaction:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. This dynamic, shape-adjusting description is exactly the induced-fit model (Koshland), as opposed to the rigid lock-and-key model.

questions.q: Exposure to which type of radiation is specifically noted to inhibit salivary amylase activity?
questions.e: The lecture notes that UV, beta, gamma, and X-rays can inactivate certain enzymes through peroxide formation, and specifically calls out UV rays as inhibiting salivary amylase.

questions.q: Which drug used in treating alcoholism works by irreversibly inhibiting acetaldehyde dehydrogenase?
questions.e: Disulfiram blocks acetaldehyde dehydrogenase irreversibly, causing acetaldehyde to build up — this produces the unpleasant hangover-like symptoms that discourage drinking.

questions.q: Organophosphorus insecticides are toxic to humans because they irreversibly inhibit which enzyme essential for nerve conduction?
questions.e: By irreversibly blocking acetylcholinesterase, organophosphorus insecticides prevent normal nerve signal termination, leading to paralysis of vital body functions.

questions.q: They are non-protein organic molecules bound to enzymes near the active site:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Coenzymes are the organic (often vitamin-derived) non-protein cofactors that assist catalysis near the active site.

questions.q: Cofactors that are tightly bound to an enzyme are known as:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. A cofactor that is permanently/tightly bound (rather than loosely associating and dissociating) is specifically called a prosthetic group; a loosely-bound organic cofactor is usually just called a coenzyme.

questions.q: Which model says the active site moulds itself around the substrate as binding occurs?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The induced fit model (Koshland, 1959) holds that the active site is flexible: substrate binding moulds it into the complementary shape, unlike the rigid pre-formed site of the lock and key model.

questions.q: ___ occurs when the inhibitory chemical, which does not have to resemble the substrate, binds to the enzyme other than at the active site:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Non-competitive inhibitors bind at a separate (allosteric) site and need not resemble the substrate at all.

questions.q: Enzymes are highly specific for a given substrate due to the shape of their:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The precise 3D shape (and charge pattern) of the active site is what makes each enzyme substrate-specific.

questions.q: Zymogens such as pepsinogen are inactive precursor forms of enzymes that require activation before they can function.
questions.e: True. Zymogens (proenzymes) like pepsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, and plasminogen must undergo irreversible peptide bond cleavage to become active (pepsin, chymotrypsin, plasmin).

questions.q: According to the lecture, amylase has a longer biological half-life than lactate dehydrogenase (LDH).
questions.e: False. The lecture states LDH has a half-life of about 5 to 6 days, while amylase's half-life is much shorter — only about 3 to 5 hours.

questions.q: Elevated serum aspartate transaminase (AST) is commonly used to help diagnose myocardial infarction (heart attack).
questions.e: True. AST (along with CPK and LDH) is listed in the lecture as a marker enzyme for heart attacks.

questions.q: Competitive inhibitors stop an enzyme from working by:
o: Blocking the active site of the enzyme
Combining with the product of the reaction
Changing the shape of the enzyme
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate closely enough to occupy (block) the active site, competing directly with the real substrate for that same site.

questions.q: Ribozymes are RNA molecules that can function as biological catalysts, as demonstrated by ribonuclease P.
questions.e: True. The RNA component of ribonuclease P was shown to exhibit true enzyme activity and even obey Michaelis-Menten kinetics, proving RNA can act as a catalyst.

questions.q: Which of the following are among the six major IUB classes of enzymes? (Select ALL that apply)
questions.e: The six official IUB classes are Oxidoreductases, Transferases, Hydrolases, Lyases, Isomerases, and Ligases. 'Proteases' and 'Nucleases' are older trivial names based on substrate, not official IUB class names.

questions.q: Which of the following is/are types of reversible inhibition?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Competitive (and non-competitive/uncompetitive) inhibition is reversible; covalent modification is the hallmark of irreversible inhibition. 'Hydrogen' and 'oxidative' inhibition aren't standard inhibition categories.

questions.q: According to the lecture, which of the following are ways enzyme activity is regulated in cells? (Select ALL that apply)
questions.e: The lecture lists five regulatory mechanisms: allosteric regulation, activation of latent enzymes, compartmentation, control of enzyme synthesis, and enzyme degradation. Random mutation is not a regulatory mechanism.

questions.q: Which of the following enzymes are used as markers to help diagnose myocardial infarction (heart attack)? (Select ALL that apply)
questions.e: AST, CPK, and LDH are all listed as heart attack markers (with CPK being an early marker). Alkaline phosphatase is linked to rickets/obstructive jaundice, and acid phosphatase to prostate cancer.

questions.q: Which of the following are examples of coenzymes/cofactors mentioned in the lecture? (Select ALL that apply)
questions.e: Thiamin, riboflavin, and biotin are organic coenzymes, and Mg++ is listed as an inorganic coenzyme. Cellulose and chlorophyll are not cofactors mentioned in the lecture.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about factors affecting enzyme activity are TRUE, according to the lecture? (Select ALL that apply)
o: Each enzyme has an optimum pH beyond which activity declines
Increasing substrate concentration raises the rate until active sites are saturated
UV, beta, gamma, and X-rays can inactivate certain enzymes
Temperature increases enzyme activity up to a point before denaturation occurs
Enzyme concentration has no effect on reaction rate
questions.e: Temperature, pH, substrate concentration, enzyme concentration, and radiation all affect enzyme activity. Only the statement claiming enzyme concentration has 'no effect' is false — increasing enzyme amount increases rate when substrate is abundant.

questions.q: Epinephrine and glucagon regulate glycolysis by which covalent-modification mechanism?

Directly binding to pyruvate kinase's active site
Increasing AMP levels to activate PFK-1
questions.e: Epinephrine and glucagon raise cAMP levels, activating cAMP-dependent protein kinase, which rapidly phosphorylates and inactivates pyruvate kinase — a fast-acting regulatory mechanism.

questions.q: PFK-1 activity is allosterically inhibited by which molecules?
questions.e: High levels of citrate and ATP signal that the cell has abundant energy, so they allosterically inhibit PFK-1 to slow glycolysis.

questions.q: Which molecule allosterically activates PFK-1, signaling low cellular energy status?
questions.e: Rising AMP indicates the cell's energy charge is low, so AMP allosterically activates PFK-1 to accelerate glycolysis and restore ATP levels.

questions.q: Why must NADH generated during glycolysis be continuously recycled back to NAD+?
o: So that NAD+ does not become limiting, allowing glycolysis to continue
So ATP can be hydrolyzed back to ADP
So that pyruvate kinase can remain active
questions.e: The glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step requires NAD+ as an electron acceptor; without recycling NADH back to NAD+, glycolysis would grind to a halt.

questions.q: Under aerobic conditions, what is the ultimate fate of pyruvate produced by glycolysis?
o: It is reduced directly to lactate
It enters the citric acid cycle, where it is oxidized to CO2, producing additional NADH and FADH2
It is excreted unchanged from the cell
It is converted back into glucose
questions.e: With oxygen available, pyruvate is fed into the citric acid cycle for full oxidation, generating further reducing equivalents (NADH and FADH2) for the electron transport chain.

questions.q: The rate-limiting step of glycolysis is:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Step 3 is the PFK-1 reaction (F6P → F1,6BP) — the committed, rate-limiting, allosterically regulated step of glycolysis.

questions.q: In the Preparatory Phase, 2 ATP molecules are generated rather than consumed.
questions.e: False. The Preparatory Phase INVESTS (consumes) 2 ATP molecules to activate glucose — ATP is only generated later, during the Pay-Off Phase.

questions.q: Glucokinase, the hepatic isozyme of hexokinase, phosphorylates glucose specifically in the liver.
questions.e: True. Glucokinase is the liver-specific isozyme that carries out the same first phosphorylation step as hexokinase, but only in hepatocytes.

questions.q: The reaction catalyzed by phosphofructokinase-1 is reversible under cellular conditions.
questions.e: False. The PFK-1 reaction is irreversible under cellular conditions, making it one of the three key regulatory control points of glycolysis.

questions.q: Aldolase catalyzes a reversible aldol condensation reaction that cleaves fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.
questions.e: True. Unlike the irreversible steps of glycolysis, the aldolase-catalyzed cleavage is a reversible aldol condensation reaction.

questions.q: The step catalyzed by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase can be inhibited by heavy metals and arsenite.
questions.e: True. The lecture specifically lists heavy metals, arsenite, and iodoacetate as inhibitors of this dehydrogenation step.

questions.q: The Rapoport-Luebering shunt and 2,3-BPG production are especially important in skeletal muscle cells.
questions.e: False. This shunt and its 2,3-BPG product are especially significant in erythrocytes (red blood cells), helping unload oxygen to peripheral tissues.

questions.q: Glycolysis is classified (metabolically) as:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Glycolysis breaks glucose down — a catabolic pathway.

questions.q: The enzyme ___ catalyses an anaplerotic reaction:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Pyruvate carboxylase (pyruvate → oxaloacetate) is the classic anaplerotic reaction, replenishing TCA cycle intermediates. ('Malate carboxykinase' and 'malate synthetase' aren't standard enzyme names — likely mean PEP carboxykinase and malate synthase respectively, neither of which is anaplerotic in the mammalian TCA sense.)

questions.q: Glycolysis in the erythrocyte produces pyruvate that is further metabolized to:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Red blood cells have no mitochondria, so pyruvate can't enter the TCA cycle — it's reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, regenerating NAD⁺ for glycolysis to continue.

questions.q: Glycolysis:

Produces 4 ATPs at the end of the reaction
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The payoff phase generates 4 ATP in total (2 per triose × 2 trioses); after subtracting the 2 ATP invested earlier in the preparatory phase, the NET yield is 2 ATP — but the gross amount produced 'at the end' (payoff phase) is 4.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true for fructolysis and glycolysis?
o: These processes share same intermediate structures
Leads to same metabolic fates for fructose and glucose
Both fructose and glucose are exclusively metabolized in the liver
Rate of fructose and glucose transport is virtually the same
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Fructolysis converges with glycolysis at the level of the triose phosphates (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate / dihydroxyacetone phosphate), so the two pathways do share common intermediate structures. Their regulation and tissue fates differ, transport uses different carriers (GLUT5 vs GLUT2/GLUT4) at different rates, and glucose is metabolised in virtually every tissue, not just the liver.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the fate of pyruvate and NADH are TRUE, according to the lecture? (Select ALL that apply)
o: NADH is directly converted into ATP without involving any other pathway
NADH must be recycled to NAD+ to avoid becoming limiting
The fate of pyruvate depends partly on the availability of oxygen

Under aerobic conditions, pyruvate enters the citric acid cycle
questions.e: Pyruvate's fate (TCA cycle vs. lactate formation) and NADH's need for recycling both depend on oxygen availability. NADH is not directly converted into ATP — it must be reoxidized via the electron transport chain (aerobic) or lactate formation (anaerobic).

questions.q: Polyol pathway
o: Pathway is present in the liver
Pathway is not related to glucose concentration
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. In the polyol pathway, aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol, and sorbitol dehydrogenase then converts sorbitol to fructose — so it does involve sorbitol dehydrogenase. Aldolase B belongs to fructose metabolism, not the polyol pathway; the pathway is most active in tissues like the lens, retina, nerve and kidney (not primarily the liver); and its flux rises with high glucose concentration (e.g. in hyperglycaemia), so it is very much related to glucose levels.

questions.q: The polyol (sorbitol) pathway is notably absent from which organ?
questions.e: Unlike many other tissues, the liver lacks significant aldose reductase activity, so the polyol pathway is essentially absent there.

questions.q: Activity of the sorbitol pathway is directly related to:
questions.e: The sorbitol pathway's activity rises in proportion to glucose concentration, becoming markedly elevated in hyperglycemic states.

questions.q: Sorbitol pathway activity is characteristically higher in:
o: Healthy individuals after an overnight fast
questions.e: Because sorbitol pathway flux is driven by glucose concentration, it is markedly increased during the hyperglycemia of uncontrolled diabetes.

questions.q: Sorbitol is subsequently oxidized to fructose by sorbitol dehydrogenase, which requires:
questions.e: Sorbitol dehydrogenase oxidizes sorbitol to fructose using NAD+ as the electron acceptor (producing NADH).

questions.q: Aldose reductase, the enzyme that initiates the polyol pathway, is found in tissues such as:
o: Lens and retina of the eye, kidney, placenta, Schwann cells, erythrocytes and seminal vesicles
questions.e: Aldose reductase is widely distributed in tissues including the lens, retina, kidney, placenta, peripheral nerve Schwann cells, erythrocytes, and seminal vesicles, but is essentially absent from the liver.

questions.q: Fructose serves as the preferred fuel substrate for which cell type?
questions.e: Fructose is the preferred energy source for sperm cells; it is generated locally in the seminal vesicles via the polyol pathway and secreted into semen.

questions.q: In the seminal vesicles, glucose is converted to:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Seminal vesicles synthesize fructose (from glucose) as the main energy fuel for sperm in seminal fluid.

questions.q: In uncontrolled diabetes (hyperglycemia), large amounts of glucose enter cells that are:
o: Strictly dependent on insulin for glucose uptake
Not dependent on insulin for glucose uptake
questions.e: Tissues such as the lens, nerves, kidney and retina take up glucose independently of insulin, so in hyperglycemia their intracellular glucose levels rise substantially.

questions.q: In hyperglycemia, tissues such as the lens, retina, nerve cells and kidney show increased flux through the polyol pathway mainly because they possess high activity of:
o: Aldose reductase, together with sufficient NADPH
questions.e: These tissues have high aldose reductase activity and adequate NADPH supply, allowing rapid conversion of the excess intracellular glucose to sorbitol.

questions.q: In the diabetic complications associated with the polyol pathway, the conversion of sorbitol onward to fructose is limited because affected tissues have:
o: Excess aldose reductase and no sorbitol dehydrogenase deficiency
Low or absent sorbitol dehydrogenase activity
questions.e: In tissues like the lens, retina and nerves, sorbitol dehydrogenase activity is low or absent, so sorbitol is not efficiently converted to fructose and instead accumulates.

questions.q: Sorbitol accumulates inside affected cells in diabetes mainly because sorbitol:
o: Cannot freely cross the cell membrane
Is degraded immediately by aldolase B
Is rapidly converted back to glucose
Is actively pumped out via GLUT5
questions.e: Sorbitol does not diffuse easily across cell membranes, so once formed it tends to accumulate within the cell where it was produced.

questions.q: Pathological changes associated with polyol pathway activity in diabetes include:
o: Cataract formation, peripheral neuropathy and nephropathy
questions.e: Accumulation of sorbitol in the lens, peripheral nerves and kidney is believed to contribute to cataract formation, peripheral neuropathy and nephropathy in diabetic patients.

questions.q: Which of the following is true about Essential fructosuria
o: A child from carrier parents has 50% chance of having this condition
Caused by deficiency in hepatic fructokinase
Fructose is trapped within the cells
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Essential fructosuria results from a deficiency of hepatic fructokinase, so ingested fructose cannot be phosphorylated in the liver and simply spills into the urine unchanged. It is a benign, largely ASYMPTOMATIC condition, and — being autosomal recessive — two carrier parents have a 25% (not 50%) chance of an affected child.

questions.q: In essential fructosuria, there is reduced or complete absence of:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Essential fructosuria = fructokinase deficiency, so fructose is never phosphorylated and simply spills into urine unchanged (harmless, unlike Hereditary Fructose Intolerance, which is aldolase B/F1P-aldolase deficiency).

questions.q: In essential fructosuria, the metabolic block prevents the phosphorylation of fructose to:
questions.e: Because fructokinase is deficient, fructose cannot be phosphorylated to fructose 1-phosphate, the normal first step of its metabolism.

questions.q: Fructose appears in the urine (fructosuria) when:
o: Plasma fructose exceeds the renal threshold for fructose reabsorption
Liver glycogen stores are completely depleted
questions.e: As plasma fructose concentration rises in essential fructosuria, it eventually exceeds the renal tubular threshold for reabsorption, leading to fructose appearing in the urine.

questions.q: Clinically, essential fructosuria is best described as:
o: A major cause of neonatal liver failure
A cause of progressive renal failure in childhood
A severe, life-threatening disorder requiring emergency treatment
questions.e: Essential fructosuria has no significant clinical manifestations and is generally considered a harmless, asymptomatic biochemical curiosity.

questions.q: Hereditary Fructose Intolerance (HFI) results from a deficiency of which enzyme?
questions.e: HFI is caused by deficiency of aldolase B, the enzyme that normally cleaves fructose 1-phosphate into DHAP and glyceraldehyde.

questions.q: Hereditary Fructose Intolerance is also known by which alternative name?
questions.e: HFI is also referred to as hereditary fructosemia, reflecting the rise in blood fructose levels seen after fructose ingestion.

questions.q: In HFI, fructose metabolism is blocked, so fructose cannot be processed further once it has been converted to:
questions.e: Fructokinase still converts fructose to fructose 1-phosphate normally in HFI, but the deficient aldolase B cannot cleave it further, so fructose 1-phosphate accumulates.

questions.q: Depletion of inorganic phosphate in HFI impairs the activity of which enzyme, contributing to hypoglycemia?
questions.e: Because Pi is trapped as part of fructose 1-phosphate, glycogen phosphorylase (which requires Pi to release glucose 1-phosphate from glycogen) cannot function properly, impairing glycogenolysis.

questions.q: Following fructose ingestion, patients with HFI characteristically develop:
questions.e: Inhibition of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis after fructose ingestion in HFI leads to profound hypoglycemia.

questions.q: The estimated prevalence of HFI in some European populations is approximately:
questions.e: HFI may be as common as 1 in 20,000 people in some European populations, making it one of the more recognizable inborn errors of carbohydrate metabolism.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT typically described as a sign or symptom following fructose ingestion in HFI?
questions.e: The classic signs after fructose ingestion in HFI include vomiting, hypoglycemia, jaundice, haemorrhage, hepatomegaly, hyperuricemia and kidney failure — not polyuria with glycosuria, which is more typical of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus.

questions.q: With very high fructose intake, fructokinase rapidly phosphorylates fructose to fructose 1-phosphate, but because aldolase B activity is comparatively limited, this leads to:
o: A marked rise in ATP production
Accumulation of fructose 1-phosphate and depletion of intracellular inorganic phosphate
questions.e: Because aldolase B cannot keep pace with fructokinase activity during high fructose loads, fructose 1-phosphate accumulates, sequestering Pi and lowering its intracellular availability.

questions.q: The binding of inorganic phosphate to organic molecules such as fructose 1-phosphate, reducing the availability of free Pi for essential metabolic reactions, is referred to as:
questions.e: This phenomenon — where Pi becomes 'trapped' bound to an organic molecule and is therefore less available for metabolism — is termed sequestering of phosphate.

questions.q: One consequence of decreased availability of inorganic phosphate during high fructose consumption is:
o: Lowered synthesis of ATP from ADP and Pi
Increased synthesis of ATP from ADP and Pi
questions.e: With less free Pi available, the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP is reduced, lowering ATP synthesis.

questions.q: Chronic high consumption of fructose is associated with increased blood levels of:
questions.e: Long-term high fructose intake is associated with increased blood uric acid levels, which can predispose to gout.

questions.q: The mechanism by which high fructose intake raises uric acid levels involves:
o: Direct conversion of fructose to uric acid by aldolase B
Decreased renal excretion of uric acid only
Excessive breakdown of ADP and AMP to uric acid
Increased synthesis of purines from glucose
questions.e: Because Pi is sequestered by fructose 1-phosphate, ADP and AMP accumulate and are excessively degraded, ultimately increasing uric acid production.

questions.q:
Galactose is produced from:
I. Glycolipids
II. Glycoproteins
III. Milk
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. While galactose is structurally found in glycolipids and glycoproteins, the major dietary/exogenous SOURCE of galactose is lactose in milk (which is hydrolysed to glucose + galactose), making milk the key answer intended here.

questions.q: The hydrolysis of lactose into glucose and galactose is catalyzed by the enzyme:
questions.e: Lactase, also called beta-galactosidase, is located on intestinal mucosal cells and hydrolyzes lactose into its component monosaccharides, glucose and galactose.

questions.q: The principal dietary source of galactose is:
questions.e: Lactose, present in milk and milk products, is the principal dietary source of galactose, which is released upon lactase digestion.

questions.q: Similar to fructose, the entry of galactose into cells is:
questions.e: Like fructose, galactose entry into cells is not regulated by insulin.

questions.q: The only physiological way to catabolize (break down) galactose is by:
o: Direct conversion to glycogen without intermediates
questions.e: Galactose catabolism proceeds exclusively through its conversion to glucose, which then enters mainstream glucose metabolism.

questions.q: How many enzymes are involved in the conversion of galactose to glucose?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The Leloir pathway uses galactokinase, galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT), and UDP-galactose-4-epimerase, plus phosphoglucomutase to convert the resulting glucose-1-phosphate to glucose-6-phosphate — four enzymes in total in the standard teaching scheme.

questions.q: Because of its role in galactose-to-glucose conversion, this metabolic capacity of the liver can be exploited as a:
questions.e: The liver's ability to convert administered galactose to glucose can be used clinically as a measure of hepatic function.

questions.q: Galactose metabolism is classified as:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The Leloir pathway converts galactose into glucose-1-phosphate for use/breakdown — catabolic.

questions.q: Galactose 1-phosphate is converted onward by exchanging with which compound, in a reaction catalyzed by galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase?
questions.e: Galactose 1-phosphate displaces glucose 1-phosphate from UDP-glucose, forming UDP-galactose and glucose 1-phosphate, in the reaction catalyzed by galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase.

questions.q:
The pathways for glucose converted from galactose include:
I. Gluconeogenesis
II. Glycolysis
III. Glycogenesis
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Once galactose is converted (via the Leloir pathway) to glucose-6-phosphate, that G6P can be used in glycolysis for energy or in glycogenesis for storage. It is not classified as entering 'gluconeogenesis', since gluconeogenesis specifically refers to synthesising new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors.

questions.q: UDP-galactose, generated during galactose metabolism, is converted back to UDP-glucose by the action of:
questions.e: UDP-galactose-4-epimerase interconverts UDP-galactose and UDP-glucose, regenerating UDP-glucose so it can again accept galactose 1-phosphate.

questions.q: Because UDP-glucose is regenerated and reused at the end of this cycle, it functions in galactose metabolism as a:
o: Coenzyme in the conversion of galactose to glucose
Structural component of cell membranes only
questions.e: Since UDP-glucose is consumed and then regenerated by UDP-galactose-4-epimerase in each turn of the cycle, it effectively acts as a coenzyme in the overall conversion of galactose to glucose.

questions.q: A deficiency of which enzyme would directly impair the exchange reaction that converts galactose 1-phosphate to glucose 1-phosphate and UDP-galactose?
questions.e: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase catalyzes the exchange of galactose 1-phosphate with UDP-glucose; its deficiency blocks this step.

questions.q: Which divalent cation is required as a cofactor in the galactokinase reaction?
questions.e: Mg2+ is required as a cofactor for the galactokinase-catalyzed phosphorylation of galactose by ATP.

questions.q:
Cataract due to galactokinase deficiency arises from:
I. Accumulation of galactitol
II. Permeable cells to water
III. Low activity of aldose reductase
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. With galactokinase deficiency, excess galactose is instead reduced by ALDOSE REDUCTASE (which is normally, not poorly, active) to galactitol. Galactitol accumulates in the lens (I), drawing water in osmotically and making the lens cells swell/permeable (II) — this is what causes the cataract. Statement III is false; it is not low aldose reductase activity that causes this — the enzyme is active enough to generate the damaging galactitol.

questions.q: Galactokinase deficiency is inherited as:
questions.e: Galactokinase deficiency is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder.

questions.q: The major clinical feature of galactokinase deficiency is:
o: Cataracts developing within the first weeks or months of life
questions.e: The hallmark clinical feature of galactokinase deficiency is the early development of cataracts in infancy.

questions.q: In galactokinase deficiency there is accumulation of:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Without galactokinase, galactose can't be phosphorylated, so it accumulates and gets shunted by aldose reductase into galactitol — the compound responsible for cataract formation in this condition.

questions.q: Galactitol contributes to cataract formation in galactokinase deficiency mainly because it:
o: Directly binds and inactivates lens crystallin enzymes
Is converted rapidly to toxic free radicals in the lens
Cannot leave the lens, causing osmotic accumulation of water and damage
questions.e: Galactitol, like sorbitol, cannot easily leave the cell once formed; its accumulation in the lens draws in water osmotically, leading to swelling and damage.

questions.q: Classical galactosemia is caused by a deficiency of which enzyme?
questions.e: Classical galactosemia results from a deficiency of galactose 1-phosphate uridyl transferase, the enzyme that converts galactose 1-phosphate to glucose 1-phosphate and UDP-galactose.

questions.q: In classical galactosemia, impaired galactose metabolism leads to elevated levels of galactose in:
questions.e: Because galactose cannot be efficiently metabolized, its levels rise in the circulation (galactosemia) and it spills over into the urine (galactosuria).

questions.q: Galactitol is formed from galactose by the enzyme:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Aldose reductase reduces excess galactose to galactitol (using NADPH); galactitol build-up in the lens is what drives cataract formation in galactosemia/galactokinase deficiency.

questions.q: Which of the following clinical symptoms of classical galactosemia is a direct result of the accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Accumulated galactose-1-phosphate is directly hepatotoxic, damaging liver cells and causing jaundice. (By contrast, the cataracts of galactosemia are attributed to galactitol, formed via aldose reductase, rather than to galactose-1-phosphate itself.)

questions.q: Early biochemical diagnosis of classical galactosemia is made by measuring the activity of galactose 1-phosphate uridyl transferase in:
questions.e: A simple and early diagnostic test for classical galactosemia involves measuring galactose 1-phosphate uridyl transferase activity in erythrocytes.

questions.q:
Galactosemia is:
I. Due to deficiency in galactokinase
II. A sex-linked hereditary disease
III. A congenital disease in infants
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Correction: Classic galactosemia is caused by deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT) — galactokinase deficiency causes a separate, milder disorder — so statement I is not accurate for 'galactosemia' as classically defined. Statement II is factually incorrect: galactosemia is inherited in an AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE pattern, not sex-linked. Only statement III is correct — it is a congenital disorder that presents in infancy. (This answer has been corrected from the original paper, which had marked 'A'.)

questions.q: The degree of fructosuria seen in essential fructosuria depends on the amount of fructose ingested in the diet.
questions.e: Since fructose is not trapped or metabolized normally, the amount excreted in urine correlates with dietary fructose intake.

questions.q: Provided that patients with hereditary fructose intolerance strictly avoid dietary fructose, the long-term prognosis is generally good.
questions.e: Treatment with a fructose-free diet, if adhered to, is associated with a good prognosis in HFI.

questions.q: In the polyol pathway, accumulation of sorbitol and related changes are believed to share a common pathogenesis underlying many of the chronic complications of diabetes.
questions.e: It appears that a majority of diabetic complications (cataracts, neuropathy, nephropathy) share a common pathogenesis as a consequence of the polyol pathway.

questions.q: Aldose reductase is NOT found in the
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Aldose reductase (the first enzyme of the polyol pathway) is present in tissues such as the retina, nerve tissue, kidney, lens and erythrocytes. The liver has comparatively negligible aldose reductase activity, making it the correct 'NOT found in' answer.

questions.q: Fructose directly and strongly stimulates pancreatic insulin secretion in the same way that glucose does.
questions.e: Fructose uptake by cells is insulin-independent, and fructose does not significantly stimulate insulin secretion, unlike glucose.

questions.q: In the normal human liver, glucokinase phosphorylation of fructose to fructose 6-phosphate is the major route of fructose metabolism.
questions.e: The major route is phosphorylation of fructose to fructose 1-phosphate by fructokinase; the glucokinase/hexokinase route to fructose 6-phosphate is only a minor pathway.

questions.q: In hereditary fructose intolerance
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by aldolase B deficiency. Fructose-1-phosphate cannot be cleaved further and accumulates, trapping cellular phosphate and secondarily inhibiting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis — leading to HYPOglycaemia (not hyperglycaemia) after fructose ingestion.

questions.q:
Fructokinase is located in:
I. Liver
II. Brain
III. Eye
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Fructokinase is found mainly in the liver (also kidney and intestine). It is not a significant enzyme in the brain or the eye -- the eye instead has notable aldose reductase activity as part of the polyol pathway.

questions.q: Lactase (beta-galactosidase) hydrolyzes the disaccharide lactose into its constituent monosaccharides, glucose and galactose.
questions.e: Lactase acts on lactose to release free glucose and galactose for absorption.

questions.q: Galactokinase deficiency (Galactosemia type 2) is generally more clinically severe than classical galactosemia, frequently presenting with liver failure in infancy.
questions.e: Galactokinase deficiency is comparatively milder, with cataracts as its main feature; classical galactosemia (transferase deficiency) is the form associated with severe hepatic and systemic manifestations.

questions.q: Sorbitol can freely diffuse across cell membranes, which prevents its accumulation within cells even during hyperglycemia.
questions.e: Sorbitol cannot freely cross cell membranes; this is precisely why it accumulates intracellularly and causes osmotic damage during hyperglycemia.

questions.q: In normal (non-pathological) galactose metabolism, conversion of galactose to galactitol via aldose reductase represents the major catabolic route for galactose.
questions.e: The conversion of galactose to galactitol is normally insignificant; the major catabolic route for galactose is its conversion to glucose via the galactokinase/uridyl transferase/epimerase pathway.

questions.q: Fructose transport into cells occurs more slowly than glucose transport.
questions.e: Overall, fructose transport across membranes is less rapid compared with glucose transport.

questions.q: Both fructose and galactose can enter cells without requiring insulin.
questions.e: Unlike glucose, whose uptake into many tissues is insulin-regulated, both fructose and galactose enter cells independently of insulin.

questions.q: Essential fructosuria and hereditary fructose intolerance are caused by deficiency of the same enzyme.
questions.e: Essential fructosuria is due to fructokinase deficiency, whereas hereditary fructose intolerance is due to aldolase B deficiency — two distinct enzymes.
