questions.q: Which allosteric signal ACTIVATES citrate synthase?
questions.e: Citrate synthase is activated by ADP (indicating low energy) and inhibited by ATP, NADH, succinyl-CoA, and citrate (its own product). This fine-tunes TCA flux to match the cell's energy state.

questions.q: Which ion activates both isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-KG dehydrogenase?
questions.e: Ca²+ activates isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-KG dehydrogenase. During muscle contraction, rising mitochondrial Ca²+ accelerates TCA cycle flux to meet increased ATP demand.

questions.q: The Krebs cycle is described as 'amphibolic'. What does this mean?
o: It serves both anabolic and catabolic functions
It only works in aquatic organisms
It uses aerobic and anaerobic pathways simultaneously
questions.e: Amphibolic = dual role. The TCA cycle catabolises Acetyl-CoA for energy AND provides anabolic precursors: α-KG (→ glutamate), OAA (→ aspartate), succinyl-CoA (→ heme), citrate (→ fatty acids).

questions.q: Succinyl-CoA is the direct precursor for synthesis of which molecule?
questions.e: Succinyl-CoA + Glycine → δ-aminolevulinate (ALA), the first step in porphyrin/heme synthesis (catalysed by ALA synthase). This is the major anabolic exit point from the TCA cycle for heme.

questions.q: α-Ketoglutarate is a biosynthetic precursor for which amino acid?
questions.e: α-KG accepts an amino group via transamination to form glutamate. Glutamate is then the precursor for glutamine, proline, arginine, and ornithine — demonstrating TCA's anabolic role.

questions.q: The following are true about the tricarboxylic acid cycle EXCEPT:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The TCA cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, NOT the cytosol — that's the false (exception) statement. It genuinely does supply biosynthetic precursors, GTP (succinyl-CoA synthetase), and (via oxidative phosphorylation) ATP.

questions.q: Anaplerotic reactions serve what primary purpose?
o: Inhibit the cycle under high-ATP conditions
Produce extra NADH for the ETC
Export excess citrate to the cytosol
questions.e: Anaplerotic ('filling up') reactions replace TCA intermediates removed for anabolism (amino acid, heme, nucleotide synthesis). Without them, the cycle would grind to a halt even with Acetyl-CoA available.

questions.q: Which enzyme is the key anaplerotic enzyme converting pyruvate to oxaloacetate in mammals?
questions.e: Pyruvate carboxylase (requires biotin + ATP) carboxylates pyruvate → OAA. It is activated by Acetyl-CoA and represents the primary anaplerotic reaction restoring OAA when TCA intermediates are depleted.

questions.q: The Glyoxylate cycle uses the derived Acetyl-CoA as:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The cycle yields one NADH (malate dehydrogenase step) plus succinate that can feed the TCA/ETC for energy, while also supplying C4 carbon skeletons for gluconeogenesis — both energy and carbohydrate roles.

questions.q: Per turn, the Krebs cycle net reaction is: Acetyl-CoA + OAA + 3NAD+ + FAD + GDP + Pi → ?
questions.e: The 2 acetyl carbons are fully oxidised to 2 CO₂, generating 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP, releasing CoA-SH, and regenerating OAA to continue the next turn.

questions.q: Which TCA enzyme does NOT generate a diffusible reducing equivalent?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Succinate dehydrogenase's FAD stays permanently bound and passes electrons directly to Complex II/ubiquinone — it never releases a free FADH₂, unlike the NADH-producing steps.

questions.q: Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency leads to elevated levels of which metabolites?
questions.e: PDC deficiency → pyruvate cannot become Acetyl-CoA → pyruvate accumulates → lactate dehydrogenase converts it to lactate → lactic acidosis → neurological disorders and potentially fatal outcome.

questions.q: Pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase deficiency results in which condition?
questions.e: Without phosphatase, PDC stays phosphorylated (inactive) → glucose → lactate (not Acetyl-CoA) → lactic acidosis → CNS dysfunction. The enzyme is always 'switched off.'

questions.q: What is the role of lipoamide in the E2 subunit of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?
o: Decarboxylates pyruvate with the help of TPP
Transfers the acetyl group to CoA
questions.e: Lipoamide (covalently attached to E2, derived from lipoic acid) is a swinging arm: it accepts the acetyl group from hydroxyethyl–TPP (on E1) and transfers it to CoASH, releasing Acetyl-CoA.

questions.q: Cellular respiration converts biochemical energy into which primary currency?
questions.e: Cellular respiration — glycolysis + TCA + oxidative phosphorylation — converts energy from nutrients to ATP, the universal cellular energy currency used by virtually every energy-requiring process.

questions.q: Approximately how many total ATP are produced from one glucose via complete aerobic oxidation?
questions.e: Glycolysis: ~2 ATP; TCA: ~2 GTP; ETC (from NADH + FADH₂ of all stages): ~26–28 ATP. Total: ~30–32 ATP per glucose. Earlier estimates of 36–38 are now considered too high.

questions.q: The α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex consists of which three enzymes?
questions.e: The α-KG dehydrogenase complex: E1 = α-KG dehydrogenase (TPP), E2 = dihydrolipoyl transsuccinylase (lipoamide + CoASH), E3 = dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (FAD + NAD+). Structurally analogous to PDC.

questions.q: Which TCA intermediate exits to the cytoplasm to provide Acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis?
questions.e: Citrate exits via the tricarboxylate carrier. Cytoplasmic ATP-citrate lyase cleaves it → Acetyl-CoA + OAA. This Acetyl-CoA is used for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis.

questions.q: Which statement about Krebs cycle regulation is CORRECT?
o: High CoA activates pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase
High NADH/NAD+ ratio inhibits three key enzymes
questions.e: High NADH/NAD+ ratio inhibits PDC, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and α-KG dehydrogenase — all NAD+-requiring steps. This product inhibition slows the cycle when energy is abundant.

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
The Krebs cycle can operate under anaerobic conditions in humans.
questions.e: FALSE. The TCA cycle requires oxygen INDIRECTLY. NAD+ and FAD must be regenerated by the electron transport chain, which requires O₂ as its final electron acceptor. Without O₂, NAD+ runs out and the cycle stops.

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
One turn of the Krebs cycle directly produces 3 ATP molecules.
questions.e: FALSE. The TCA cycle directly produces only 1 GTP (equivalent to 1 ATP) per turn via substrate-level phosphorylation at Step 5. The 3 NADH and 1 FADH₂ yield ATP indirectly via the ETC (~9 ATP total per turn).

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
Acetyl-CoA can be directly converted back to pyruvate in humans.
questions.e: FALSE. The conversion of pyruvate → Acetyl-CoA by PDC is IRREVERSIBLE. This is why even-chain fatty acids (producing only Acetyl-CoA) cannot be used for net glucose synthesis in humans.

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
Fumarase acts on both fumarate and its cis-isomer maleate.
questions.e: FALSE. Fumarase is highly stereospecific and acts ONLY on trans-fumarate (not cis-maleate). It produces exclusively L-Malate. This stereospecificity is cited in the lecture as a key enzyme property.

questions.q: The Glyoxylate cycle:
o: Uses one acetyl-CoA per turn of the cycle
Is a source for carbohydrate synthesis in some yeast
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The glyoxylate cycle lets plants, some fungi/yeast and bacteria convert fatty-acid-derived acetyl-CoA into carbohydrate. It uses TWO acetyl-CoA per turn and does NOT occur in mammals (they lack malate synthase/isocitrate lyase).

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
Malonate inhibits succinate dehydrogenase non-competitively.
questions.e: FALSE. Malonate is a COMPETITIVE inhibitor. It resembles succinate structurally (both are C4 dicarboxylic acids) and competes for the active site without being oxidised, blocking FADH₂ production.

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
In thiamine deficiency, both pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-KG dehydrogenase are impaired.
questions.e: TRUE. Both enzyme complexes require TPP (from thiamine). Deficiency impairs both, causing pyruvate and α-KG accumulation, reduced NADH/ATP production, and neurological dysfunction (Wernicke's encephalopathy in alcoholics).

questions.q: The Glyoxylate cycle occurs in the ___ of some bacteria:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Classically the glyoxysome (a specialised peroxisome) houses this cycle in plants/fungi; note that true bacteria (no organelles) generally run these reactions in the cytosol, so this is a point worth clarifying with your lecturer.

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
Citrate synthase is inhibited by its own product, citrate.
questions.e: TRUE. Citrate product-inhibits citrate synthase — a classic feedback mechanism. High citrate (and ATP, NADH, succinyl-CoA) slows the enzyme when energy is plentiful; ADP activates it.

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
Pyruvate carboxylase is the key mammalian anaplerotic enzyme converting pyruvate to OAA.
questions.e: TRUE. Pyruvate carboxylase (biotin-dependent, ATP-requiring) carboxylates pyruvate → OAA, replenishing TCA intermediates when they are depleted for biosynthetic purposes. It is activated by Acetyl-CoA.

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
α-Ketoglutarate is a 4-carbon compound.
questions.e: FALSE. α-Ketoglutarate (2-oxoglutarate) is a 5-CARBON compound. It is formed from 6C isocitrate (Step 3, –1 CO₂) and converted to 4C succinyl-CoA (Step 4, –1 CO₂).

questions.q: This enzyme of the TCA cycle generates a reducing equivalent:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Isocitrate dehydrogenase oxidatively decarboxylates isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate, generating the first NADH of the cycle.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a cofactor of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?
questions.e: Biotin is NOT a PDC cofactor. It belongs to pyruvate CARBOXYLASE (the anaplerotic enzyme). PDC uses five cofactors: TPP, lipoamide, CoASH, FAD, and NAD+.

questions.q: During strenuous exercise, which signal would INCREASE the rate of the Krebs cycle?
o: High ATP with high NADH levels
questions.e: Exercise raises mitochondrial Ca²+ (from muscle contraction), activating isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-KG dehydrogenase. Falling ATP/rising ADP also relieves product inhibition on TCA enzymes, accelerating flux.

questions.q: How many carbons are in oxaloacetate?
questions.e: OAA has 4 carbons. It condenses with 2-carbon Acetyl-CoA to form 6-carbon citrate. At the end of each cycle turn, OAA is regenerated with its original 4 carbons intact — it acts as a catalytic carrier.

questions.q: Hans Adolf Krebs was born in which year?
questions.e: Hans Adolf Krebs was born in 1900 and died in 1981. He described the citric acid cycle in 1937 at Sheffield University and won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1953.

questions.q: HCl has specific gravity 1.5 and purity 78% (MW = 36.5 g/mol). What volume is needed to prepare a 1M solution?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Stock molarity = (1.5 × 1000 × 0.78) / 36.5 ≈ 32.05 M. To get 1 mol in solution: V = 1000 mL × 1M / 32.05M ≈ 31.2 mL → 31 mL.

questions.q: Which TCA enzyme links directly to Complex II of the mitochondrial ETC?
questions.e: Succinate dehydrogenase IS Complex II. It is physically embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and transfers electrons from FADH₂ to ubiquinone (CoQ), feeding them directly into the ETC.

questions.q: The TCA cycle is a/an ___ pathway:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Amphibolic: it serves both catabolic (energy release) and anabolic (biosynthetic precursor supply) roles.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: The Krebs cycle is the final common oxidative pathway for carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.
REASON: All three macronutrients can be converted to Acetyl-CoA or other TCA intermediates before oxidation.
o: Both true — reason correctly explains assertion
Both true — reason does NOT explain assertion
questions.e: Both are true and causally linked. Carbohydrates → pyruvate → Acetyl-CoA; fats → Acetyl-CoA (β-oxidation); amino acids → pyruvate, Acetyl-CoA, or TCA intermediates directly. All converge on the TCA cycle for final oxidation.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Malonate inhibition of succinate dehydrogenase can block cellular respiration.
REASON: Malonate prevents FADH₂ production, which is needed to donate electrons to the ETC.
o: Both true — reason correctly explains assertion
Both true — reason does NOT explain assertion
questions.e: Both are true and correctly linked. Malonate → blocks succinate dehydrogenase → no FADH₂ → no electron donation at Complex II → succinate accumulates → ETC partially impaired → reduced ATP → impaired cellular respiration.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: PDH kinase is activated by high Acetyl-CoA.
REASON: Acetyl-CoA signals adequate TCA substrate, making further pyruvate conversion unnecessary.
o: Both true — reason correctly explains assertion
Both true — reason does NOT explain
questions.e: Both correct. High Acetyl-CoA signals surplus TCA substrate. PDH kinase phosphorylates/inactivates E1, preventing further Acetyl-CoA formation — classic product feedback inhibition of the PDC.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: The TCA cycle produces more ATP indirectly than directly.
REASON: NADH and FADH₂ from TCA are oxidised by the ETC generating far more ATP than the single GTP from substrate-level phosphorylation.
o: Both true — reason correctly explains assertion
Both true — reason does NOT explain
questions.e: Per turn: 1 GTP direct. But 3 NADH → ~7.5 ATP and 1 FADH₂ → ~1.5 ATP via ETC — total ~9 ATP indirect vs 1 GTP direct. The ETC accounts for ~90% of TCA-derived energy.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Enzymes are able to lower the activation energy of a reaction
REASON: enzymes increase the degree of entropy.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The ASSERTION is true but the REASON is false. Enzymes do lower activation energy, by binding and stabilising the transition state. But they do not increase entropy — the opposite: by holding substrates in a fixed orientation in the active site they REDUCE translational and rotational entropy, which is part of how they overcome the entropic barrier to reaction.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Fumarase can convert maleate (cis-fumarate) to malate.
REASON: Fumarase is a stereospecific enzyme acting only on trans-fumarate.
o: Both true — reason correctly explains assertion
questions.e: The ASSERTION is FALSE — fumarase cannot convert cis-maleate. The REASON is TRUE — fumarase acts only on the trans-isomer (fumarate). The true reason actually disproves the assertion, making the assertion incorrect.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: PDC phosphatase deficiency causes lactic acidosis.
REASON: Without phosphatase, PDC stays phosphorylated and inactive, so pyruvate is reduced to lactate instead of entering TCA.
o: Both true — reason correctly explains assertion
Both true — reason does NOT explain
questions.e: Both true and causally linked. PDC phosphatase activates PDC. Without it, PDC is permanently inactivated → pyruvate → lactate → lactic acidosis → CNS damage. The reason mechanistically explains the assertion.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Glucagon secretion favours gluconeogenesis
REASON: Glucagon secretion leads to phosphorylation of phosphofructokinase 2, which reduces the production of an inhibitor in gluconeogenesis.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Both statements are true and connected: glucagon activates PKA, which phosphorylates the bifunctional PFK-2/FBPase-2 enzyme. This inactivates its kinase domain (less F2,6BP made) and activates its phosphatase domain — lowering F2,6BP, an inhibitor of the gluconeogenic enzyme fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase — thereby favouring gluconeogenesis.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: ATP is an allosteric inhibitor of gluconeogenesis
REASON: ATP inhibits the conversion of Fructose-6-phosphate to Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate by phosphofructokinase 1.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The ASSERTION is false and the REASON is true. ATP does not inhibit gluconeogenesis — high ATP signals plenty of energy, which SHUTS DOWN glycolysis and permits gluconeogenesis. The reason describes the real effect correctly: ATP allosterically inhibits phosphofructokinase-1, the enzyme converting fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate — a glycolytic step, not a gluconeogenic one.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is a major regulatory point of the TCA cycle.
REASON: It has a large negative ΔG under cellular conditions, committing isocitrate to further oxidation.
o: Both true — reason correctly explains assertion
Both true — reason does NOT explain
questions.e: Both true. Isocitrate dehydrogenase (Step 3) is allosterically regulated (activated by ADP/Ca²+, inhibited by ATP/NADH) and thermodynamically irreversible under cellular conditions — making it a committed, flux-controlling step.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: The Lineweaver-Burk plot makes it easier to calculate the Km and Vmax of a reaction
REASON: the Lineweaver-Burk plot uses a double reciprocal plot.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Both statements are true. Plotting 1/V against 1/[S] (the double-reciprocal transform) turns the Michaelis-Menten hyperbola into a straight line, from which Km and Vmax can be read directly from the slope and intercepts — a correct explanation.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Gluconeogenesis occurs mainly in the liver
REASON: gluconeogenesis helps to maintain glucose levels in the blood.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Both statements are true, but the reason explains WHY gluconeogenesis matters generally, not WHY the liver specifically is the main site (that's because the liver -- and to a lesser extent the kidney cortex -- has the full enzyme set: pyruvate carboxylase, PEP carboxykinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, and glucose-6-phosphatase).

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is an allosteric regulator of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis
REASON: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activates Fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase and inhibits phosphofructokinase 1.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F2,6BP) is indeed a key allosteric regulator that reciprocally controls glycolysis and gluconeogenesis — it activates PFK-1 (glycolysis) and inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (gluconeogenesis), tipping metabolism towards glycolysis when it is high.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Active sites are usually denoted by crevices
REASON: active sites are small parts of an enzyme.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Both statements are true — active sites are commonly found in clefts/crevices, and they do occupy a small part of the total enzyme structure. However, being small does not explain WHY they appear as crevices, so the reason is not a correct explanation of the assertion.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: PDC deficiency is most dangerous to the brain.
REASON: The brain relies almost exclusively on glucose oxidation for energy and cannot efficiently use fatty acids as fuel.
o: Both true — reason correctly explains assertion
Both true — reason does NOT explain
questions.e: Both true. The blood-brain barrier limits fatty acid entry; the brain depends on glucose → pyruvate → Acetyl-CoA → TCA for ATP. When PDC is deficient, this pathway fails and the brain is disproportionately affected — causing the neurological symptoms seen in PDC deficiency.

questions.q: Starting molecule for the Krebs cycle:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Each turn begins when acetyl-CoA condenses with oxaloacetate (citrate synthase) to form citrate. Oxaloacetate is regenerated/recycled rather than being the fresh 'starting' input — acetyl-CoA is the new carbon source that kicks off each turn.

questions.q: A stock solution is diluted 10-fold to 9 mL total to prepare X2 (X2 = 0.16 M ÷ 10; FW = 250 g/mol). What volume of stock was used, and what is X2’s mass concentration?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. DF=10 on 9 mL total → stock volume = 9/10 = 0.9 mL. Molarity of X2 = 0.16/10 = 0.016 M → mass conc = 0.016 × 250 = 4 g/L.

questions.q: Why is the TCA pathway called a 'cycle' rather than a pathway?
o: It generates energy in circular pulses
OAA is consumed and regenerated each turn
questions.e: It is a cycle because OAA is the acceptor molecule at Step 1 and is regenerated at Step 8. This allows continuous oxidation of acetyl groups without net consumption of the carbon-carrying molecule.

questions.q: The TCA cycle:
o: Is coupled with the release of NADPH
Uses 2 molecules of acetyl-CoA per turn of the cycle
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Corrected: the TCA cycle uses only ONE acetyl-CoA per turn, is net energy-YIELDING (not consuming), and produces NADH (not NADPH). It does produce high-energy compounds: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP/ATP per turn.

questions.q: E3 (dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase) in the PDC uses which cofactors?
questions.e: E3 uses FAD and NAD+. It re-oxidises reduced lipoamide (dihydrolipoamide) → oxidised lipoamide (disulfide), transferring electrons: FADH₂ → FAD, then NADH → NAD+. This restores lipoamide for the next catalytic cycle.

questions.q: Which correctly describes CoA's role in the Krebs cycle?
o: Carrier for acyl groups, regenerated each cycle
questions.e: CoA-SH is a carrier that forms thioester bonds with acyl groups (Acetyl-CoA, succinyl-CoA). It is released as free CoA-SH at Steps 1 and 5 respectively, making it available for reuse — a catalytic, not consumable, role.

questions.q: A malnourished alcoholic has elevated blood pyruvate and neurological symptoms. Most likely deficiency?
questions.e: Alcoholism commonly causes thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency. Without TPP, pyruvate dehydrogenase cannot convert pyruvate → Acetyl-CoA. Pyruvate accumulates and is reduced to lactate. Neurological features = Wernicke's encephalopathy.

questions.q: Which TCA intermediate is NOT used up by other synthetic pathways?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Citrate feeds fatty-acid synthesis, succinyl-CoA feeds heme synthesis, oxaloacetate feeds gluconeogenesis/amino acids — malate is mainly retained within the cycle/shuttle systems.

questions.q: Comparing the Glyoxylate cycle to the TCA cycle, it bypasses the ___ of the TCA cycle:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Isocitrate lyase cleaves isocitrate straight to succinate + glyoxylate, skipping the two oxidative decarboxylation steps (isocitrate DH & α-KGDH) and their CO₂ loss.

questions.q: The TCA cycle is:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Amphibolic — it serves both catabolic (energy-releasing) and anabolic (precursor-supplying) roles.

questions.q: The by-passing enzymes in the Glyoxylate cycle are:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Malate synthase and isocitrate lyase are the two unique enzymes that bypass the CO₂-releasing steps of the TCA cycle.

questions.q: Which is an example of an anaplerotic reaction replenishing OAA for TCA?
questions.e: PEP carboxylase (plants/bacteria) and pyruvate carboxylase (mammals) are anaplerotic. In mammals, pyruvate + CO₂ + ATP → OAA (pyruvate carboxylase) is the primary anaplerotic reaction. PEP+CO₂→OAA by PEP carboxylase is the plant equivalent.

questions.q: E2 of the PDC is named:
questions.e: E2 = dihydrolipoamide acetyltransferase. It transfers the acetyl group from lipoamide to CoASH forming Acetyl-CoA. Summary: E1(TPP)→E2(lipoamide+CoASH)→E3(FAD+NAD+).

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
Succinyl-CoA is the immediate precursor for porphyrin and heme biosynthesis.
questions.e: TRUE. Succinyl-CoA + Glycine → δ-ALA (catalysed by ALA synthase in mitochondria). This is the first committed step in porphyrin synthesis. B12 deficiency indirectly impairs succinyl-CoA production via methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
FADH₂ yields more ATP than NADH when oxidised by the ETC.
questions.e: FALSE. FADH₂ yields ~1.5 ATP (enters at CoQ, bypasses Complex I). NADH yields ~2.5 ATP (enters at Complex I). NADH is the more energy-rich electron carrier because it has a more negative reduction potential.

questions.q: The TCA cycle is NOT inhibited by:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Fluoride inhibits enolase — a glycolytic enzyme, not a TCA cycle enzyme — so it doesn't directly inhibit the TCA cycle itself. Fluoroacetyl-CoA (via fluorocitrate) blocks aconitase, and PDH deficiency starves the cycle of acetyl-CoA, so both of those genuinely impair it.

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
The ΔG'° of malate dehydrogenase (Step 8) is negative.
questions.e: FALSE. ΔG'° = +29.7 kJ/mol (positive = thermodynamically UNFAVOURABLE). The reaction is driven forward by the immediately following citrate synthase reaction (ΔG'° = –32.2 kJ/mol) which rapidly removes OAA.

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
Acetyl-CoA cannot contribute to net gluconeogenesis in humans.
questions.e: TRUE. Humans lack glyoxylate cycle enzymes (isocitrate lyase and malate synthase). Therefore Acetyl-CoA cannot be converted to net OAA/glucose. Even-chain fatty acids (→ only Acetyl-CoA) are NOT gluconeogenic in humans.

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
Hans Adolf Krebs received the Nobel Prize for describing the TCA cycle.
questions.e: TRUE. Krebs won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1953, shared with Fritz Lipmann (who discovered CoA). Krebs described the citric acid cycle in 1937 while at Sheffield University.

questions.q: During isocitrate → α-KG, which enzyme-bound intermediate is formed transiently?
questions.e: Isocitrate dehydrogenase first oxidises isocitrate to OXALOSUCCINATE (a transient, enzyme-bound intermediate), which is then decarboxylated to α-KG + CO₂. Oxalosuccinate is not released into solution.

questions.q: Which best describes the Krebs cycle's role in aerobic metabolism?
o: Generates most ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation
The central hub linking major pathways
It operates independently of the ETC
questions.e: The TCA cycle is the central metabolic hub connecting carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism; providing biosynthetic precursors; and supplying NADH/FADH₂ to the ETC. It does NOT directly generate most ATP.

questions.q: Which amino acid donates its nitrogen to α-KG during glutamate synthesis by transamination?
questions.e: Transamination: ANY amino acid can donate its α-amino group to α-KG → glutamate + the corresponding α-keto acid. This is catalysed by aminotransferases (transaminases). It links amino acid catabolism to TCA.

questions.q: What happens to TCA flux when NADH/NAD+ ratio is very high?
o: The cycle switches to using NADP+
Cycle speeds up to consume NADH
questions.e: High NADH/NAD+ means NAD+ is scarce. Steps 3 (isocitrate dehydrogenase), 4 (α-KG dehydrogenase), and 8 (malate dehydrogenase) all require NAD+ and are product-inhibited. TCA flux drops dramatically.

questions.q: After GTP is produced in Step 5, how does it contribute to the cellular ATP pool?
o: GTP is stored as a cellular energy reserve
GTP is used exclusively for protein synthesis
GTP transfers its phosphate to ADP
questions.e: Nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDPK): GTP + ADP ↔ GDP + ATP. This reaction is near-equilibrium and rapidly interconverts GTP and ATP, allowing the single TCA-produced GTP to contribute to the cellular ATP pool.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Citrate exits mitochondria to provide Acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis.
REASON: ATP-citrate lyase in the cytoplasm cleaves citrate into OAA and Acetyl-CoA for lipogenesis.
o: Both true — reason correctly explains assertion
Both true — reason does NOT explain
questions.e: Both true and causally linked. When energy is abundant, citrate exits via the tricarboxylate carrier. Cytoplasmic ATP-citrate lyase → Acetyl-CoA (→ fatty acids/cholesterol) + OAA. This is the Acetyl-CoA shuttle from mitochondria to cytoplasm.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Enzymes are known as biological catalysts
REASON: enzymes speed up biological reactions.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Both statements are true, and speeding up reaction rates (by lowering activation energy) is exactly why enzymes are classified as catalysts — a correct explanation.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: The brain is especially vulnerable to thiamine deficiency.
REASON: The brain depends heavily on glucose oxidation via PDC and TCA, both requiring TPP.
o: Both true — reason correctly explains assertion
Both true — reason does NOT explain
questions.e: Both true. The brain cannot efficiently use fat/ketones (blood-brain barrier limits fatty acid entry). It is critically dependent on glucose → pyruvate → Acetyl-CoA (PDC, needs TPP) → TCA. TPP deficiency → Wernicke's encephalopathy.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Aconitase converts citrate → isocitrate via a dehydration-rehydration mechanism.
REASON: Although citrate appears symmetric, aconitase treats its two arms differently (prochiral specificity).
o: Both true — reason correctly explains assertion
Both true — reason does NOT explain
questions.e: Both true and related. Aconitase: citrate → cis-aconitate (–H₂O) → isocitrate (+H₂O). Despite citrate's apparent symmetry, aconitase distinguishes its two –CH₂COO⁻ arms by 3-point attachment (prochirality), making the reaction stereospecific.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Metabolism in living organisms is very important
REASON: metabolism is carried out by organisms to sustain life.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Both statements are true. Metabolism is indeed vital, and it is true precisely because metabolism (the sum of catabolic and anabolic reactions) is what sustains life — so the reason correctly explains the assertion.

questions.q: The TCA cycle is NOT inhibited by:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Fluoride inhibits enolase — a glycolytic enzyme, not a TCA cycle enzyme. Fluoroacetate (via fluorocitrate) blocks aconitase, and PDH deficiency starves the cycle of acetyl-CoA.

questions.q: Which cofactor does E2 (dihydrolipoamide acetyltransferase) of PDC require?
questions.e: E2 requires lipoamide (covalently attached, derived from lipoic acid — acts as swinging arm) and CoASH (acceptor of the acetyl group). Together they release Acetyl-CoA and reduced lipoamide (for E3 to re-oxidise).

questions.q: The TCA cycle:
o: Uses 2 molecules of pyruvate per turn of the cycle
Produces energy in the form of ADP
Is coupled with the release of NADPH
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Corrected: the cycle doesn't use pyruvate directly (it uses 1 acetyl-CoA/turn), is net energy-YIELDING (not consuming), releases NADH (not NADPH), and produces ATP/GTP (ADP is what's consumed to make ATP, not a product). Only 'produces high-energy compounds' (3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP per turn) is true.

questions.q: Succinyl-CoA product-inhibits which TCA enzyme?
o: Both citrate synthase and α-KG dehydrogenase
questions.e: Succinyl-CoA inhibits both: (1) α-KG dehydrogenase (its own producing enzyme — direct product inhibition) and (2) citrate synthase (slowing cycle entry). This prevents overaccumulation when downstream steps are slow.

questions.q: What fraction of per-turn TCA energy is captured DIRECTLY as GTP?
questions.e: 1 GTP ≈ 1 ATP directly. But 3 NADH → ~7.5 ATP and 1 FADH₂ → ~1.5 ATP via ETC = ~9 ATP total. GTP = 1/10 = ~10%. The ETC (via NADH/FADH₂) captures ~90% of TCA-derived energy.

questions.q: A student says 'the Krebs cycle directly produces 38 ATP per glucose.' What is wrong?
o: The cycle itself yields only 2 GTP
The TCA cycle produces NADPH, not ATP
The correct figure is nearer 100 ATP
questions.e: TCA (2 turns per glucose) directly yields only 2 GTP (substrate-level phosphorylation, Step 5 ×2). Total ~30–32 ATP comes from all stages: ~2 ATP (glycolysis) + ~2 GTP (TCA) + ~26–28 ATP (ETC from NADH/FADH₂). Attributing 38 to TCA alone is incorrect.

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
All eight steps of the Krebs cycle take place in the mitochondrial matrix.
questions.e: FALSE. Seven steps are in the matrix. Step 6 (succinate dehydrogenase) is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane. This enzyme is also Complex II of the electron transport chain.

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
Isocitrate dehydrogenase is activated by ADP and Ca²+ and inhibited by ATP.
questions.e: TRUE. Isocitrate dehydrogenase (Step 3) is a key allosteric regulatory enzyme: activated by ADP (low energy) and Ca²+ (high demand) and inhibited by ATP and NADH (energy sufficiency). It is a major flux-controlling point.

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
Prokaryotes carry out the Krebs cycle in their cytoplasm.
questions.e: TRUE. Prokaryotes lack mitochondria, so all TCA enzymes are cytoplasmic (soluble) except succinate dehydrogenase which is in the plasma membrane. The cycle functions identically — oxidising Acetyl-CoA for energy and biosynthesis.

questions.q: Why is the TCA cycle essential even in non-energy-producing states?
o: It drives protein folding in mitochondria
It provides the body's only source of CO₂
questions.e: Even in resting cells, TCA intermediates are continuously withdrawn for amino acid synthesis, heme production, nucleotide synthesis, and gluconeogenesis. Anaplerotic reactions replenish them to maintain cycle function.

questions.q: If aconitase (Step 2) were competitively inhibited, which metabolite would accumulate?
questions.e: Blocking aconitase stops citrate → isocitrate conversion, so CITRATE accumulates immediately. (Clinically, fluorocitrate — derived from fluoroacetate rat poison — inhibits aconitase, causing citrate accumulation and TCA cycle failure.)

questions.q: 'Respiratory control' of the TCA cycle means:
o: Cycle speed is controlled by lung capacity
The cycle is controlled by respiratory hormones
Cycle speed depends on CO₂ exhalation
TCA rate is limited by NAD+ and ADP supply
questions.e: Respiratory control links TCA to ETC and O₂. When O₂ is available and ADP is high, ETC oxidises NADH → NAD+ and ADP→ATP. This regenerates NAD+ and consumes ADP, accelerating TCA. No O₂ → no NAD+ → TCA stops.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Gluconeogenesis and glycolysis are considered opposing pathways
REASON: Gluconeogenesis is a direct reversal of glycolysis.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The assertion is true but the reason is false. Gluconeogenesis is NOT a direct reversal of glycolysis. Three glycolytic steps are irreversible — hexokinase/glucokinase, phosphofructokinase-1 and pyruvate kinase — and gluconeogenesis bypasses them with four different enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase, then fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase. The other seven steps are shared and reversible.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Fatty acids are a major cardiac fuel during aerobic conditions.
REASON: The heart has constant O₂ supply and high mitochondrial density, enabling efficient β-oxidation and TCA cycle activity.
o: Both true — reason correctly explains assertion
Both true — reason does NOT explain
questions.e: Both true. The heart is almost always aerobic, has the highest mitochondrial density of any tissue, and preferentially oxidises fatty acids: FA → Acetyl-CoA (β-oxidation) → TCA → NADH/FADH₂ → ETC → ATP. Cardiac metabolism is highly TCA-dependent.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Enzymes are reusable
REASON: enzymes are specific for the reaction they catalyze.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The assertion is true -- enzymes are released unchanged after catalysis and can be used repeatedly. But the reason given doesn't explain that: specificity is about WHICH reaction an enzyme catalyzes, not about why it can be reused. Reusability comes from the enzyme not being consumed or permanently altered during catalysis.

questions.q: A certain enzyme will hydrolyze egg white but not starch. Which statement best explains this observation?
o: Starch is composed of amino acids
Starch molecules are too large to be hydrolyzed
Enzyme molecules are specific in their actions
Egg white acts as a coenzyme for hydrolysis
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Working on protein (egg white) but not carbohydrate (starch) is a textbook demonstration of enzyme substrate specificity.

questions.q: Which statement BEST describes E3 (dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase) of PDC?
o: It transfers acetyl group from lipoamide to CoASH
questions.e: E3 re-oxidises reduced lipoamide (–SH form) → oxidised disulfide form: FADH₂ formed, then NAD+ reduces it → NADH. The restored lipoamide disulfide is then ready to accept the next acetyl group from E1.

questions.q: Pyruvate carboxylase is most active when:
o: Acetyl-CoA is high but OAA is limiting
The NADH/NAD+ ratio is very low
ATP is low and ADP is high
Glucose is abundant and energy is in excess
questions.e: Pyruvate carboxylase is allosterically activated by Acetyl-CoA. When Acetyl-CoA accumulates (high fat oxidation) but OAA is depleted (used for gluconeogenesis), pyruvate carboxylase replenishes OAA — ensuring TCA flux is maintained.

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
OAA from TCA can support gluconeogenesis during fasting.
questions.e: TRUE. During fasting, hepatic OAA → PEP (PEPCK, using GTP) → glucose (gluconeogenesis). Gluconeogenic amino acids (alanine, aspartate, glutamate) feed into TCA as OAA or malate, then support glucose production — critical for fasting glucose homeostasis.

questions.q:
TRUE or FALSE:
Both PDC and α-KG dehydrogenase are activated by Ca²+ ions.
questions.e: TRUE. Ca²+ activates PDC indirectly (by activating PDC phosphatase, which dephosphorylates/activates PDC) and directly activates α-KG dehydrogenase and isocitrate dehydrogenase. This coordinates TCA activity with cellular energy demand.

questions.q: Which intervention would most directly replenish TCA if OAA is depleted during amino acid synthesis?
questions.e: Pyruvate carboxylase (activated by Acetyl-CoA) converts pyruvate → OAA, directly replenishing the depleted TCA intermediate. This is the primary mammalian anaplerotic response to OAA depletion.

questions.q: During hepatic gluconeogenesis from amino acids, which TCA intermediate is most directly the gluconeogenic substrate?
questions.e: OAA is the direct gluconeogenic precursor. PEPCK converts OAA + GTP → PEP + CO₂ + GDP. PEP then proceeds through the remaining gluconeogenic steps to glucose. Amino acids that form OAA (or malate → OAA) are therefore gluconeogenic.

questions.q: Which single vitamin deficiency would simultaneously impair BOTH PDC and α-KG dehydrogenase?
questions.e: Both complexes require TPP derived from thiamine (B1). A single B1 deficiency cripples both, simultaneously blocking: (1) pyruvate entry into TCA and (2) Step 4 of TCA. The result is impaired TCA flux and catastrophic energy failure, especially in the brain.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Coenzymes are also known as co-substrates
REASON: coenzymes influence substrate binding.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The ASSERTION is true but the REASON is false. Coenzymes are called co-substrates because they behave like a second substrate: they bind loosely, are chemically ALTERED stoichiometrically during the reaction and must be regenerated — NAD⁺ becomes NADH, CoASH becomes acetyl-CoA. Their job is to carry electrons or chemical groups, not to influence how the primary substrate binds. Helping to bind and orient substrate is the role of tightly bound prosthetic groups and metal-ion cofactors, not of coenzymes acting as co-substrates.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: The Krebs cycle is the final common oxidative pathway for carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.
REASON: All three macronutrients can be converted to Acetyl-CoA or other TCA intermediates before oxidation.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both are true and causally linked. Carbohydrates → pyruvate → Acetyl-CoA; fats → Acetyl-CoA (β-oxidation); amino acids → pyruvate, Acetyl-CoA, or TCA intermediates directly. All converge on the TCA cycle for final oxidation.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Malonate inhibition of succinate dehydrogenase can block cellular respiration.
REASON: Malonate prevents FADH₂ production, which is needed to donate electrons to the ETC.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both are true and correctly linked. Malonate → blocks succinate dehydrogenase → no FADH₂ → no electron donation at Complex II → succinate accumulates → ETC partially impaired → reduced ATP → impaired cellular respiration.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: PDH kinase is activated by high Acetyl-CoA.
REASON: Acetyl-CoA signals adequate TCA substrate, making further pyruvate conversion unnecessary.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both correct. High Acetyl-CoA signals surplus TCA substrate. PDH kinase phosphorylates/inactivates E1, preventing further Acetyl-CoA formation — classic product feedback inhibition of the PDC.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: The TCA cycle produces more ATP indirectly than directly.
REASON: NADH and FADH₂ from TCA are oxidised by the ETC generating far more ATP than the single GTP from substrate-level phosphorylation.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Per turn: 1 GTP direct. But 3 NADH → ~7.5 ATP and 1 FADH₂ → ~1.5 ATP via ETC — total ~9 ATP indirect vs 1 GTP direct. The ETC accounts for ~90% of TCA-derived energy.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: PDC phosphatase deficiency causes lactic acidosis.
REASON: Without phosphatase, PDC stays phosphorylated and inactive, so pyruvate is reduced to lactate instead of entering TCA.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true and causally linked. PDC phosphatase activates PDC. Without it, PDC is permanently inactivated → pyruvate → lactate → lactic acidosis → CNS damage. The reason mechanistically explains the assertion.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is a major regulatory point of the TCA cycle.
REASON: It has a large negative ΔG under cellular conditions, committing isocitrate to further oxidation.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true. Isocitrate dehydrogenase (Step 3) is allosterically regulated (activated by ADP/Ca²+, inhibited by ATP/NADH) and thermodynamically irreversible under cellular conditions — making it a committed, flux-controlling step.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: PDC deficiency is most dangerous to the brain.
REASON: The brain relies almost exclusively on glucose oxidation for energy and cannot efficiently use fatty acids as fuel.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true. The blood-brain barrier limits fatty acid entry; the brain depends on glucose → pyruvate → Acetyl-CoA → TCA for ATP. When PDC is deficient, this pathway fails and the brain is disproportionately affected — causing the neurological symptoms seen in PDC deficiency.

questions.q:
ASSERTION: Citrate exits mitochondria to provide Acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis.
REASON: ATP-citrate lyase in the cytoplasm cleaves citrate into OAA and Acetyl-CoA for lipogenesis.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE

questions.q: NADPH is important for maintaining adequate levels of which molecule in the cell?
questions.e: NADPH is essential for maintaining adequate levels of reduced glutathione (GSH), a key cellular antioxidant.

questions.q: Reduced glutathione (GSH) is critical for destroying which type of harmful molecule, exemplified by hydrogen peroxide?
questions.e: GSH destroys reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as hydrogen peroxide, protecting the cell from oxidative damage.

questions.q: GSH also helps maintain the iron in hemoglobin in which oxidation state?
questions.e: GSH helps maintain hemoglobin iron in the ferrous (Fe2+) state, which is required for normal oxygen binding.

questions.q: Chemically, glutathione is best described as a:
o: Single amino acid derivative of cysteine
Tripeptide of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine
questions.e: Glutathione is a tripeptide made of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine, and functions as a potent antioxidant.

questions.q: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) can damage red blood cell membranes by reacting with:
o: the globin chains of hemoglobin directly
double bonds in fatty acid moieties of membrane lipids
questions.e: ROS react with double bonds in the fatty acid components of membrane lipids, weakening the membrane and predisposing to haemolysis.

questions.q: Because mature RBCs lack mitochondria, they are totally dependent on NADPH from the PPP to regenerate GSH from GSSG via which enzyme?
questions.e: Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to regenerate reduced glutathione (GSH) from its oxidized form (GSSG).

questions.q: In the reaction 2GSH + H2O2 → GSSG + 2H2O, reduced glutathione is acting to detoxify:
questions.e: This reaction shows reduced glutathione detoxifying hydrogen peroxide, a type of peroxide, producing oxidized glutathione and water.

questions.q: Cells with low levels of GSH are especially susceptible to:
questions.e: Low GSH levels leave cells, especially RBCs, vulnerable to oxidative damage and hemolysis.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed among the causes of reduced glutathione levels in the notes?
questions.e: The notes list stress, poor nutrition, environmental toxins, and ageing as factors that may reduce glutathione — not regular moderate exercise.

questions.q: Carriers of the G6PD deficiency mutation have been found to have increased resistance to which disease?
questions.e: G6PD deficiency carriers show increased resistance to malaria, similar to other red-cell conditions like sickle cell trait.

questions.q: The geographic distribution of G6PD deficiency is highest in which regions, according to the notes?
o: Tropical Africa, Asia, Middle East, Mediterranean, and Papua New Guinea
questions.e: G6PD deficiency is most prevalent in tropical Africa, Asia, the Middle East, the Mediterranean, and Papua New Guinea — regions historically affected by malaria.

questions.q: Most people with G6PD deficiency are usually asymptomatic, but a severe haemolytic episode can be triggered within hours of exposure to:
questions.e: G6PD-deficient individuals are usually asymptomatic until exposed to certain drugs or other oxidative stressors, which can trigger acute haemolysis rapidly.

questions.q: Which pair of antimalarial/antibiotic-related drug classes is listed as a precipitating factor for haemolysis in G6PD deficiency?
questions.e: Sulfonamide antibiotics and certain antimalarial drugs are listed as precipitating oxidative stressors in G6PD deficiency.

questions.q: Which commonly used analgesic/fever-reducing agents are listed as precipitating factors for G6PD-related haemolysis?
questions.e: Aspirin and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are listed among the drugs that can precipitate haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

questions.q: Naphthalene balls, commonly known as 'moth repellant', are listed as a precipitating factor for G6PD-related haemolysis. What is their common household name?
questions.e: Naphthalene balls are commonly known as mothballs and are a recognized oxidative stressor in G6PD deficiency.

questions.q: True or False: Fava beans, soybeans, and other legumes are listed as precipitating factors for haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
questions.e: True — the notes list fava beans, soybeans, and some other legumes among the oxidative stressors that can precipitate haemolysis (favism).

questions.q: True or False: The Pentose Phosphate Pathway occurs mainly in the mitochondria of the cell.
questions.e: False — the notes clearly state that the reactions of the PPP occur in the cytosol, not the mitochondria.

questions.q: True or False: The oxidative phase of the PPP generates NADPH, while the non-oxidative phase interconverts sugars of different carbon-chain lengths.
questions.e: True — the oxidative phase produces NADPH, and the non-oxidative phase handles the interconversion of 3-, 4-, 5-, 6-, and 7-carbon sugars.

questions.q: True or False: Mature red blood cells contain mitochondria, which allows them to regenerate NADPH independently of the PPP.
questions.e: False — mature RBCs lack mitochondria entirely, making them completely dependent on the PPP for NADPH generation.

questions.q: True or False: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is described as a rare enzyme abnormality affecting very few people worldwide.
questions.e: False — the notes state G6PD deficiency is quite a common enzyme abnormality, affecting more than 400 million people worldwide.

questions.q: True or False: Symptoms of G6PD deficiency can include paleness, extreme tiredness, rapid heartbeat, and dark tea-coloured urine.
questions.e: True — these are all listed as symptoms of G6PD deficiency in the notes, alongside jaundice and shortness of breath.

questions.q: True or False: G6PD deficiency during pregnancy is associated with a reduced risk of anaemia and better pregnancy outcomes.
questions.e: False — the notes state that G6PD deficiency can lead to poor pregnancy outcomes, including an increased risk of anaemia in pregnancy, not a reduced risk.

questions.q: True or False: Management of G6PD deficiency usually involves avoiding oxidative stressors, and may include folic acid, iron supplementation, oxygen therapy, or blood transfusion.
questions.e: True — the notes describe exactly these management strategies for G6PD deficiency.

questions.q: True or False: Haemolysis in G6PD deficiency is described as always being a long-term, chronic process that never resolves.
questions.e: False — the notes state that haemolysis is usually short-term but can be life-threatening, not that it is always chronic.

questions.q: True or False: Glutathione is described in the notes as a potent antioxidant that reduces oxidative stress in cells.
questions.e: True — glutathione is explicitly described as a potent antioxidant that reduces oxidative stress.

questions.q: True or False: According to the notes, a high concentration of NADP+ inhibits the Pentose Phosphate Pathway to conserve glucose.
questions.e: False — a high concentration of NADP+ actually stimulates the PPP so that NADPH can be replenished, rather than inhibiting the pathway.

questions.q:

I. Hexose Monophosphate Shunt
II. Phosphogluconate Pathway
III. Cori Cycle
questions.e: I and II are correct — the Hexose Monophosphate Shunt and Phosphogluconate Pathway are alternative names for the PPP. The Cori Cycle (III) is a separate, unrelated pathway.

questions.q:
Which of the following are functions of the Pentose Phosphate Pathway, according to the notes?
I. Generation of pentose sugars for nucleotide/nucleic acid synthesis
II. Generation of NADPH for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defense
III. Direct generation of large amounts of ATP as the main pathway product
questions.e: I and II are correct functions of the PPP. Statement III is false — the PPP is not primarily an ATP-generating pathway; that is the role of glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.q:
Which of the following tissues are listed as using PPP-derived NADPH mainly for steroid synthesis?
I. Adrenal gland
II. Testes
III. Liver
questions.e: I and II are correct — the adrenal gland, testes, and ovary are listed for steroid synthesis. The liver (III) is listed for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis, not primarily steroid synthesis.

questions.q:

II. The oxidative phase begins with oxidation of glucose-6-phosphate.
III. The non-oxidative phase is the step that generates the pathway's NADPH.
questions.e: I and II are correct. Statement III is false — NADPH is generated in the OXIDATIVE phase, not the non-oxidative phase.

questions.q:
Which of the following are true regarding G6PD deficiency, according to the notes?
I. It affects more than 400 million people worldwide.
II. Carriers show increased resistance to malaria.
III. It is caused by a deficiency of glutathione reductase.
questions.e: I and II are correct. Statement III is false — G6PD deficiency is a deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, not glutathione reductase.

questions.q:
Which of the following are listed as precipitating factors/oxidative stressors for G6PD-related haemolysis?
I. Fava beans and other legumes
II. Sulfonamide antibiotics and antimalarial drugs
III. Regular consumption of fresh fruit
questions.e: I and II are correct precipitating factors. Statement III (fresh fruit) is not listed as a stressor in the notes.

questions.q: In the reaction that prevents accumulation of hydrogen peroxide within cells, catalase functions as an:

Indicator in the detection of hydrogen peroxide
Enzyme in the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Catalase rapidly breaks down toxic H₂O₂ into water and oxygen, protecting cells from oxidative damage.

II. Dark, tea-coloured urine
III. Excessive weight gain
questions.e: I and II are listed symptoms of G6PD deficiency. Excessive weight gain (III) is not mentioned in the notes.

questions.q:

I. Avoiding oxidative stressors
II. Folic acid and iron supplementation
III. Regular chemotherapy
questions.e: I and II are correct management strategies, along with oxygen therapy and blood transfusion when needed. Chemotherapy (III) is not part of G6PD deficiency management.

questions.q:
Assertion: Metabolism in living organisms is very important
Reason: metabolism is carried out by organisms to sustain life.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion

questions.e: Both statements are true. Metabolism is indeed vital, and it is true precisely because metabolism (the sum of catabolic and anabolic reactions) is what sustains life — so the reason correctly explains the assertion.
questions.t: Basic Concept & Design of Metabolism / Enzymes

questions.q:
Assertion: Anabolism produces energy in living organisms
Reason: anabolism supplies energy for use in catabolic process in living organisms.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both statements are false. Anabolism is the energy-CONSUMING (endergonic) arm of metabolism — it uses energy to build complex molecules from simpler ones. It is catabolism that breaks molecules down and releases energy, some of which is then used to drive anabolic reactions — the reverse of what is stated here.
questions.t: Basic Concept & Design of Metabolism / Enzymes

questions.q:
Assertion: Metabolic pathways are in equilibrium
Reason: metabolic pathways are in a steady state.

questions.e: The assertion is false: living metabolic pathways are deliberately kept away from true chemical equilibrium (equilibrium would mean the reaction has stopped net flow). The reason is true — pathways operate at a steady state, where intermediates are maintained at fairly constant concentrations even as flux continues through the pathway.
questions.t: Basic Concept & Design of Metabolism / Enzymes

questions.q:

questions.t: Basic Concept & Design of Metabolism / Enzymes

questions.e: Both statements are true, and speeding up reaction rates (by lowering activation energy) is exactly why enzymes are classified as catalysts — a correct explanation.
questions.t: Basic Concept & Design of Metabolism / Enzymes

questions.q:

questions.t: Basic Concept & Design of Metabolism / Enzymes

questions.e: The assertion is false — hexokinase is a TRANSFERASE (a kinase), not an isomerase. The reason is actually true: transferring a phosphate group from ATP to glucose is the defining feature of a transferase, which describes hexokinase correctly (just not as an 'isomerase').
questions.t: Basic Concept & Design of Metabolism / Enzymes

questions.q:
Assertion: Coenzymes are usually loosely bound to an enzyme

questions.e: The assertion is true — coenzymes typically associate loosely/transiently (non-covalently) with enzymes, unlike prosthetic groups. The reason is false: covalent, tight binding describes prosthetic groups, not the loose association of coenzymes.
questions.t: Basic Concept & Design of Metabolism / Enzymes

questions.q:
Assertion: The lock and key model of enzymes is accepted
Reason: the lock and key model was able to explain the kinetic behavior of enzymes.

Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: The assertion is true but the reason is false. Enzymes lower activation energy by binding and STABILISING the transition state — orienting substrates correctly, straining bonds and excluding water. If anything they REDUCE entropy, because holding two substrates in a fixed orientation makes the system more ordered, not less. Note also that an enzyme changes neither ΔG nor the equilibrium position; it only lowers the barrier to reaching it.

questions.e: The assertion is true but the reason is false. Enzymes lower activation energy by binding and STABILISING the transition state — orienting substrates, straining bonds, excluding water. If anything they REDUCE entropy, since holding substrates in a fixed orientation makes the system more ordered. An enzyme changes neither ΔG nor the equilibrium position.

questions.q:
Assertion: The Lineweaver-Burk plot makes it easier to calculate the Km and Vmax of a reaction
Reason: the Lineweaver-Burk plot uses a double reciprocal plot.

Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both statements are true. Plotting 1/V against 1/[S] (the double-reciprocal transform) turns the Michaelis-Menten hyperbola into a straight line, from which Km and Vmax can be read directly from the slope and intercepts — a correct explanation.
questions.t: Basic Concept & Design of Metabolism / Enzymes

questions.q:
The major macromolecules that are usually studied in biochemistry include
I. Proteins
II. Nucleic Acids
III. Carbohydrates
questions.e: All three — proteins, nucleic acids, and carbohydrates (plus lipids) — are the major classes of biomolecules central to biochemistry.

questions.q:
Which of the following is/are TRUE about Proteins?
I. Basic functional units are amino acids.
II. There are three levels of structure in Proteins.
III. Amino acid sequences in proteins are stabilized by carbon bonding.
questions.e: Statement I is true (amino acids are the building blocks). Statement II is true in the sense intended here (primary, secondary, tertiary — quaternary applies only to multi-subunit proteins). Statement III is false: the primary sequence is held together by peptide (amide) bonds, not 'carbon bonding'.

questions.q:
Metabolism is important because
I. It allows the transformation of energy
II. Provides intermediates as waste material
III. Energy is produced solely for cell repair
questions.e: Metabolism does allow transformation and interconversion of energy (I) and it does generate/consume intermediates that link pathways together (II, as understood here). Statement III is false — energy produced from metabolism is used for many purposes (movement, biosynthesis, transport, thermoregulation), not solely for cell repair.

questions.q:
In predicting spontaneity of reactions, if ΔG is negative and large, the reaction is
I. Exergonic
II. Spontaneous
III. Proceed in forward direction
questions.e: A large negative ΔG means the reaction releases free energy (exergonic, I) and will proceed spontaneously (II). Statement III is considered not an automatic consequence purely of the sign/magnitude of ΔG in the way the other two are, hence it is excluded here.

questions.q:
Which of the following is/are the common monosaccharide(s)?
I. Cellulose
II. Glucose
III. Fructose
questions.e: Glucose and fructose are monosaccharides (simple sugars). Cellulose is a polysaccharide (a polymer of glucose units), not a monosaccharide, so statement I is false.

questions.q:
In metabolism
I. There is coordination.
II. There are several pathways.
III. Substrates are transformed to products via non-specific intermediates.
questions.e: Metabolism is highly coordinated (I) and consists of many interconnected pathways (II). Statement III is false — intermediates in metabolic pathways are generally highly SPECIFIC, not non-specific, which is part of what allows tight regulation.

questions.q:
Characteristics of enzymes include(s)
I. being highly specific.
II. activity being lost when denatured.
III. the acceleration in the rate of breaking of bonds.
questions.e: All three are core enzyme characteristics: high specificity for substrates, loss of activity on denaturation (loss of 3D structure), and acceleration of bond-breaking/making steps of a reaction.

questions.q:
Classes of enzymes include (s)
I. hydrolysis.
II. ligases.
III. transferases.
questions.e: Ligases and transferases are genuine enzyme class names. 'Hydrolysis' is the name of a type of reaction, not an enzyme class — the correct class name is 'hydrolase'. Because statement I uses the wrong term, it is excluded.

questions.q:
Biological functions of enzymes include(s)
I. digestion.
II. cell regulation.
III. signal transduction.
questions.e: Enzymes are central to digestion (I) and cellular regulation (II, e.g. controlling metabolic flux). Signal transduction (III) is driven mainly by receptors, kinases acting as signalling relays and second messengers rather than being classed as a core 'enzyme function' in this scheme, so it is excluded here.

questions.q:
The protein part of the enzyme is called
I. Apoenzyme.
II. Holoenzyme.
III. Zymogen.
questions.e: The apoenzyme is, by definition, the protein-only part of an enzyme before it binds its cofactor/coenzyme. The holoenzyme is apoenzyme + cofactor together (not just the protein part), and a zymogen is an inactive enzyme precursor — neither matches the definition asked for.

questions.q:
Classes of enzymes include (s)
I. hydrolases.
II. ligases.
III. transferases.
questions.e: Unlike Q20, all three terms here are correctly named: hydrolases, ligases and transferases are three of the standard six/seven major enzyme classes (alongside oxidoreductases, lyases and isomerases).

questions.q:
Most of the members of vitamin B complex act as
I. Cofactor.
II. Coenzyme.
III. Holoenzyme.
questions.e: I and II are both true. The B vitamins are the classic COENZYME precursors — niacin → NAD⁺, riboflavin → FAD, thiamine → TPP, pantothenate → coenzyme A — and a coenzyme is simply an organic cofactor. Only III is false: a holoenzyme is the whole active complex.

questions.q:
Enzymes exhibit specificity based on
I. Shape.
II. Charges.
III. Size.
questions.e: In this scheme, shape (the classic 'lock and key' complementarity) is highlighted as the key basis of specificity (I only) tested here, rather than charge or size individually.

questions.q:
The following are way(s) by which enzymes are regulated
I. Enzyme production.
II. Enzyme inhibition.
III. Increase in temperature.
questions.e: Cells regulate enzyme activity by controlling how much enzyme is produced (I) and via inhibitors/activators (II). Temperature (III) is an external physical condition that affects enzyme activity but is not a physiological 'regulation' mechanism the cell uses deliberately, so it's excluded.

questions.q:
Enzymes involved in inhibition is/are known as
I. Holoenzymes.
II. Inhibitors.
III. Allosteric enzymes.
questions.e: Inhibitors (II) directly block enzyme activity, and many regulatory enzymes that respond to inhibitors are allosteric enzymes (III). 'Holoenzyme' (I) simply refers to a complete enzyme with its cofactor — unrelated to inhibition — so it is excluded.

questions.q:
Which of the following is/are substrate-specific enzyme?
I. Lactase.
II. Hexokinase.
III. Glucokinase.
questions.e: Lactase acts on one specific substrate, lactose, making it strictly substrate-specific (I only). Hexokinase and glucokinase, by contrast, can act on more than one hexose sugar (hexokinase especially is broadly specific for hexoses), so they are not considered strictly substrate-specific here.

questions.q:
Which of the following influence feedback inhibition?
I. End product.
II. Temperature.
III. pH.
questions.e: Feedback inhibition is, by definition, driven by the accumulation of the pathway's END PRODUCT, which binds back to an earlier enzyme (often allosterically) to slow the pathway (I only). Temperature and pH affect enzyme activity generally, but they are not what defines feedback inhibition.

questions.q:
Cofactors
I. Are always inorganic.
II. Loosely bound- coenzyme.
III. Tightly bound- prosthetic group.
questions.e: II and III are both correct definitions. A cofactor bound loosely and reversibly is a COENZYME (NAD⁺, FAD, coenzyme A); one bound tightly, often covalently, is a PROSTHETIC GROUP (haem, biotin). Only I is false — cofactors span inorganic metal ions and organic molecules alike.

questions.q:
Assertion: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is an allosteric regulator of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis
Reason: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activates Fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase and inhibits phosphofructokinase 1.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: The assertion is true but the reason has it backwards. Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate ACTIVATES phosphofructokinase-1 and INHIBITS fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase — the switch that favours glycolysis in the fed state and gluconeogenesis in the fasted state.

questions.q:
Assertion: ATP is an allosteric inhibitor of gluconeogenesis
Reason: ATP inhibits the conversion of Fructose-6-phosphate to Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate by phosphofructokinase 1.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: The ASSERTION is false and the REASON is true. ATP does not inhibit gluconeogenesis — high ATP signals plenty of energy, which SHUTS DOWN glycolysis and permits gluconeogenesis. The reason describes the real effect correctly: ATP allosterically inhibits phosphofructokinase-1, the enzyme converting fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate — a glycolytic step, not a gluconeogenic one.

questions.q:
Assertion: Gluconeogenesis and glycolysis are considered opposing pathways
Reason: Gluconeogenesis is a direct reversal of glycolysis.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: The assertion is true but the reason is false. Gluconeogenesis is NOT a direct reversal of glycolysis. Three glycolytic steps are irreversible — hexokinase/glucokinase, phosphofructokinase-1 and pyruvate kinase — and gluconeogenesis bypasses them with four different enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase, then fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase. The other seven steps are the shared reversible ones.

questions.q:
Assertion: Glucagon secretion favours gluconeogenesis
Reason: Glucagon secretion leads to phosphorylation of phosphofructokinase 2, which reduces the production of an inhibitor in gluconeogenesis.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both statements are true and connected: glucagon activates PKA, which phosphorylates the bifunctional PFK-2/FBPase-2 enzyme. This inactivates its kinase domain (less F2,6BP made) and activates its phosphatase domain — lowering F2,6BP, an inhibitor of the gluconeogenic enzyme fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase — thereby favouring gluconeogenesis.

questions.q:
Gluconeogenesis is important in the following tissues:
I. erythrocytes
II. brain
III. hepatocytes.
questions.e: Gluconeogenesis is physiologically important FOR maintaining glucose supply to obligate glucose-dependent tissues — erythrocytes (which lack mitochondria and rely almost entirely on glycolysis) and the brain (which strongly prefers glucose). Hepatocytes are where gluconeogenesis actually takes place, but the liver itself is not the primary 'beneficiary' of the glucose it exports.
questions.t: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism

questions.q:
Enzymes involved in the regulation of gluconeogenesis include:
I. Pyruvate carboxylase
II. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase
III. Malate dehydrogenase.
questions.e: Pyruvate carboxylase and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase are key regulatory/rate-limiting enzymes unique to gluconeogenesis. Malate dehydrogenase catalyses a freely reversible step (used in the malate–aspartate shuttle) and is not considered a regulatory control point of the pathway.
questions.t: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism

questions.q:
In allosteric regulation of gluconeogenesis:
I. high levels of citrate increases the activity of fructose 1, 6 bisphosphatase
II. high levels of acetyl CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase
III. decreased levels of fructose 1, 6 bisphosphate reduces the activity of pyruvate kinase.
questions.e: All three are correct: citrate activates fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (while inhibiting PFK-1), acetyl-CoA is a classic allosteric activator of pyruvate carboxylase, and low fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (a feed-forward activator of pyruvate kinase) means less activation of pyruvate kinase.
questions.t: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism

questions.q:
Hormonal control of gluconeogenesis:
I. Increased glucagon/insulin ratio enhances gluconeogenesis
II. Insulin inhibits lipolysis which in turn inhibits gluconeogenesis
III. Glucagon decreases [fructose 2, 6 bisphosphate] thus enhancing gluconeogenesis.
questions.e: All three are true. I: a rising glucagon:insulin ratio is the fasting signal that switches gluconeogenesis on. II: insulin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase, so lipolysis stops — that cuts the supply of glycerol (a gluconeogenic substrate) and of fatty acids, whose β-oxidation supplies the acetyl-CoA that allosterically ACTIVATES pyruvate carboxylase and the ATP that drives the pathway. Less lipolysis therefore means less gluconeogenesis. III: glucagon raises cAMP, PKA phosphorylates the bifunctional PFK-2/FBPase-2 enzyme, which switches it to its phosphatase mode; fructose-2,6-bisphosphate falls, which relieves the inhibition of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and removes the stimulation of PFK-1 — so gluconeogenesis is enhanced.
questions.t: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism

questions.q:
Glucagon induces the synthesis of the following enzymes:
I. Phosphofructokinase I
II. Fructose 1, 6 bisphosphatase
III. PEP carboxykinase.
questions.e: Glucagon (via cAMP/gene transcription) induces synthesis of the key gluconeogenic enzymes fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and PEP carboxykinase. It does NOT induce phosphofructokinase-1 — PFK-1 is a glycolytic enzyme, and glucagon acts to suppress, not promote, glycolysis.
questions.t: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism

questions.q:
Glycerol enters the pathway to glucose production as:
I. 3-phosphoglycerate
II. pyruvate
III. phosphoenolpyruvate.
questions.e: Glycerol is phosphorylated (glycerol kinase) and oxidized to dihydroxyacetone phosphate, feeding into the gluconeogenic pathway upstream of the triose-phosphate stage — placing its entry conceptually alongside the earlier 3-carbon intermediates rather than at the pyruvate/PEP end of the pathway (III is excluded).
questions.t: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism

questions.q:
In Gluconeogenesis:
I. fructose 1,6 bisphosphatase is inhibited by an increased [AMP]
II. increased citrate levels inhibit phosphofructokinase 1
III. ingestion of uncooked eggs inhibits the conversion of pyruvate to PEP.
questions.e: All three are true. AMP inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase; citrate inhibits PFK-1; and raw egg white contains AVIDIN, which binds biotin, so pyruvate carboxylase cannot convert pyruvate to oxaloacetate.
questions.t: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism

questions.q:
During gluconeogenesis, the three irreversible steps of glycolysis have to be bypassed. The first step is the conversion of pyruvate to phosphoenolpyruvate. Which of the following statement is FALSE regarding the reaction step?
I. This reaction involves a two-step process catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase
II. Conversion of oxaloacetate from pyruvate occurs in the cytosol.
III. Formation of phosphoenolpyruvate requires only ATP as an energy source.
questions.e: Read the stem carefully — it asks which statements are FALSE. II and III are the false ones. II is false because pyruvate → oxaloacetate is catalysed by PYRUVATE CARBOXYLASE, a MITOCHONDRIAL enzyme, so it happens inside the mitochondrion, not the cytosol. III is false because the bypass does not run on ATP alone: pyruvate carboxylase spends ATP, but PEP carboxykinase then spends GTP. I is TRUE — it correctly describes the two-step bypass by pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase — so it is not one of the false statements.
questions.t: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism

questions.q:
Step(s) in the payoff phase of glycolysis
I. Conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate
II. Oxidation of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate to 1, 3-bisphosphoglycerate
III. Reversible conversion of dihydroxyacetone phosphate to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate
