questions.e: PEP → pyruvate and G3P oxidation → 1,3-BPG are both substrate-level phosphorylation/oxidation steps that occur in the payoff (energy-generating) phase. The DHAP ↔ G3P isomerisation (triose phosphate isomerase) happens immediately after aldolase cleavage and is considered part of the earlier preparatory (investment) phase, not the payoff phase.
questions.t: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism

questions.q:
Intermediate(s) involved in substrate level phosphorylation in glycolysis
I. 2-phosphoglycerate
II. Phosphoenolpyruvate
III. 1, 3-bisphosphoglycerate
questions.e: 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate and phosphoenolpyruvate are the two high-energy intermediates that directly donate a phosphate group to ADP (substrate-level phosphorylation), generating ATP. 2-phosphoglycerate is only an intermediate of the enolase/mutase steps and does not itself donate a phosphate to ADP.
questions.t: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism

questions.q:
Which of the following enzymes participate in the 1st phase of glycolysis?
I. Enolase
II. Phosphoglycerate mutase
III. Phosphoglucose isomerase
questions.e: Phosphoglucose isomerase (glucose-6-P → fructose-6-P) acts in the preparatory (1st) phase of glycolysis. Enolase and phosphoglycerate mutase act later, in the payoff phase — so only statement III belongs to the 1st phase.
questions.t: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism

questions.q:
The pathways for glucose converted from galactose include
I. Gluconeogenesis
II. Glycolysis
III. Glycogenesis
questions.e: Once galactose is converted (via the Leloir pathway) to glucose-6-phosphate, that G6P can be used in glycolysis for energy or in glycogenesis for storage. It is not classified as entering 'gluconeogenesis', since gluconeogenesis specifically refers to synthesising new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors.
questions.t: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism

questions.q:
Cataract due to galactokinase deficiency arises from
I. Accumulation of galactitol
II. Permeable cells to water
III. Low activity of aldose reductase
questions.e: With galactokinase deficiency, excess galactose is instead reduced by ALDOSE REDUCTASE (which is normally, not poorly, active) to galactitol. Galactitol accumulates in the lens (I), drawing water in osmotically and making the lens cells swell/permeable (II) — this is what causes the cataract. Statement III is false; it is not low aldose reductase activity that causes this — the enzyme is active enough to generate the damaging galactitol.
questions.t: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism

questions.q:
Galactosemia is
I. Due to deficiency in galactokinase
II. A sex-linked hereditary disease
III. A congenital disease in infants
questions.e: Correction: Classic galactosemia is caused by deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT) — galactokinase deficiency causes a separate, milder disorder — so statement I is not accurate for 'galactosemia' as classically defined. Statement II is factually incorrect: galactosemia is inherited in an AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE pattern, not sex-linked. Only statement III is correct — it is a congenital disorder that presents in infancy. (This answer has been corrected from the original paper, which had marked 'A'.)
questions.t: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism

questions.q:
Galactose is produced from
I. Glycolipids
II. Glycoproteins
III. Milk
questions.e: While galactose is structurally found in glycolipids and glycoproteins, the major dietary/exogenous SOURCE of galactose is lactose in milk (which is hydrolysed to glucose + galactose), making milk the key answer intended here.
questions.t: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism

questions.q: Polyol pathway
o: Pathway is present in the liver
Pathway is not related to glucose concentration
questions.e: In the polyol pathway, aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol, and sorbitol dehydrogenase then converts sorbitol to fructose — so it does involve sorbitol dehydrogenase. Aldolase B belongs to fructose metabolism, not the polyol pathway; the pathway is most active in tissues like the lens, retina, nerve and kidney (not primarily the liver); and its flux rises with high glucose concentration (e.g. in hyperglycaemia), so it is very much related to glucose levels.
questions.t: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option

questions.q: Which of the following is true about Essential fructosuria
o: Fructose is trapped within the cells
Caused by deficiency in hepatic fructokinase
A child from carrier parents has 50% chance of having this condition
questions.e: Essential fructosuria results from a deficiency of hepatic fructokinase, so ingested fructose cannot be phosphorylated in the liver and simply spills into the urine unchanged. It is a benign, largely ASYMPTOMATIC condition, and — being autosomal recessive — two carrier parents have a 25% (not 50%) chance of an affected child.
questions.t: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option

questions.q: In hereditary fructose intolerance
questions.e: Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by aldolase B deficiency. Fructose-1-phosphate cannot be cleaved further and accumulates, trapping cellular phosphate and secondarily inhibiting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis — leading to HYPOglycaemia (not hyperglycaemia) after fructose ingestion.
questions.t: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option

questions.q: Aldose reductase is NOT found in the
questions.e: Aldose reductase (the first enzyme of the polyol pathway) is present in tissues such as the retina, nerve tissue, kidney, lens and erythrocytes. The liver has comparatively negligible aldose reductase activity, making it the correct 'NOT found in' answer.
questions.t: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option

questions.q: How many enzymes are involved in the conversion of galactose to glucose?
questions.e: The Leloir pathway uses galactokinase, galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT), and UDP-galactose-4-epimerase, plus phosphoglucomutase to convert the resulting glucose-1-phosphate to glucose-6-phosphate — four enzymes in total in the standard teaching scheme.
questions.t: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option

questions.q: Which enzyme phosphorylates fructose to fructose-6-phosphate
questions.e: In extrahepatic tissues (muscle, adipose), broadly-specific hexokinase phosphorylates fructose directly to fructose-6-phosphate. This is distinct from the LIVER pathway, where fructokinase instead produces fructose-1-phosphate — a classic distinction question.
questions.t: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option

questions.q: Transporter involved in shuttling fructose into intestinal cells
questions.e: GLUT5 is the fructose-specific transporter located on the apical (luminal) membrane of intestinal enterocytes, mediating fructose absorption from the gut lumen.
questions.t: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true for fructolysis and glycolysis?
o: These processes share same intermediate structures
Leads to same metabolic fates for fructose and glucose
Rate of fructose and glucose transport is virtually the same
Both fructose and glucose are exclusively metabolized in the liver
questions.e: Fructolysis converges with glycolysis at the level of the triose phosphates (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate / dihydroxyacetone phosphate), so the two pathways do share common intermediate structures. Their regulation and tissue fates differ, transport uses different carriers (GLUT5 vs GLUT2/GLUT4) at different rates, and glucose is metabolised in virtually every tissue, not just the liver.
questions.t: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option

questions.q: Fructose
o: In its free form is absorbed directly by intestines
Uptake occurs along a concentration gradient
questions.e: Dietary fructose (both free, and bound in sucrose) is estimated to make up roughly a fifth of typical carbohydrate/caloric intake in many modern diets. Fructose is not found only in the free form (it is also part of sucrose), and its intestinal absorption depends on the GLUT5 transporter rather than being unassisted.
questions.t: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option

questions.q: Fructose is
questions.e: Fructose is a ketose — a polyhydroxyketone — whereas glucose is an aldose (a polyhydroxyaldehyde). They are structural isomers of one another, not epimers (epimers differ at a single stereocentre while retaining the same functional-group type).
questions.t: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option

questions.q: Which of the following clinical symptoms of classical galactosemia is a direct result of the accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate?
questions.e: Accumulated galactose-1-phosphate is directly hepatotoxic, damaging liver cells and causing jaundice. (By contrast, the cataracts of galactosemia are attributed to galactitol, formed via aldose reductase, rather than to galactose-1-phosphate itself.)
questions.t: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option

questions.q:
Assertion: The Leloir pathway serves as the principal route for galactose metabolism
Reason: it converts galactose into glucose-1-phosphate, which can then enter glycolysis or glycogenesis.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both statements are true, and the reason correctly explains the assertion: the Leloir pathway (galactokinase, GALT, epimerase) is indeed the main way the body converts galactose into a usable glucose derivative.

questions.q:
Assertion: Gluconeogenesis occurs mainly in the liver
Reason: gluconeogenesis helps to maintain glucose levels in the blood.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both statements are true, but the reason explains WHY gluconeogenesis matters generally, not WHY the liver specifically is the main site (that's because the liver -- and to a lesser extent the kidney cortex -- has the full enzyme set: pyruvate carboxylase, PEP carboxykinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, and glucose-6-phosphatase).

questions.q: Damage to the red blood cells of an individual with G6PD deficiency can be reduced by adequate activity of which of the following?
questions.e: Glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione (GSH) to detoxify peroxides and protect the red cell membrane from oxidative damage. Fever and infection are actually triggers of hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, not protective factors, and reactive oxygen species are what cause the damage in the first place.

questions.q:
Assertion: Gluconeogenesis is inhibited by high ATP levels
Reason: high ATP indicates a low cellular energy charge.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both statements are false. High ATP actually PROMOTES gluconeogenesis (pyruvate carboxylase requires ATP, and a high energy charge favors glucose synthesis) rather than inhibiting it -- and high ATP indicates a HIGH, not low, energy charge.

questions.q: Which of the following is TRUE about the TCA cycle?
o: It uses fluoroacetyl-CoA as a normal substrate
It regenerates its own oxaloacetate, allowing it to keep running
It permanently degenerates oxaloacetate at its final stage
questions.e: The TCA cycle regenerates oxaloacetate at the end of every turn, which is exactly what allows it to keep cycling. Fluoroacetate is a poison (converted to fluorocitrate, which inhibits the cycle) rather than a normal substrate; the cycle is more accurately described as amphibolic (both catabolic and anabolic) rather than purely catabolic; and oxaloacetate is regenerated, not permanently destroyed.

questions.q:
Glycolysis:
I. Occurs in the mitochondrion
II. Is considered catabolic
III. Is a linear pathway
questions.e: Statement I is false -- glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, not the mitochondrion. Statements II and III are true: glycolysis is a catabolic (energy-yielding) pathway, and it proceeds as a linear sequence of 10 steps.

questions.q:
Assertion: Coenzymes are also known as co-substrates
Reason: coenzymes influence substrate binding.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: The ASSERTION is true but the REASON is false. Coenzymes are called co-substrates because they behave like a second substrate: they bind loosely, are chemically ALTERED stoichiometrically during the reaction and must be regenerated — NAD⁺ becomes NADH, CoASH becomes acetyl-CoA. Their job is to carry electrons or chemical groups, not to influence how the primary substrate binds. Helping to bind and orient substrate is the role of tightly bound prosthetic groups and metal-ion cofactors, not of coenzymes acting as co-substrates.

questions.q:
In non-competitive inhibition:
I. The inhibitor binds to the free enzyme only
II. The inhibitor does not bind to the substrate
III. Vmax decreases but Km remains the same
questions.e: Statement I is false as written -- a non-competitive inhibitor can bind either the free enzyme or the enzyme-substrate complex, not the free enzyme only. Statements II and III are true: the inhibitor doesn't resemble or bind the substrate, and classic non-competitive inhibition lowers Vmax while leaving Km unchanged.

questions.q: Nana is glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficient. He is most likely prone to:
questions.e: G6PD deficiency impairs NADPH production, so red blood cells can't maintain reduced glutathione and become vulnerable to oxidative damage and haemolysis -- causing haemolytic anaemia. (Ironically, G6PD deficiency is associated with increased RESISTANCE to malaria, not susceptibility to it.)

questions.q:
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE with regard to fructolysis?
I. Its transport into cells is insulin independent
II. Deficiency of the relevant enzyme can lead to fructosuria or fructosaemia
III. In muscle, conversion of fructose to fructose-1-phosphate is done by fructokinase
questions.e: Statements I and II are true: fructose transport is insulin-independent, and enzyme deficiencies along this pathway (e.g. fructokinase deficiency) can cause fructosuria. Statement III is false -- fructokinase is concentrated in the liver (also kidney and intestine), not muscle; muscle instead uses the low-affinity hexokinase pathway, and its product is fructose-6-phosphate, not fructose-1-phosphate.

questions.q:
Assertion: Enzymes are reusable
Reason: enzymes are specific for the reaction they catalyze.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: The assertion is true -- enzymes are released unchanged after catalysis and can be used repeatedly. But the reason given doesn't explain that: specificity is about WHICH reaction an enzyme catalyzes, not about why it can be reused. Reusability comes from the enzyme not being consumed or permanently altered during catalysis.

questions.q:
Fructokinase is located in:
I. Liver
II. Brain
III. Eye
questions.e: Fructokinase is found mainly in the liver (also kidney and intestine). It is not a significant enzyme in the brain or the eye -- the eye instead has notable aldose reductase activity as part of the polyol pathway.

questions.q:
Assertion: Severe alcoholism can affect α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
Reason: α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase requires thiamine pyrophosphate as a cofactor.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — chronic alcoholism causes thiamine deficiency, which impairs TPP-dependent enzymes like α-KGDH, a correct explanation.

questions.q:
Assertion: In type 2 diabetes, the activity of GLUT-4 is reduced
Reason: in type 2 diabetes, there is increased insulin resistance in skeletal tissues.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — insulin resistance directly impairs insulin-stimulated GLUT-4 translocation/activity, a correct explanation.

questions.q:
Assertion: Fluoride is used as an additive in blood fructose checks
Reason: it is an inhibitor in fructolysis.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both false as written — fluoride-oxalate tubes are used to preserve blood GLUCOSE (not fructose) samples, and fluoride works by inhibiting enolase, a glycolysis enzyme, not a fructolysis enzyme (fructokinase, aldolase B, triokinase). This looks like a typo for 'glucose check' in the original question.

questions.q:
Regarding the Cori cycle:
I. Lactate travels from muscle to the liver
II. The liver converts lactate back to glucose
III. It operates only during exercise, never at rest
questions.e: I and II are true, describing the core Cori cycle. III is false -- some level of lactate/glucose cycling can occur outside of intense exercise as well.

questions.q:
Regarding the Pyruvate Dehydrogenase complex:
I. It uses five different cofactors
II. It converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA
III. Its reaction is reversible
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is irreversible under physiological conditions.

questions.q:
Regarding Gibbs Free Energy:
I. A large negative ΔG means the reaction is exergonic
II. A ΔG of zero means the reaction is at equilibrium
III. A large positive ΔG means the reaction is spontaneous
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- a large positive ΔG means the reaction is endergonic and non-spontaneous, requiring energy input.

questions.q:
The pathway enzymes involved in glycolysis include:
I. Enolase
II. Hexokinase
III. Phosphoglycerate mutase
questions.e: All three are genuine glycolytic enzymes (steps 9, 1, and 8 respectively).

questions.q:
Assertion: Thiamine deficiency leads to high levels of pyruvate in the blood
Reason: high levels of pyruvate lead to decreased ATP production.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both statements are true, but the causal logic runs backwards for an explanation — it's the thiamine (TPP) deficiency impairing PDH that causes pyruvate to build up, not the other way around.

questions.q:
Regarding regulation of the Krebs cycle:
I. High NADH/NAD+ ratio slows the cycle down
II. Isocitrate dehydrogenase is inhibited by ATP
III. Malonate is a substrate of succinate dehydrogenase
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- malonate is a competitive INHIBITOR of succinate dehydrogenase (it resembles succinate), not a normal substrate.

questions.q: Malonate inhibits the Krebs cycle by competitively inhibiting:
questions.e: Malonate closely resembles succinate and competitively inhibits succinate dehydrogenase, blocking FADH2 production.

questions.q:
In metabolism:
I. There is coordination
II. There are several pathways
III. Substrates are transformed to products via non-specific intermediates
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false — metabolic pathways use SPECIFIC intermediates at each defined step, not non-specific ones.

questions.q:
Assertion: The cells in the eye do not solely depend on glycolysis for energy supply
Reason: the cells in the eye have mitochondria which serve as an alternative source of energy.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. The retina is among the most metabolically active tissues in the body and its photoreceptor inner segments are packed with mitochondria. Having mitochondria is precisely why these cells are not restricted to glycolysis. (The lens is the exception — its mature fibre cells shed their mitochondria to stay transparent.)

questions.q: The first step of fructose metabolism in the liver, trapping it for further processing, is catalyzed by:
questions.e: Fructokinase phosphorylates fructose to fructose-1-phosphate, essentially trapping it for liver metabolism.

questions.q:
Gluconeogenesis:
I. Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase is inhibited by increased [AMP]
II. Alcohol abuse is an antagonist
III. Ingestion of uncooked eggs inhibits the conversion of pyruvate to PEP
questions.e: All three are true: AMP inhibits FBPase-1 (reciprocal to its activation of PFK-1); alcohol's excess NADH impairs gluconeogenic substrate conversion; and raw-egg avidin binds biotin, impairing biotin-dependent pyruvate carboxylase (pyruvate→OAA→PEP).

questions.q: Uncompetitive inhibition is characterized by the inhibitor binding:
questions.e: In uncompetitive (anti-competitive) inhibition, the inhibitor binds ONLY to the enzyme-substrate complex, usually at an allosteric site.

questions.q: Which tissue determines whether glucose-6-phosphate can be released as free glucose into the blood?
o: Liver and kidney, since they have glucose-6-phosphatase
questions.e: Glucose-6-phosphatase is present in liver and kidney (allowing glucose release to blood) but absent in muscle, brain, and adipose tissue.

questions.q: Which tissues rely most heavily on PPP-derived NADPH for reductive biosynthesis of fatty acids and steroids?
o: Liver, adrenal gland, and adipose tissue
questions.e: Tissues like liver, adrenal gland, testes, ovary, and adipose tissue use PPP-derived NADPH heavily for fatty acid and steroid synthesis.

questions.q:
Assertion: Galactose cannot be produced in the cell
Reason: galactose is only obtained from dietary sources.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both false — the body can make galactose endogenously from glucose via UDP-glucose 4-epimerase, even without dietary galactose.

questions.q:
Arsenate:
I. Inhibits glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase competitively
II. Is a structural analogue of inorganic orthophosphate
III. Impairs the substrate-level phosphorylation step catalyzed by phosphoglycerate kinase
questions.e: Arsenate mimics phosphate (ii) and competes with it in the GAPDH reaction (i), forming an unstable 1-arseno-3-phosphoglycerate that decomposes spontaneously BEFORE reaching phosphoglycerate kinase — so it bypasses/wastes that step rather than directly 'impairing' PGK's catalysis (iii is the weaker/false statement here).

questions.q:
Regarding cofactors:
I. A prosthetic group is tightly bound to the enzyme
II. A coenzyme is loosely bound to the enzyme
III. All cofactors are strictly organic molecules
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- cofactors can be inorganic (e.g. metal ions) or organic (e.g. vitamin-derived coenzymes).

questions.q:
Assertion: Holoenzyme is called a functional enzyme
Reason: holoenzyme is made up of an apoenzyme and a coenzyme.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — the holoenzyme (apoenzyme + cofactor) is the complete, catalytically active form, which is exactly why it's 'functional'.

questions.q:
Regarding fructose metabolism:
I. Fructose transport into cells is insulin independent
II. Fructokinase is concentrated mainly in the liver
III. Fructose is metabolized primarily in muscle
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- fructose is metabolized almost completely in the liver, not muscle.

questions.q:
Assertion: The Krebs cycle derives its acetyl units from only carbohydrates
Reason: the Krebs cycle is solely carbohydrate dependent.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both false — acetyl-CoA feeding the cycle can come from carbohydrates, fats, and proteins; the TCA cycle is amphibolic, not carbohydrate-exclusive.

questions.q: An elevated blood LDH level after tissue damage can be a clue pointing toward:
questions.e: LDH is released into the blood when cells are damaged, so an abnormally high LDH level can point toward conditions like a heart attack.

questions.q:
Assertion: The Krebs cycle is called the tricarboxylic acid cycle
Reason: the first tricarboxylic acid produced is isocitrate.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion true. Reason false — the first tricarboxylic acid formed is CITRATE (via citrate synthase); isocitrate is formed one step later by aconitase.

questions.q:
Assertion: Enzymes are crucial to metabolism
Reason: enzymes drive desirable reactions that cannot occur on their own (at a biologically useful rate).
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true, and this is exactly why enzymes are crucial — they make otherwise-too-slow reactions happen fast enough for life.

questions.q: Organophosphorus insecticides act as irreversible inhibitors mainly by blocking:
questions.e: Organophosphorus insecticides block acetylcholinesterase, essential for nerve conduction, causing paralysis of vital functions.

questions.q:
Gluconeogenesis is important for the following tissues:
I. Erythrocytes
II. Brain
III. Reticulocytes
questions.e: These tissues don't perform gluconeogenesis themselves (only liver/kidney do), but they critically DEPEND ON its glucose output, especially during fasting — hence gluconeogenesis is 'important' to them.

questions.q:
The following TCA intermediates are used up by other synthetic pathways:
I. Citrate
II. Succinate
III. Malate
questions.e: Only citrate is a major biosynthetic exit point (feeding fatty-acid/cholesterol synthesis via the citrate shuttle); succinate and malate stay mostly within the cycle/shuttle systems.

questions.q: Enzymes are best described as:
o: Structural components of the cell wall
questions.e: Enzymes are biocatalysts synthesized by living cells; they are almost all protein in nature (with the exception of ribozymes).

questions.q:
Regarding glucose transporters (GLUTs):
I. GLUT4 is the only insulin-dependent transporter
II. GLUT1 is found in red blood cells
III. GLUT2 is insulin-dependent
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- GLUT2 (found in kidney, liver, pancreas) is insulin-independent, like GLUT1 and GLUT3.

questions.q:
Regulation of gluconeogenesis:
I. High citrate increases fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase activity
II. High acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase
III. Decreased fructose 1,6-bisphosphate reduces pyruvate kinase activity
questions.e: All three are correct: citrate activates FBPase-1, acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase, and less F1,6BP (a feed-forward activator of pyruvate kinase) means less PK activity.

questions.q:
Assertion: Fructose absorption does not depend on sodium concentration in blood
Reason: fructose absorption is insulin independent.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true (fructose uses facilitated diffusion via GLUT5, unlike Na⁺-dependent glucose transport, and doesn't need insulin) — but insulin-independence doesn't explain sodium-independence; they're separate properties.

questions.q: Which body appointed the Enzyme Commission in 1961 to standardize enzyme classification?
questions.e: The IUB appointed an Enzyme Commission in 1961, leading to the six-class enzyme system in force since 1964.

questions.q:
Assertion: Metabolism in living organisms is very important
Reason: metabolism is organized into several discrete pathways.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both statements are true, but organization into pathways doesn't explain WHY metabolism is important — that's about sustaining life processes.

questions.q:
Regarding galactose metabolism:
I. Lactase hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose
II. Classical galactosemia is due to GALT deficiency
III. Galactokinase deficiency causes classical galactosemia
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- galactokinase deficiency causes a separate, milder disorder (Galactosemia type 2), not classical galactosemia.

questions.q: ATP's high-energy phosphoanhydride bonds release large amounts of energy on hydrolysis mainly because of:
o: High resonance stabilization and low electrostatic repulsion
Less resonance stabilization and high electrostatic repulsion
questions.e: The high-energy character comes from less resonance stabilization of the phosphoanhydride bonds and high electrostatic repulsion between the charged phosphate groups.

questions.q:
High glucagon/insulin ratio in the blood:
I. Increased enzymatic capacity for gluconeogenesis
II. Represses transcription of glucokinase
III. Represses transcription of pyruvate kinase
questions.e: All three are true — this hormonal state favours gluconeogenic gene expression while repressing glycolytic genes (glucokinase, pyruvate kinase).

questions.q:
Regarding metabolism:
I. Catabolism is energy-yielding
II. Anabolism is energy-requiring
III. Amphibolic pathways serve only catabolic roles
questions.e: Catabolism releases energy (I, true) and anabolism consumes it (II, true). Amphibolic pathways serve BOTH catabolic and anabolic roles, not only catabolic, so III is false.

questions.q: Lactose is hydrolyzed to glucose and galactose by the enzyme:
questions.e: Lactase hydrolyzes the disaccharide lactose into its two monosaccharide components, glucose and galactose.

questions.q: G6PD deficiency mainly causes disease by predisposing red blood cells to:
o: Acute hemolytic anemia under oxidative stress
questions.e: Without adequate NADPH, RBCs cannot maintain reduced glutathione, making them vulnerable to oxidative damage and hemolysis when stressed.

questions.q:
Glycolysis is regulated by:
I. Aldolase
II. Hexokinase
III. Phosphofructokinase
questions.e: Hexokinase and PFK-1 are genuine allosteric control points of glycolysis; aldolase is not considered a regulated/rate-controlling enzyme in the classic scheme, so only II and III hold.

questions.q: G6PD deficiency is clinically significant partly because carriers show increased resistance to:
questions.e: G6PD deficiency carriers have increased resistance to malaria, which is why the trait remains common in malaria-endemic regions.

questions.q:
The enzyme responsible for splitting the glucose (fructose-1,6-bisphosphate) molecule in glycolysis is:
I. Aldolase
II. Enolase
III. Phosphoglycerate Mutase
questions.e: Only aldolase splits F1,6BP into DHAP + G3P; enolase and phosphoglycerate mutase act later and don't cleave carbon-carbon bonds.

questions.q:
Regarding the Pentose Phosphate Pathway:
I. It occurs in the cytosol
II. G6PD catalyzes the committed step
III. The non-oxidative phase produces NADPH
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- NADPH is produced only in the oxidative phase; the non-oxidative phase interconverts sugars without touching NADPH.

questions.q:
Regarding enzyme active sites:
I. They are typically flexible, not rigid
II. Serine is the most frequently found active-site residue
III. The active site makes up most of the enzyme's mass
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- only a small portion (about 2-6 amino acids) of the much larger enzyme is directly involved in catalysis.

questions.q:
Regarding hereditary disorders of carbohydrate metabolism:
I. Essential fructosuria is caused by fructokinase deficiency
II. Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by aldolase B deficiency
III. Essential fructosuria is a severe, symptomatic disease
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- essential fructosuria is a benign, largely asymptomatic condition, unlike hereditary fructose intolerance which can be severe.

questions.q:
Assertion: In the Krebs cycle, aconitase isomerizes citrate to isocitrate
Reason: aconitase is an isomerase.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — aconitase catalyzes the isomerization of citrate to isocitrate (via cis-aconitate), consistent with its isomerase classification.

questions.q:
Assertion: Irreversible inhibitors are easily dissociated from enzymes
Reason: irreversible inhibitors bind to enzymes through non-covalent forces.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: The assertion is true but the reason is false. Gluconeogenesis is NOT a direct reversal of glycolysis. Three glycolytic steps are irreversible — hexokinase/glucokinase, phosphofructokinase-1 and pyruvate kinase — and gluconeogenesis gets around them with four different enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase, then fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase. The other seven steps are the shared reversible ones.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three purposes requiring a continual input of free energy in living organisms?
questions.e: The three purposes are mechanical work in cellular movements, biosynthesis of macromolecules, and active transport of molecules and ions across membranes. Storage of genetic information is not one of them — DNA stores information without a continual free-energy input.

questions.q:
Enzyme inhibitors:
I. Usually don't affect the activity of enzymes
II. Most drugs are inhibitors
III. Decrease the activity of enzymes
questions.e: I is false — inhibitors by definition DO affect (reduce) activity. II and III are true: many drugs act as enzyme inhibitors, and by definition inhibitors decrease enzyme activity.

questions.q:
In catabolism:
I. There are four main stages
II. Lipids are broken down to fatty acids
III. Polysaccharides are broken down to monosaccharides
questions.e: I is false — catabolism is classically described in THREE main stages (Lehninger), not four. II and III are true.

questions.q:
Substrates of gluconeogenesis in humans include:
I. Lactate
II. Glycerol
III. Aspartate
questions.e: All three feed gluconeogenesis: lactate (via pyruvate), glycerol (from fat breakdown), and aspartate (a glucogenic amino acid, via oxaloacetate).

questions.q:
Regarding enzyme inhibition:
I. Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate
II. Irreversible inhibitors bind covalently
III. Non-competitive inhibitors always increase Vmax
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- non-competitive inhibition decreases Vmax while Km stays the same, it does not increase Vmax.

questions.q:
Regarding glycolysis:
I. It takes place in the cytoplasm
II. It produces a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose
III. All ten steps are reversible
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- three steps (hexokinase, PFK-1, pyruvate kinase) are irreversible under physiological conditions.

questions.q: Fructose is transported into intestinal cells mainly by:
questions.e: GLUT5 mediates facilitated diffusion of fructose across the apical membrane of intestinal cells.

questions.q: The Pyruvate Dehydrogenase complex requires how many cofactors?
questions.e: PDH uses five cofactors: TPP, CoASH, lipoic acid, FAD, and NAD+.

questions.q:
Assertion: Increase in alanine transaminase (ALT) in the blood is a result of liver damage
Reason: increase in ALT in the blood results from leakage from damaged hepatocytes.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — ALT is a liver-enriched cytosolic enzyme, so it normally stays inside hepatocytes; injury lets it leak into the bloodstream, which is exactly why elevated ALT signals liver damage.

questions.q:
Galactose is found in the following:
I. Chitin
II. Sugar beets
III. Cane sugar
questions.e: This item is genuinely tricky/debated: galactose-containing oligosaccharides (e.g. raffinose) occur in sugar beet, but chitin (poly-N-acetylglucosamine) and cane sugar (sucrose = glucose+fructose) don't actually contain galactose. Treat this one with a pinch of salt and confirm the intended source list with your lecturer.

questions.q: A prosthetic group differs from a coenzyme mainly in that it is:
o: Tightly and stably bound to the enzyme
questions.e: Prosthetic groups are tightly, stably incorporated into the enzyme's structure (covalently or noncovalently), unlike loosely-bound coenzymes.

questions.q:
Regarding glycolytic regulation:
I. PFK-1 is inhibited by ATP and citrate
II. PFK-1 is activated by AMP
III. Pyruvate kinase is activated by ATP
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- pyruvate kinase is INHIBITED by ATP (and alanine), not activated by it; high energy charge turns glycolysis off.

questions.q:
Assertion: Epimerase converts ribulose-5-phosphate to xylulose-5-phosphate in the hexose monophosphate shunt
Reason: epimerase is an isomerase.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — ribulose-5-phosphate 3-epimerase inverts the configuration at one carbon to make xylulose-5-phosphate, and epimerases are indeed a subclass of isomerases (EC 5), which is exactly why it can perform this interconversion.

questions.q: Anaplerotic reactions serve to:
o: Break down the Krebs cycle entirely
Replenish Krebs cycle intermediates drawn off for biosynthesis
questions.e: Anaplerotic ("filling up") reactions replenish TCA cycle intermediates, allowing the cycle to keep running even as biosynthesis draws intermediates away.

questions.q:
Regarding the Krebs cycle:
I. It occurs in the mitochondrial matrix
II. It generates 3 NADH per turn
III. It is a purely catabolic pathway
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- the Krebs cycle is amphibolic, serving both catabolic and anabolic (biosynthetic) roles.

questions.q:
Which statement(s) is/are TRUE about enzymes?
I. Apoenzyme = Holoenzyme − Coenzyme
II. Holoenzyme = Apoenzyme + Coenzyme
III. Coenzyme = Holoenzyme − Apoenzyme
questions.e: All three are just algebraic rearrangements of the same true relationship: Holoenzyme = Apoenzyme + Coenzyme.

questions.q: The major site of gluconeogenesis in mammals is the:
questions.e: The liver is the major site of gluconeogenesis; the kidney cortex is a secondary site at about 1/10 the liver's capacity.

questions.q: Which enzyme is unique to gluconeogenesis and bypasses the irreversible PFK-1 step of glycolysis?
questions.e: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase dephosphorylates fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to fructose-6-phosphate, bypassing PFK-1.

questions.q:
Regarding organization of metabolic pathways:
I. A cyclic pathway regenerates its intermediates each turn
II. A spiral pathway uses different enzymes at each stage
III. A linear pathway's product feeds into the next reaction as substrate
questions.e: II is false -- spiral pathways (like fatty acid synthesis) use the SAME set of enzymes repeatedly, not different enzymes at each stage. I and III correctly describe cyclic and linear pathways.

questions.q:
Assertion: The phosphofructokinase reaction in glycolysis is the rate-limiting step
Reason: the phosphofructokinase reaction is not regulated.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion true (PFK-1 is the committed/rate-limiting step). Reason false — PFK-1 is in fact heavily regulated (by ATP, AMP, citrate, F2,6BP).

questions.q:
Glucagon induces the synthesis of the following enzymes:
I. PEP carboxykinase
II. Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase
III. Phosphofructokinase-1
questions.e: Glucagon induces the gluconeogenic enzymes PEPCK and FBPase-1; it would NOT induce PFK-1, a glycolytic enzyme it actually opposes.

questions.q:
Regarding G6PD deficiency:
I. It can cause acute hemolytic anemia
II. Red blood cells are especially affected because they lack mitochondria
III. It decreases resistance to malaria
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- G6PD deficiency is actually associated with INCREASED resistance to malaria, not decreased resistance.

questions.q:
Regarding enzyme classification:
I. Oxidoreductases catalyze oxidation-reduction reactions
II. Ligases join two molecules together using ATP
III. Hydrolases catalyze isomerization reactions
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- hydrolases catalyze hydrolysis reactions; isomerization is carried out by isomerases.

questions.q:
Assertion: The isocitrate dehydrogenase reaction of the TCA cycle produces the first reducing equivalent of the pathway
Reason: the isocitrate dehydrogenase reaction produces NADPH.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion true (it is indeed the first NADH-producing step). Reason false — the mitochondrial TCA-cycle isocitrate dehydrogenase produces NADH, not NADPH.

questions.q: A high glucagon:insulin ratio has which overall effect?
o: Has no effect on either pathway
questions.e: A high glucagon:insulin ratio increases the enzymatic capacity for gluconeogenesis and decreases that for glycolysis.

questions.q:
The salient features of galactosemia include:
I. Galactosuria
II. Development of cataract
III. Deficiency of galactokinase
questions.e: Classical galactosemia is caused by GALT deficiency, not galactokinase deficiency (galactokinase deficiency is the separate, milder Galactosemia type 2). So III is false here; I and II (galactosuria, cataracts) are true.

questions.q:
Assertion: Hexokinase is an isomerase
Reason: hexokinase is involved in the transfer of a functional group from one molecule to another.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Hexokinase is a transferase/kinase (EC 2.7.1.1), not an isomerase — assertion false. The reason correctly describes what a transferase/kinase does (transfers the phosphate group) — reason true.

questions.q:
Which of the following is/are TRUE about fructose uptake?
I. Is insulin dependent
II. Taken up in the liver by GLUT2
III. Uptake goes against a concentration gradient
questions.e: Corrected: I is false (insulin-independent) and III is false (GLUT-mediated transport is facilitated diffusion, WITH the concentration gradient, not against it). Only II — uptake in the liver via GLUT2 — is true.

questions.q: Which enzyme class catalyzes the transfer of functional groups between molecules?
questions.e: Transferases (EC 2) catalyze the transfer of functional groups from one molecule to another.

questions.q: How many NADPH molecules are produced in the oxidative phase of the PPP per glucose-6-phosphate?
questions.e: Two NADPH are produced in the oxidative phase -- one at the G6PD step and one at the 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase step.

questions.q: Which THREE enzymes catalyze the irreversible steps of glycolysis?
questions.e: Steps 1 (hexokinase), 3 (PFK-1), and 10 (pyruvate kinase) are the pathway's irreversible, regulated control points.

questions.q:
Enzyme inhibitors:
I. Usually don't affect enzyme activity
II. Most drugs are enzyme inhibitors
III. Are compounds that decrease the activity of enzymes
questions.e: I is false — inhibitors by definition DO affect (reduce) activity. II and III are true: many drugs work as enzyme inhibitors, which by definition decrease enzyme activity.

questions.q:
Assertion: ATP has high energy bonds
Reason: ATP is formed from ADP and phosphate.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both statements are true, but simply being 'formed from ADP + Pi' doesn't explain why the phosphoanhydride bonds are high-energy (that's due to charge repulsion/resonance effects) — not a correct explanation.

questions.q:
Fluoride inhibits which enzyme(s) and arrests glycolysis?
I. Aldolase
II. Hexokinase
III. Enolase
questions.e: Fluoride specifically inhibits enolase (by binding Mg²⁺ in its active site as a fluorophosphate complex), not aldolase or hexokinase.

questions.q:
Regarding gluconeogenesis:
I. It occurs mainly in the liver
II. Pyruvate carboxylase requires biotin
III. It is simply the reverse of glycolysis
questions.e: I and II are true. III is false -- gluconeogenesis bypasses the three irreversible glycolytic steps using different enzymes; it is not a direct reversal.

questions.q: Which of the following is a known trigger of hemolysis in G6PD-deficient individuals?
questions.e: Fava beans (and certain drugs like sulfonamides, antimalarials, and NSAIDs) are classic oxidative stressors that can trigger hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

questions.q: Which enzyme transfers 2-carbon units between sugars in the non-oxidative phase, using a thiamine-derived cofactor?
questions.e: Transketolase transfers 2-carbon units and requires TPP (a thiamine-derived cofactor); transaldolase transfers 3-carbon units.

questions.q: Substrate-level phosphorylation occurs in glycolysis at which two steps?
questions.e: Step 7 (phosphoglycerate kinase) and Step 10 (pyruvate kinase) both directly transfer a phosphate to ADP, generating ATP.

questions.q:
Which of the following is/are correct about the reaction: Fructose-6-P + ATP → Fructose-1,6-bisP + ADP?
I. It is the rate-limiting step of glycolysis
II. Is the 2nd priming (ATP-investing) step of glycolysis
III. Is catalysed by phosphofructokinase
questions.e: All three are correct: this PFK-1 reaction is glycolysis's committed, rate-limiting step, it's the second ATP-consuming ('priming') reaction (after hexokinase's), and PFK-1 (phosphofructokinase) is indeed the enzyme responsible.

questions.q:
Assertion: Essential fructosuria results in the inability to metabolize fructose beyond fructose-1-phosphate
Reason: essential fructosuria is caused by a deficiency of fructose-1-phosphate aldolase.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both false — that description is Hereditary Fructose Intolerance (aldolase B deficiency). Essential fructosuria is caused by fructokinase deficiency, so fructose is never even phosphorylated to F1P.

questions.q:
Assertion: Lactose intolerance results in bloating of the stomach after ingestion of lactose
Reason: lactose intolerance results from a lack of lactase.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — without lactase, undigested lactose ferments in the gut, producing gas and bloating; a correct explanation.

questions.q:
Consider the following:
I. Pyruvate kinase deficiency leads to swelling and lysis of erythrocytes
II. Hexokinase deficiency leads to non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia
III. Hexokinase deficiency shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right
questions.e: PK deficiency (i) and hexokinase deficiency (ii) are both real causes of hereditary haemolytic anaemia. But hexokinase deficiency REDUCES 2,3-BPG production, which shifts the O₂ curve LEFT (higher O₂ affinity), not right — iii is false.

questions.q:
Assertion: Papain can be used as a therapeutic agent
Reason: papain has anti-cancer properties.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion true (papain is used clinically, e.g. wound debridement, digestive aid). Its established therapeutic basis is its proteolytic activity, not anti-cancer effects — reason is false/unsubstantiated as the main basis.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the first, committed step of glycolysis in most tissues?
questions.e: Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate in Step 1, an essentially irreversible reaction under physiological conditions.

questions.q:
Iodoacetate:
I. Is an irreversible inhibitor of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase
II. Its action is similar to that of mercury
III. It is an allosteric inhibitor of phosphoglycerate kinase
questions.e: Iodoacetate covalently alkylates GAPDH's catalytic cysteine (i), the same thiol-reactive mechanism mercury uses on enzymes (ii). It doesn't act on phosphoglycerate kinase at all (iii is false).

questions.q:
Assertion: All enzymes are denatured by heat
Reason: all enzymes have a three-dimensional structure.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: The word 'all' makes the assertion false — thermostable enzymes (e.g. from thermophilic organisms) resist heat denaturation. The reason (3D structure) is true.

questions.q:
Assertion: Free ATP is a potent non-competitive inhibitor in glycolysis
Reason: free ATP inhibits hexokinase in glycolysis.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. In pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle, so it accumulates and is shunted to lactate, producing the acidosis. This is why PDH deficiency shows a NORMAL lactate:pyruvate ratio — both rise together.

questions.q:
Assertion: Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Deficiency results in metabolic acidosis
Reason: the metabolic acidosis is a result of the build-up of pyruvic acid.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. In PDH deficiency pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle, so it accumulates and is shunted to lactate, producing the acidosis. This is why PDH deficiency shows a NORMAL lactate:pyruvate ratio — both rise together.

questions.q:
Enzymes involved in the regulation of gluconeogenesis include:
I. Pyruvate carboxylase
II. PEP carboxykinase
III. Malate dehydrogenase
questions.e: Pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase are key regulated/rate-controlling enzymes; malate dehydrogenase is reversible and not a major control point.

questions.q:
Assertion: The α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase reaction of the TCA cycle is the 3rd oxidative decarboxylation step of the pathway
Reason: it is the 5th step of the pathway.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion true when counting pyruvate dehydrogenase (pyruvate→acetyl-CoA) as the 1st oxidative decarboxylation, isocitrate DH as the 2nd, and α-KGDH as the 3rd. Reason false — within the 8-step TCA cycle itself, α-KGDH is step 4, not step 5 (corrected from the commonly circulated 'E' answer).

questions.q:
Assertion: Galactose cannot be made in the body
Reason: galactose can only be obtained from dietary sources.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both false — the body can synthesize galactose endogenously from glucose via UDP-glucose 4-epimerase, even without any dietary galactose.

questions.q: Glycolysis converts one molecule of glucose into:
questions.e: Glycolysis is a 10-step pathway converting one 6-carbon glucose into two 3-carbon pyruvate molecules.

questions.q:
In non-competitive inhibition:
I. The inhibitor binds to only free enzyme
II. The inhibitor does not bind to the substrate
III. There is a decrease in Vmax but Km remains the same
questions.e: I is false — a non-competitive inhibitor can bind BOTH free enzyme and the enzyme-substrate complex, not only free enzyme. II and III correctly describe non-competitive inhibition.

questions.q:
Enzyme mechanism involves:
I. Providing an alternative pathway
II. Reducing the reaction entropy change
III. Not lowering the energy of the transition state
questions.e: Only I is a standard named mechanism here. III is definitely false — enzymes work precisely BY lowering the transition-state energy.

questions.q: An elevated blood alanine transaminase (ALT) level is most closely associated with:
questions.e: ALT is a classic marker for liver disease/hepatitis, since it's released when hepatocytes are damaged.

questions.q:
Hormonal control of gluconeogenesis:
I. Increased glucagon/insulin ratio enhances gluconeogenesis
II. Insulin inhibits lipolysis, which in turn inhibits gluconeogenesis
III. Glucagon decreases [fructose 2,6-bisphosphate], enhancing gluconeogenesis
questions.e: All three are true. I: a rising glucagon:insulin ratio is the fasting signal that switches gluconeogenesis on. II: insulin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase, so lipolysis stops — that cuts the supply of glycerol (a gluconeogenic substrate) and of fatty acids, whose β-oxidation supplies the acetyl-CoA that allosterically ACTIVATES pyruvate carboxylase and the ATP that drives the pathway. Less lipolysis therefore means less gluconeogenesis. III: glucagon raises cAMP, PKA phosphorylates the bifunctional PFK-2/FBPase-2 enzyme, which switches it to its phosphatase mode; fructose-2,6-bisphosphate falls, which relieves the inhibition of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and removes the stimulation of PFK-1 — so gluconeogenesis is enhanced.

questions.q:
Assertion: The Krebs cycle is an amphibolic pathway
Reason: the Krebs cycle serves in both catabolic and anabolic pathways.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — that dual catabolic/anabolic role is exactly the definition of 'amphibolic'.

questions.q:
Fructokinase can be found in:
I. Liver
II. Brain
III. Eye
questions.e: Fructokinase (ketohexokinase) is concentrated in liver, kidney and intestine — not significantly in brain or eye.

questions.q: The non-oxidative phase of the PPP is best described as:
o: Reversible and does not touch NADPH
questions.e: The non-oxidative phase is entirely reversible and interconverts 3- to 7-carbon sugars without using or producing NADPH.

questions.q: Which enzyme classification describes chymotrypsinogen before it is activated?
questions.e: Chymotrypsinogen is a zymogen (proenzyme) -- an inactive precursor activated by proteolytic cleavage into chymotrypsin.

questions.q:
The synthesis of PEP from pyruvate requires:
I. Pyruvate carboxylase
II. PEP carboxykinase
III. Biotin
questions.e: Pyruvate carboxylase (biotin-dependent) converts pyruvate→OAA, then PEP carboxykinase converts OAA→PEP — all three are required.

questions.q:
Assertion: The Lineweaver-Burk plot makes it easier to calculate Km and Vmax of a reaction
Reason: the Lineweaver-Burk plot gives a straight line.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — plotting 1/v vs 1/[S] linearises the Michaelis-Menten curve, and reading the slope/intercepts of that straight line is exactly how Km and Vmax are extracted.

questions.q: The major dietary source of fructose is the disaccharide:
questions.e: Sucrose (cane sugar) contains equimolar fructose and glucose and is the major dietary source of fructose.

questions.q: The net ATP yield per glucose molecule through glycolysis is:
questions.e: 2 ATP are invested in the preparatory phase and 4 are produced in the payoff phase, giving a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose.

questions.q: The Krebs cycle is also known as the:
questions.e: The Krebs cycle is also called the Citric Acid Cycle or Tricarboxylic Acid (TCA) Cycle.

questions.q:
Assertion: Fats are preferred over glycogen as a source of energy
Reason: fat can be rapidly metabolized.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both false — glycogen/glucose is actually mobilized and metabolized FASTER (better for quick energy needs), while fat oxidation (β-oxidation) is comparatively slow to ramp up, even though it yields more energy per gram over the long haul.

questions.q: Heavy ethanol consumption can cause hypoglycemia mainly because ethanol metabolism:
o: Generates excess NADH, pushing pyruvate toward lactate and inhibiting gluconeogenesis
questions.e: Ethanol oxidation consumes large amounts of NAD+, generating excess NADH, which favors lactate formation over pyruvate and blocks gluconeogenesis.

questions.q: Metformin helps treat type 2 diabetes partly by suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis through activation of:
questions.e: Metformin activates AMPK, which suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis and increases insulin sensitivity.

questions.q:
PEP carboxykinase activity:
I. Is an inducible enzyme
II. Is enhanced by glucagon
III. Is enhanced by insulin
questions.e: PEPCK is induced/enhanced by glucagon (favouring gluconeogenesis) and REPRESSED, not enhanced, by insulin — III is false.

questions.q: Gluconeogenesis is the synthesis of glucose from:
o: Non-carbohydrate precursors such as lactate, glycerol, and amino acids
questions.e: Gluconeogenesis synthesizes new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors like lactate, pyruvate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids.

questions.q: GLUT4, the insulin-dependent glucose transporter, is found mainly in:
o: Red blood cells and the brain
questions.e: GLUT4 is the only insulin-dependent GLUT transporter, found in muscle and fat/adipose tissue.

questions.q:
Which of the following enzymes is/are involved in galactose metabolism?
I. Glucose-1-phosphatase
II. Galactose-4-epimerase (UDP-galactose 4-epimerase)
III. Glucose-6-phosphatase
questions.e: Note: 'Glucose 1 phosphate' as originally written isn't an enzyme, and is read here as a likely typo for 'glucose-6-phosphatase' — the enzyme that ultimately frees glucose from the pathway's end-product. 'Glucose-1-phosphatase' (i) isn't a standard enzyme of this pathway (phosphoglucomutase handles that interconversion instead), so I is excluded. UDP-galactose 4-epimerase (ii) is a genuine, essential enzyme of galactose metabolism (Leloir pathway).

questions.q:
Usefulness of enzyme kinetics includes:
I. Measuring rate of reactions
II. Use in clinical assays to detect disease
III. Helping understand the mechanism of catalysis
questions.e: All three are genuine applications of enzyme kinetics.

questions.q:
Assertion: All enzymes are immortal
Reason: all enzymes have half-lives.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion false (enzymes degrade over time, they aren't immortal). Reason true — having a half-life is exactly why they're not immortal.

questions.q:
The reaction catalyzed by PFK-1:
I. Is an example of an isomerization reaction
II. Catalyzes the phosphorylation of fructose-1-phosphate
III. Is allosterically inhibited by ATP and citrate
questions.e: I and II are false — PFK-1 phosphorylates fructose-6-phosphate (not F1P), and this is a phosphorylation, not an isomerization. III is true: ATP and citrate are classic allosteric inhibitors of PFK-1.

questions.q:
Assertion: Gluconeogenesis mainly occurs in the kidney
Reason: gluconeogenesis helps release glucose for use by cells.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion false — the liver is the main site of gluconeogenesis (the kidney contributes more only during prolonged fasting). The reason is essentially true: gluconeogenesis exists to supply glucose that other tissues can take up and use.

questions.q:
Assertion: The Krebs cycle is halted by fluoroacetate
Reason: fluoroacetate binds tightly to citrate synthase.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion true. Reason false — fluoroacetate is actually converted BY citrate synthase into fluorocitrate, and it's the fluorocitrate that then tightly inhibits aconitase, halting the cycle.

questions.q: The Cori cycle describes the recycling of:
o: Fatty acids between liver and adipose tissue
Lactate between muscle/erythrocytes and the liver
Amino acids between kidney and pancreas
Ketone bodies between brain and liver
questions.e: In the Cori cycle, lactate from anaerobic glycolysis in muscle/erythrocytes travels to the liver, is converted back to glucose, and returns to those tissues.

questions.q:
Assertion: The succinyl-CoA synthetase reaction is a substrate-level phosphorylation reaction
Reason: succinyl-CoA synthetase uses 5 enzymes and 3 cofactors.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion true (it directly generates GTP/ATP). Reason false — that '5 enzymes, 3 cofactors' description actually belongs to the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, not succinyl-CoA synthetase (a single enzyme).

questions.q: Catabolism is best described as:
o: Pathways that link anabolism and catabolism
questions.e: Catabolism breaks down complex molecules into smaller units and is generally energy-yielding.

questions.q:
Assertion: Fructolysis occurs mainly in the liver
Reason: fructolysis is mainly directed towards glycogen replenishment.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both statements are commonly taught as true, with liver fructose metabolism feeding glycogen stores — though note the deeper reason liver dominates fructolysis is really its unique enzyme complement (fructokinase, GLUT2, aldolase B).

questions.q:
Which statement(s) is/are TRUE about glycolysis?
I. Occurs only in aerobic organisms
II. ATPs are produced in the preparatory phase
III. Yields two molecules of ATP and NADH
questions.e: I and II are false (glycolysis occurs in both aerobic and anaerobic organisms; the preparatory phase CONSUMES 2 ATP, it doesn't produce any). III is true: net yield is 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose.

questions.q:
Salient features of classical galactosemia include:
I. Galactosuria
II. Development of cataract
III. Deficiency of galactokinase
questions.e: Corrected: classical galactosemia is caused by GALT deficiency, not galactokinase deficiency (that's Galactosemia type 2 — see Q48). So III is false; I and II (galactosuria, cataracts) are true.

questions.q:
Galactosemia type 2:
I. Leads to hepatic complications
II. Is an autosomal dominant disorder
III. Leads to the development of cataract
questions.e: Type 2 (galactokinase deficiency) is autosomal RECESSIVE and, unlike classical galactosemia, does NOT cause hepatic damage — it mainly causes cataracts. Only III is true.

questions.q: The committed, rate-limiting step of the PPP is catalyzed by:
questions.e: G6PD catalyzes the irreversible, committed first step of the oxidative phase, oxidizing glucose-6-phosphate and producing the first NADPH.

questions.q:
Assertion: Essential fructosuria results in fructose appearing in the urine
Reason: it is an autosomal recessive disorder.
o: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — fructokinase deficiency (essential fructosuria) is indeed autosomal recessive, and unmetabolized fructose does spill into urine. But the inheritance pattern doesn't explain WHY fructose ends up in urine — that's due to the enzyme deficiency itself, not how the condition is inherited.

questions.q: Thiamine deficiency (as in Beriberi) impairs the Krebs cycle mainly because thiamine is needed to make:
questions.e: Thiamine is required to synthesize TPP, a cofactor for both pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.

questions.q: Compared to hexokinase, glucokinase has:
questions.e: Glucokinase has a high Km (low affinity, only active when glucose is abundant) and high Vmax, unlike hexokinase's low Km/low Vmax profile.

questions.q: Biochemistry is best defined as the science concerned with:
questions.e: Biochemistry is the science concerned with the chemical basis of life -- the chemical constituents of living cells and the reactions they undergo.

questions.q:
Arsenic (arsenite) inhibits the following biosynthetic reactions:
I. Conversion of pyruvate to Acetyl-CoA
II. Conversion of α-ketoglutarate to succinyl-CoA
III. Conversion of citrate to isocitrate
questions.e: Arsenite binds the dithiol groups of lipoamide, disabling lipoamide-dependent complexes — PDH (i) and α-KGDH (ii). Aconitase (iii, citrate→isocitrate) doesn't use lipoamide and is unaffected by this mechanism.

questions.q: If ΔG for a reaction is negative and large, the reaction is:
questions.e: The assertion is true but the reason is false. Gluconeogenesis is NOT a direct reversal of glycolysis. Three glycolytic steps are irreversible — hexokinase/glucokinase, phosphofructokinase-1 and pyruvate kinase — and gluconeogenesis gets around them with four different enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase, then fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase. The other seven steps are the shared reversible ones.

questions.q: Sorbitol accumulation in diabetic tissues (lens, nerve, kidney) causes damage mainly through:
o: Osmotic swelling, since sorbitol cannot cross the membrane
questions.e: The assertion is true but the reason is false. Gluconeogenesis is NOT a direct reversal of glycolysis. Three glycolytic steps are irreversible — hexokinase/glucokinase, phosphofructokinase-1 and pyruvate kinase — and gluconeogenesis gets around them with four different enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase, then fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase. The other seven steps are the shared reversible ones.

questions.q: The three organizational forms of metabolic pathways are:
questions.e: Metabolic pathways can be organized as linear (e.g. serine biosynthesis), cyclic (e.g. citric acid cycle), or spiral (e.g. fatty acid synthesis).

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the condensation of acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to form citrate?
questions.e: Citrate synthase catalyzes the first step of the cycle, condensing acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate to form citrate.

questions.q:
Which of the following are by-products of fructolysis?
I. Pyruvate
II. Acetyl-CoA
III. Glycogen
questions.e: Fructose-derived DHAP/glyceraldehyde can be routed through glycolysis (→ pyruvate → acetyl-CoA) or gluconeogenesis (→ glycogen), so all three are plausible metabolic fates, especially in the liver.

questions.q: Who first introduced the term "Biochemistry", and in what year?
questions.e: German chemist Carl Neuberg introduced the term in 1903, from the Greek "bios" meaning life.

questions.q:
Anabolism:
I. Reactions do not require energy
II. Is a divergent process occurring in 3 stages
III. Is mainly powered by adenosine triphosphate
questions.e: I is false — anabolic (biosynthetic) reactions are energy-REQUIRING. II and III are true: anabolism diverges from a few precursors into many products, powered largely by ATP.

questions.q: The Krebs cycle is described as "amphibolic" because it:
o: Serves both catabolic and anabolic roles
questions.e: Amphibolic pathways serve dual roles -- both energy production (catabolic) and biosynthesis (anabolic); the Krebs cycle is the classic example.

questions.q: The Pentose Phosphate Pathway is also known as the:
questions.e: The PPP is also called the Hexose Monophosphate Shunt or the Phosphogluconate Pathway.

questions.q: What is the overall stoichiometric "cost" of synthesizing one glucose molecule via gluconeogenesis?
o: 6 high-energy phosphates (4 ATP + 2 GTP) and 2 NADH
questions.e: The pathway requires 4 ATP, 2 GTP, and 2 NADH per glucose molecule produced from 2 pyruvate -- confirming it is not a simple reversal of glycolysis.

questions.q:
Gluconeogenesis is facilitated by:
I. Acetyl-CoA
II. ATP
III. Citrate
questions.e: Acetyl-CoA allosterically activates pyruvate carboxylase, ATP supplies the energy the pathway needs, and citrate activates fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase — all three facilitate gluconeogenesis.

questions.q: Classical Galactosemia is caused by a deficiency of:
questions.e: Classical Galactosemia is due to deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase, causing galactosemia and galactosuria.

questions.q:
Fructose:
I. Entry into cells is insulin dependent
II. Intolerance leads to fructosuria and fructosaemia
III. In the liver, the first step of its metabolism is phosphorylation by fructokinase
questions.e: I is false — fructose uptake (GLUT5/GLUT2) is insulin-independent. II and III are true.

questions.q: Which enzyme converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate in the mitochondrion, bypassing pyruvate kinase?
questions.e: Pyruvate carboxylase carboxylates pyruvate to oxaloacetate, requiring ATP and biotin -- the first of two steps bypassing pyruvate kinase.

questions.q: In competitive inhibition, the inhibitor:
o: Binds only to the enzyme-substrate complex
Binds at an allosteric site distant from the active site
Resembles the substrate and competes for the active site
Permanently and covalently inactivates the enzyme
questions.e: A competitive inhibitor is a substrate analogue that competes with the true substrate for binding at the active site.

questions.q: In Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Phosphatase Deficiency, PDH remains permanently:
questions.e: Without functional PDH phosphatase, PDH stays phosphorylated and inactive, diverting glucose to lactic acid and causing lactic acidosis.

questions.q: How many NADH molecules are generated per turn of the Krebs cycle?
questions.e: Three NADH are generated per turn: at isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-KG dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase.

questions.q: Under anaerobic conditions, pyruvate is reduced to lactate mainly in order to:
o: Regenerate NAD+ so glycolysis can continue
Produce citrate for the TCA cycle
questions.e: Lactate dehydrogenase regenerates NAD+ from NADH, which is essential for glycolysis to keep running without oxygen.

questions.q: A multienzyme complex increases metabolic efficiency mainly through:
o: Channeling of intermediates directly between enzymes
questions.e: Multienzyme complexes cluster enzymes together so intermediates are channeled directly between active sites, reducing loss and speeding up the overall reaction sequence.

questions.q: Essential fructosuria is caused by a deficiency of:
questions.e: Essential fructosuria is due to hepatic fructokinase deficiency, an autosomal recessive but benign, asymptomatic condition.

questions.q: PPP-derived NADPH is especially critical in red blood cells because it:
o: Regenerates reduced glutathione to defend against oxidative damage
questions.e: RBCs lack mitochondria and depend entirely on PPP-derived NADPH to regenerate reduced glutathione (GSH) via glutathione reductase.

questions.q: In Hereditary Fructose Intolerance, the deficient enzyme is:
