questions.e: Hereditary Fructose Intolerance results from deficiency of aldolase B, causing fructose-1-phosphate to accumulate and trap phosphate.

questions.q: Besides ATP, which of the following is also considered an important cellular "energy currency"?
questions.e: GTP is another energy-rich molecule, important in processes like protein synthesis and signal transduction.

questions.q: According to the Induced Fit model of enzyme action, the active site:
o: Is rigid and pre-shaped like a lock
Is reshaped by interactions with the substrate
questions.e: Koshland's Induced Fit model proposes that the active site is flexible and is continuously reshaped as the substrate binds, unlike the rigid Lock and Key model.

questions.q: Which step of the Krebs cycle is a substrate-level phosphorylation, producing GTP/ATP?
questions.e: Succinyl-CoA synthetase converts succinyl-CoA to succinate, generating GTP (or ATP) directly via substrate-level phosphorylation.

questions.q: PFK-1 is allosterically inhibited by:
questions.e: PFK-1 is inhibited by high ATP and citrate (signs of abundant energy) and activated by AMP.

questions.q: Where in the cell does the Krebs cycle take place?
questions.e: The Krebs cycle enzymes reside in the mitochondrial matrix, the innermost compartment of the mitochondrion.

questions.q: In the polyol (sorbitol) pathway, aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol using:
questions.e: Aldose reductase uses NADPH to reduce glucose to sorbitol; sorbitol dehydrogenase then uses NAD+ to oxidize sorbitol to fructose.

questions.q: The major clinical symptom of galactokinase deficiency (Galactosemia type 2) is:
questions.e: Galactokinase deficiency causes galactitol accumulation in the lens, leading to cataracts in the first weeks/months of life.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyses the final cleavage step in beta-oxidation?
questions.e: β-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase, the enzyme that shortens the chain by two carbons.

questions.q: Which vitamin-derived coenzyme is required for the carboxylation of propionyl-CoA to D-methylmalonyl-CoA?
questions.e: Biotin — the standard cofactor for carboxylases. B12 is needed later, by the mutase.

questions.q: The conversion of D-methylmalonyl-CoA to L-methylmalonyl-CoA is catalysed by which enzyme?
o: Succinyl-CoA synthetase of the TCA cycle
questions.e: The epimerase simply flips the stereochemistry from D to L. Only then can the B12-dependent MUTASE rearrange L-methylmalonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA.

questions.q: What is the fate of acetyl-CoA produced during the beta-oxidation of fatty acids?
o: It enters the citric acid cycle
It is used in ketone body formation
questions.e: Both — TCA entry when oxaloacetate is available, ketogenesis in the liver when it is not (fasting, uncontrolled diabetes).

questions.q: Which intermediate of the citric acid cycle is used for the synthesis of fatty acids?
questions.e: Citrate carries acetyl units out to the cytosol, where ATP-citrate lyase releases acetyl-CoA. Citrate also allosterically activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase.

questions.q: What is the rate-limiting step of fatty acid oxidation?
o: Transport of fatty acids into the mitochondria
Activation of fatty acids to acyl-CoA
questions.e: The CPT I step of the carnitine shuttle — the regulated gate, inhibited by malonyl-CoA.

questions.q: Which of the following is not an intermediate of beta-oxidation?
questions.e: Malonyl-CoA belongs to fatty acid SYNTHESIS, and in fact blocks β-oxidation by inhibiting CPT I.

questions.q: How many ATP molecules are produced from the complete oxidation of one molecule of stearic acid (18:0)?
questions.e: C18 gives 9 acetyl-CoA × 10 = 90, plus 8 rounds × (1.5 + 2.5) = 32, total 122 — minus 2 ATP equivalents for activation = 120 net.

questions.q: What is the immediate fate of glycerol released during the breakdown of triacylglycerols?
o: It enters the citric acid cycle
questions.e: Glycerol kinase phosphorylates it to glycerol-3-phosphate. Only after that does it feed via DHAP into glycolysis or gluconeogenesis.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyses the phosphorylation of glycerol to glycerol-3-phosphate?
questions.e: Glycerol kinase, found in liver and kidney but essentially absent from adipose tissue — which is why adipocytes cannot recycle their own glycerol.

questions.q: Which fatty acid oxidation pathways occur in the peroxisomes?
questions.e: Peroxisomes run alpha-oxidation (branched acids such as phytanic acid) and beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids. Omega-oxidation is a smooth ER pathway using cytochrome P450.

questions.q: What is the primary difference between peroxisomal and mitochondrial beta-oxidation?
questions.e: All three differ: peroxisome vs matrix; VLCFA/branched vs long- and medium-chain; and peroxisomal acyl-CoA oxidase passes electrons straight to O₂, giving H₂O₂ instead of ATP.

questions.q: In the liver, excess acetyl-CoA produced during beta-oxidation can be converted to:
questions.e: Ketone bodies, when oxaloacetate has been drained into gluconeogenesis and the TCA cycle cannot absorb the acetyl-CoA.

questions.q: Which ketone body is most abundant in the blood during ketosis?
questions.e: β-hydroxybutyrate. A high mitochondrial NADH/NAD⁺ ratio during heavy fat oxidation pushes acetoacetate towards it.

questions.q: What is the role of hormone-sensitive lipase in lipid metabolism?
o: Hydrolyses triacylglycerols to free fatty acids
Converts fatty acids to ketone bodies
questions.e: It mobilises stored fat in adipocytes. Activated by glucagon and adrenaline via PKA phosphorylation; inhibited by insulin.

questions.q: Which pathway is used for the synthesis of fatty acids from acetyl-CoA?
questions.e: De novo lipogenesis in the cytosol — a distinct pathway with distinct enzymes, not β-oxidation run backwards.

questions.q: What enzyme converts malonyl-CoA to fatty acids during fatty acid synthesis?
questions.e: Fatty acid synthase, a multi-enzyme complex that repeatedly condenses malonyl-CoA units to build palmitate.

questions.q: Which molecule inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT I), regulating beta-oxidation?
questions.e: Malonyl-CoA — the reciprocal switch. When synthesis is running, malonyl-CoA is high and the mitochondrial gate is shut.

questions.q: How is acetyl-CoA transported from the mitochondria to the cytosol for fatty acid synthesis?
questions.e: The citrate shuttle. Acetyl-CoA itself cannot cross the inner membrane.

questions.q: The oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids occurs in:
questions.e: Peroxisomes shorten VLCFAs (C22 and above) before the product is handed to mitochondria. Failure of VLCFA import causes X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.

questions.q: Which enzyme is required for the breakdown of branched-chain fatty acids such as phytanic acid?
questions.e: A methyl group on the β carbon blocks normal β-oxidation, so alpha-hydroxylase (phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase — see Q67) removes one carbon first.

questions.q: The presence of which molecule indicates ongoing beta-oxidation in cells?
questions.e: Acetyl-CoA is the direct product of every round. Lactate and pyruvate point to glucose metabolism instead.

questions.q: Which molecule serves as the acyl-group acceptor in the reaction catalysed by carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT I)?
questions.e: CPT I moves the acyl group from CoA onto carnitine, forming acyl-carnitine for the translocase to carry across.

questions.q: Which fatty acid oxidation process produces hydrogen peroxide as a byproduct?
questions.e: Peroxisomal acyl-CoA oxidase gives its electrons to O₂ directly, making H₂O₂, which catalase then destroys. Energy is lost as heat rather than captured as ATP.

questions.q: Which clinical feature results from a deficiency in carnitine?
questions.e: Muscle weakness with cramps after exercise, plus lipid accumulation in muscle, because long-chain fatty acids cannot reach the matrix.

questions.q: The conversion of fatty acids to acyl-CoA requires how many ATP molecules?
questions.e: Two ATP EQUIVALENTS. One ATP is used, but it is cleaved to AMP + PPi, and hydrolysing PPi costs the cell a second high-energy bond.

questions.q: What is the primary function of adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL)?
questions.e: ATGL removes the first fatty acid. HSL then takes DAG to MAG, and monoacylglycerol lipase finishes the job.

questions.q: In what cellular location does the initial activation of fatty acids occur?
questions.e: On the cytosolic face of the outer mitochondrial membrane, by acyl-CoA synthetase — before any transport happens.

questions.q: Which enzyme is inhibited by malonyl-CoA to prevent the simultaneous occurrence of fatty acid synthesis and beta-oxidation?
questions.e: CPT I. This is the classic reciprocal-regulation point that stops a futile cycle.

questions.q: What is the consequence of a deficiency in acyl-CoA dehydrogenase?
questions.e: Blocking the first step stops the spiral, so less acetyl-CoA is made and ketogenesis fails — hence the hypoketotic hypoglycaemia of MCAD deficiency.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyses the rate-limiting step of ketogenesis?
questions.e: Mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase. Do not confuse it with the cytosolic isoform used in cholesterol synthesis.

questions.q: In the context of lipid metabolism, what does the acronym HSL stand for?
questions.e: Hormone-sensitive lipase — hormone-sensitive because glucagon and adrenaline switch it on through PKA.

questions.q: Which ketone body is spontaneously produced from acetoacetate?
questions.e: Acetone, by non-enzymatic decarboxylation. It is exhaled, giving the fruity breath of ketoacidosis, and cannot be used as fuel.

questions.q: Which enzyme is involved in the conversion of HMG-CoA to acetoacetate?
questions.e: HMG-CoA lyase splits HMG-CoA into acetoacetate and acetyl-CoA. HMG-CoA reductase is the cholesterol pathway (the statin target).

questions.q: The production of ketone bodies primarily occurs in which organ?
questions.e: The liver makes them but cannot use them — it lacks thiophorase (SCOT), so the ketones are exported to other tissues.

questions.q: Which enzyme converts acetoacetate to beta-hydroxybutyrate?
questions.e: β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase, using NADH. The reaction is reversible and reflects the mitochondrial redox state.

questions.q: Which enzyme deficiency leads to Refsum disease?
questions.e: Phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase, the peroxisomal alpha-oxidation enzyme. Phytanic acid accumulates, causing retinitis pigmentosa, neuropathy and ataxia.

questions.q: What is the primary energy source for the brain during prolonged fasting?
questions.e: Ketone bodies, which supply most of the brain's fuel after several days and spare muscle protein. Fatty acids cannot cross the blood-brain barrier in useful amounts.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a ketone body?
questions.e: Pyruvate is a glycolytic product. Note the naming quirk: β-hydroxybutyrate is counted as a ketone body although chemically it is not a ketone.

questions.q: The enzyme carnitine palmitoyltransferase II (CPT II) is located in:
questions.e: CPT II sits on the matrix side of the inner membrane and converts acyl-carnitine back to acyl-CoA. CPT I is on the outer membrane.

questions.q: Which metabolic process is upregulated during fasting and leads to the production of ketone bodies?
questions.e: β-oxidation floods the liver with acetyl-CoA, which is diverted to ketogenesis once oxaloacetate has been drawn off for gluconeogenesis.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyses the initial step in the beta-oxidation of fatty acids?
questions.e: Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, the FAD-linked first oxidation. (Repeat of Q4.)

questions.q: What is the primary role of adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL)?
questions.e: First step of lipolysis: TAG → DAG. (Repeat of Q57.)

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyses the phosphorylation of glycerol to glycerol-3-phosphate?
questions.e: Glycerol kinase, mainly hepatic. (Repeat of Q40.)

questions.q: What molecule inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT I) to regulate beta-oxidation?
questions.e: Malonyl-CoA. (Repeat of Q48.)

questions.q: The beta-oxidation of odd-chain fatty acids produces which additional product not formed during the oxidation of even-chain fatty acids?
questions.e: Propionyl-CoA, the 3-carbon leftover. It is glucogenic, so odd-chain fats do give a small yield of glucose carbon.

questions.q: Which clinical presentation is characteristic of medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency?
questions.e: Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia after fasting: fat cannot be burnt, so glucose is consumed and ketones fail to rise. It can present as sudden infant collapse.

questions.q: What is the main energy source for muscles during prolonged, moderate-intensity exercise?
questions.e: Fatty acids. Glycogen dominates early and at high intensity, but fat takes over as duration lengthens.

questions.q: Which enzyme converts acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA during fatty acid synthesis?
questions.e: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase — biotin-dependent, and the rate-limiting step of lipogenesis. Activated by citrate and insulin.

questions.q: During beta-oxidation, the double bond in the enoyl CoA intermediate is:
questions.e: Trans-Δ2. Natural unsaturated fatty acids carry CIS bonds, which is exactly why an isomerase is needed to process them.

questions.q: Which metabolic pathway is responsible for the conversion of propionyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA?
questions.e: Carboxylase (biotin) → epimerase → mutase (B12). This is why B12 deficiency raises methylmalonic acid.

questions.q: What is the main role of peroxisomes in fatty acid metabolism?
o: Conversion of fatty acids to glucose
Oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids
questions.e: They chain-shorten VLCFAs until mitochondria can finish the job.

questions.q: How many rounds of beta-oxidation are required to completely oxidise palmitic acid (C16:0)?
questions.e: n/2 − 1 = 7 rounds, giving 8 acetyl-CoA. The final round produces two acetyl-CoA from one 4-carbon acyl-CoA.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyses the conversion of L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA?
questions.e: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, one of only two human enzymes requiring vitamin B12 (the other is methionine synthase).

questions.q: Which enzyme is responsible for the initial activation of fatty acids to acyl-CoA?
questions.e: Acyl-CoA synthetase (thiokinase). Synthetase = uses ATP; dehydrogenase = removes hydrogens. Different jobs entirely.

questions.q: What is the consequence of a deficiency in carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT I)?
questions.e: Long-chain fatty acids never reach the matrix, so oxidation and ketogenesis both fail — presenting as hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with hepatomegaly.

questions.q: Which molecule is an inhibitor of acetyl-CoA carboxylase, thus regulating fatty acid synthesis?
questions.e: Palmitoyl-CoA, the end product — classic feedback inhibition. Citrate does the opposite and activates the enzyme.

questions.q: What is the primary source of NADPH for fatty acid synthesis?
questions.e: The oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway, with malic enzyme contributing a share as well.

questions.q: The accumulation of which molecule can inhibit the citric acid cycle during high rates of fatty acid oxidation?
questions.e: NADH inhibits isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, slowing the cycle and pushing acetyl-CoA towards ketogenesis.

questions.q: The oxidation of unsaturated fatty acids requires additional enzymes compared to saturated fatty acids. What are these additional enzymes?
questions.e: An isomerase repositions cis bonds to trans-Δ2; a 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase (NADPH-dependent) handles even-numbered double bonds in polyunsaturated acids.

questions.q: Which coenzyme is required for the conversion of propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA?
questions.e: Biotin, the CO₂ carrier for propionyl-CoA carboxylase. (Compare Q32.)

questions.q: What is the role of peroxisomes in the oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids?
questions.e: They perform the initial alpha-oxidation to strip the blocking methyl group; mitochondria then complete the breakdown.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyses the hydrolysis of stored triacylglycerols in adipose tissue?
questions.e: HSL acts on stored fat inside the adipocyte. Lipoprotein lipase works outside, on the capillary endothelium, clearing circulating chylomicrons and VLDL.

questions.q: During the oxidation of odd-chain fatty acids, what is the ultimate fate of propionyl-CoA?
questions.e: It becomes succinyl-CoA and enters the TCA cycle — making it the one genuinely glucogenic fragment from a fatty acid.

questions.q: What is the primary function of carnitine in fatty acid metabolism?
o: Activation of fatty acids to acyl-CoA
Synthesis of fatty acids from acetyl-CoA
Transport of fatty acids into mitochondria
Oxidation of fatty acids in peroxisomes
questions.e: Transport across the inner mitochondrial membrane. (Repeat of Q7.)

questions.q: How many ATP molecules are required for the activation of one molecule of palmitic acid (C16:0)?
questions.e: Two ATP equivalents — activation happens once for the whole molecule, not once per round.

questions.q: Which enzyme is responsible for the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA?
questions.e: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex — irreversible, which is why fat cannot be turned back into glucose.

questions.q: In fatty acid synthesis, what molecule is used to elongate the growing fatty acid chain?
questions.e: Malonyl-CoA donates each 2-carbon unit; its decarboxylation drives the condensation forward. Only the very first unit comes from acetyl-CoA.

questions.q: Which enzyme converts fatty acyl-CoA to fatty acyl-carnitine for transport into the mitochondria?
questions.e: CPT I on the outer membrane. CPT II reverses the swap once inside.

questions.q: What is the net ATP yield from the complete oxidation of one molecule of palmitic acid (C16:0)?
questions.e: 108 gross minus 2 ATP equivalents for activation = 106 net. Compare Q5: palmitoyl-CoA is pre-activated, so it gives the full 108.

questions.q: Chemiosmotic theory, proposed by Mitchell, states that coupling of electron transfer to ATP synthesis is:
o: Direct, by physical contact between complexes and ATP synthase

questions.e: The coupling is indirect: electron transport creates a proton electrochemical gradient, and it is the return flow of those protons that drives ATP synthesis.

questions.q: As protons are driven out of the matrix, the matrix becomes:
o: More alkaline and negatively charged relative to the cytosol
questions.e: Proton ejection raises matrix pH and leaves the matrix negatively charged relative to the cytosol, generating both a pH gradient and a membrane potential.

questions.q: The combined pH gradient and electrical gradient across the inner membrane is known as the:
questions.e: Together the chemical (pH) and electrical gradients constitute the proton-motive force, which drives protons back into the matrix through ATP synthase.

questions.q: Why is ATP synthase essential to the coupling process?
o: It is the only channel through which H⁺ can diffuse back into the matrix
It pumps protons out of the matrix
questions.e: ATP synthase provides the only route for protons to return to the matrix. Because every returning proton must pass through it, the exergonic flow is harnessed to make ATP.

questions.q: Which part of ATP synthase forms the membrane proton channel?
questions.e: F₀ is the membrane-embedded proton channel; F₁ is the catalytic head where ADP and Pi are joined. Protons flowing through F₀ cause rotation that drives catalysis in F₁.

questions.q: After ATP is synthesised in the mitochondrion, it must:
o: Be stored in the intermembrane space
Exit to the cytosol, while ADP and Pi re-enter the mitochondrion
questions.e: ATP is exported to the cytosol for cellular work, while ADP and Pi produced by its hydrolysis re-enter to be recycled — a continuous exchange across the inner membrane.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Electron transport and ATP synthesis are said to be 'coupled'.
Reason (R): Electrons are physically transferred from the ETC complexes directly onto ADP to form ATP.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.e: The assertion is true but the reason is false. Coupling is indirect: the link between electron transport and ATP synthesis is the proton gradient, not any direct electron transfer to ADP.

questions.q: By convention, the oxidation of 1 FADH₂ yields approximately:
questions.e: FADH₂ yields about 1.5–2 ATP because it enters at Complex II and bypasses the proton pumping of Complex I. NADH yields about 2.5–3 ATP.

questions.q: Substrate-level phosphorylation differs from oxidative phosphorylation in that it:
o: Transfers a phosphoryl group directly from a substrate to ADP or GDP
Occurs only in the inner mitochondrial membrane
questions.e: Substrate-level phosphorylation transfers a phosphoryl group directly from a substrate to a nucleoside diphosphate. It occurs in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle and can proceed with or without oxygen.

questions.q: In the overall equation of aerobic respiration, the water produced originates from:
o: O₂ after it accepts electrons in the ETC
questions.e: Water is formed at Complex IV when O₂ accepts electrons and picks up protons — which is why oxygen is indispensable.

questions.q: Which product of cellular respiration is NOT shown in the summary equation C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP?
questions.e: Heat is produced but omitted from the equation, as are the regenerated carriers NAD⁺ and FAD.

questions.q: Rotenone, an insecticide, inhibits the electron transport chain at:
questions.e: Rotenone blocks Complex I. Amytal/amobarbital, MPP⁺ and piericidin act at the same site.

questions.q: Cyanide, azide and carbon monoxide inhibit oxidative phosphorylation by blocking:
questions.e: These agents bind tightly to the ferric (Fe³⁺) form of haem a₃ in Complex IV, halting the reduction of oxygen and therefore the entire chain.

questions.q:
Which of the following is/are the common monosaccharide(s)?:
I. Cellulose
II. Glucose
III. Fructose
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Glucose and fructose are monosaccharides (simple sugars). Cellulose is a polysaccharide (a polymer of glucose units), not a monosaccharide, so statement I is false.

questions.q: Enzyme complex involved in alcoholic fermentation is:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Zymase is the multi-enzyme complex (in yeast) that converts sugars into ethanol and CO₂ during alcoholic fermentation.

questions.q: Oligomycin and DCCD inhibit oxidative phosphorylation by:
o: Blocking the proton channel of ATP synthase
questions.e: Oligomycin and DCCD are phosphorylation inhibitors that plug the F₀ proton channel. DCCD binds a c subunit and sterically hinders rotation of F₀.

questions.q: Atractyloside exerts its effect by inhibiting the:
questions.e: Atractyloside blocks the ATP/ADP antiporter, so ATP cannot leave the matrix and ADP cannot enter — indirectly halting oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.q: Why do inhibitors of ATP synthase also inhibit electron transport when coupling is intact?
o: Protons cannot return, so the gradient becomes too steep to pump against and the chain stalls
They bind directly to Complex I
questions.e: If protons cannot flow back through ATP synthase, the proton-motive force builds until further pumping is impossible, so electron flow stops. Respiration inhibitors such as cyanide, by contrast, suppress oxygen uptake regardless of coupling.

questions.q: An uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation acts by:
o: Carrying protons across the inner membrane, dissipating the gradient
Preventing oxygen from binding Complex IV
Blocking electron flow at Complex III
questions.e: Uncouplers are hydrophobic molecules with a dissociable proton. They shuttle H⁺ back across the membrane, collapsing the proton-motive force without blocking the chain itself.

questions.q: In the presence of an uncoupler, which of the following occurs?
o: Electron transport stops and ATP synthesis continues
Electron transport continues and oxygen is consumed, but ATP is not formed and energy is released as heat
Both electron transport and oxygen consumption cease
questions.e: Uncoupled mitochondria continue to transport electrons and consume NADH and oxygen — in fact respiration is stimulated — but the energy escapes as heat instead of being captured as ATP.

questions.q: Thermogenin, found in brown adipose tissue of newborns and hibernating mammals, functions as:
o: A physiological uncoupling protein producing non-shivering thermogenesis
questions.e: Thermogenin is the body's own regulated uncoupler. It dissipates the gradient deliberately to generate heat — costly in ATP terms, but valuable for warming the organism.

questions.q: 2,4-Dinitrophenol was once marketed as a diet drug but was withdrawn because:
o: It uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation, causing dangerous hyperthermia
questions.e: As an unregulated chemical uncoupler, DNP wastes fuel as heat. Users developed temperatures around 107 °F and deaths occurred, so it was abandoned as a weight-loss agent.

questions.q:
Which of the following are classified as uncouplers of oxidative phosphorylation?I. 2,4-Dinitrophenol
II. Thermogenin
III. Salicylate
IV. Oligomycin
questions.e: DNP, thermogenin, dicoumarol, CCCP, salicylate and Ca²⁺ act as uncouplers. Oligomycin is not an uncoupler — it is an ATP synthase inhibitor.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the presence of an uncoupler, oxygen consumption by mitochondria increases.
Reason (R): Dissipating the proton gradient removes the back-pressure that normally restrains electron transport.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.e: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion: with the gradient collapsed, the chain is free to run faster, so respiration is stimulated even though no ATP is produced.

questions.q: What is the terminal electron acceptor of the mitochondrial electron transport chain?
questions.e: Oxygen sits at the end of the chain, accepting electrons at Complex IV and picking up protons to form water.

questions.q: If oxygen becomes unavailable, the immediate consequence is that:
o: ATP synthase reverses to make NADH
The ETC backs up, proton pumping stops and ATP production ceases
questions.e: Without a terminal acceptor the carriers remain reduced, electron flow halts, the gradient collapses and ATP synthesis stops — leading rapidly to cell dysfunction and death.

questions.q: Which of the following can serve as a terminal electron acceptor in anaerobic respiration?
questions.e: Microbial ecosystems use alternatives such as NO₃⁻, Mn⁴⁺, Fe³⁺, SO₄²⁻ and CO₂. Oxygen yields the most energy (ΔG ≈ −479 kJ/mol); sulfate the least (≈ −77 kJ/mol).

questions.q: Mitochondrial diseases are inherited:
questions.e: Only the mother contributes mitochondrial DNA, so all offspring of an affected female are affected, whereas an affected male transmits nothing.

questions.q: Mitochondrial diseases most often present as neuropathies and myopathies because:
o: Brain and muscle are highly dependent on oxidative phosphorylation
Only nerve and muscle contain Complex IV
Mitochondrial DNA is only found in nerve and muscle
questions.e: Brain and muscle rely most heavily on oxidative phosphorylation, so defects in mitochondrially encoded ETC components affect them first and most severely.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): All the children of a woman with a mitochondrial disorder are at risk of the condition.
Reason (R): Mitochondrial DNA is contributed to the zygote almost exclusively by the ovum.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.e: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Sperm mitochondria are located in the tail and are lost at fertilisation, so mitochondrial DNA is inherited maternally.

questions.q: Statins have been associated with mitochondrial effects including:
o: Reduction of coenzyme Q10 levels and inhibition of respiratory chain complexes
questions.e: Reported effects include reduced coenzyme Q10, inhibition of respiratory complexes, increased oxidative stress and dysregulated Ca²⁺ metabolism — offered as one explanation for statin-associated muscle symptoms.

questions.q:
Which statements about the inner mitochondrial membrane are correct?I. It is impermeable to protons under normal conditions
II. It contains the electron transport complexes and ATP synthase
III. It is folded into cristae
IV. It is freely permeable to NADH
questions.e: The inner membrane is impermeable (including to NADH, which is why shuttles are needed), contains the respiratory machinery, and is folded into cristae.

questions.q: Which statement(s) about the blue top (sodium citrate) tube is/are TRUE?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Blue top citrate tubes are for coagulation/PT studies (ii ✓), contain ~3.2–3.8% trisodium citrate (iii ✓), and citrate chelates calcium = clotting factor IV (iv ✓). It is NOT suited for trace-element/toxicology work (i is false — those need special metal-free tubes).

II. Uses UDP-glucose as the activated donor
III. Glycogen phosphorylase catalyses chain extension
IV. Glycogen synthase catalyses chain extension
questions.e: 2 and 4 → C. UDP-glucose is the donor and synthase extends the chain; phosphorylase is a breakdown enzyme, and Pi is used in breakdown not synthesis.

questions.q: Glucagon triggers glycogen breakdown in which tissue?
questions.e: The liver responds to glucagon (a 'blood-sugar-is-low' signal). Muscle has no glucagon receptors.

questions.q: Epinephrine (adrenaline) acts on:
questions.e: The 'fight-or-flight' signal mobilises both stores at once.

questions.q: In muscle, glycogen phosphorylase b is switched on allosterically (without hormones) by:
questions.e: Rising AMP signals that ATP is running low, so muscle can start breaking glycogen instantly during hard exercise — a low-fuel warning light.

questions.q: In muscle, which ion links phosphorylase activation directly to contraction?
questions.e: The same Ca²⁺ that triggers contraction also activates phosphorylase kinase — fuel supply matched to the moment of demand.

questions.q:

I. It lacks glucose-6-phosphatase
II. It cannot directly raise blood glucose
III. It supplies G6P for the muscle's own glycolysis
IV. It is broken down in response to glucagon
questions.e: 1,2,3 → A. Statement 4 is false: muscle has no glucagon receptors, so glucagon does not act on it.

questions.q: The ACTIVE form of glycogen phosphorylase is:
questions.e: Phosphorylase a = phosphorylated = active. Adding phosphate flips the breakdown enzyme ON.

questions.q: The ACTIVE form of glycogen synthase is:
questions.e: Synthase a = dephosphorylated = active. Note the OPPOSITE logic: the same phosphate that turns breakdown ON turns synthesis OFF — one switch, coordinated so the cell never builds and burns at once.

questions.q: The intracellular second messenger of the breakdown cascade is:
questions.e: Glucagon/epinephrine → adenylate cyclase → cAMP, the relay signal inside the cell.

questions.q: cAMP activates which enzyme?
questions.e: cAMP → PKA → phosphorylase kinase → phosphorylase. A cascade that AMPLIFIES: one hormone molecule triggers a chain that mobilises millions of glucose units — like one alarm switch activating a whole relay of pumps.

questions.q: Which enzyme reverses the cascade by removing phosphate groups (favouring synthesis, storage)?
questions.e: PP1 dephosphorylates: it turns phosphorylase OFF and synthase ON — the 'stand-down' after the alarm.

questions.q: Glucose-6-phosphate acts as an allosteric signal that:
questions.e: Plenty of G6P = plenty of fuel, so the cell shifts to STORE: synthase ON, phosphorylase OFF.

questions.q: A central whole-body role of LIVER glycogen is to:
questions.e: Liver glycogen is the buffer/reservoir that keeps blood glucose steady during fasting — filling when fed, draining when fasting.

questions.q: Von Gierke disease (Type Ia) results from deficiency of:
questions.e: No G6-phosphatase → liver can't release glucose → fasting hypoglycaemia + enlarged, glycogen-loaded liver.

questions.q: McArdle disease (Type V) is caused by a defect in:
questions.e: Muscle can't break its own glycogen → exercise-induced cramps, pain, and myoglobin in urine.

questions.q:

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the first step of glycolysis?

questions.q: This enzyme of the TCA cycle generates a reducing equivalent:
questions.e: Isocitrate dehydrogenase oxidatively decarboxylates isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate, generating the first NADH of the cycle.

questions.q: Which TCA enzyme does NOT generate a diffusible reducing equivalent?
questions.e: Succinate dehydrogenase's FAD stays permanently bound and passes electrons directly to Complex II/ubiquinone — it never releases a free FADH₂, unlike the NADH-producing steps.

questions.q: Malic enzyme converts:
questions.e: Malic enzyme catalyses the oxidative decarboxylation of malate: malate + NADP⁺ → pyruvate + CO₂ + NADPH — a major source of cytosolic NADPH for fatty acid synthesis. The paper printed this option backwards (pyruvate to malate); it now reads in the direction the enzyme actually runs.

questions.q: The Glyoxylate cycle uses ___ derived Acetyl-CoA:
questions.e: β-oxidation of stored fat produces the acetyl-CoA that the glyoxylate cycle converts into carbohydrate precursors (classic in germinating oil-seeds).

questions.q: The Glyoxylate cycle uses ___ Acetyl-CoA per turn of each cycle:
questions.e: Two acetyl-CoA molecules combine (via citrate synthase + malate synthase) each turn — unlike the TCA cycle's one.

questions.q: Which statement(s) about the gray top/oxalate-fluoride tube is/are TRUE?
questions.e: Fluoride inhibits enolase (preserving glucose) while oxalate chelates calcium (ii ✓); the tube is processed within roughly 30 min–2 hrs (iii ✓) and is used mainly for glucose estimation (iv ✓). It does NOT use silica (i is false — that's the gold-top additive).
