questions.q: The Pentose phosphate pathway is organized as a:
questions.e: ⚠️ Contested. The paper’s key says linear, and the oxidative branch certainly is. But many texts class the PPP as CYCLIC, because the non-oxidative branch feeds carbon back so that 6 glucose-6-phosphate can regenerate 5 glucose-6-phosphate + 6 CO₂ — a genuine loop. Check which your lecturer wants; if the classification trio is linear / cyclic / spiral, “cyclic” is the commoner answer for the PPP.

questions.q: Enzyme inhibitors:
o: Increase the rate of the reaction
Do not affect the rate of the reaction
Decrease the rate of the reaction
questions.e: By definition, an inhibitor reduces enzyme activity and therefore decreases reaction rate.

questions.q: The 'lock and key' model of enzymes suggested that ___ were rigid in nature:
questions.e: Fischer's lock-and-key model pictured the enzyme's active site as a rigid, pre-shaped mould that only a perfectly complementary substrate could fit — later revised by Koshland's induced-fit model.

questions.q: The general term used for the anaerobic degradation of glucose to obtain energy is:
questions.e: Fermentation is the general term for anaerobic glucose breakdown for energy (e.g. lactic acid or alcoholic fermentation).

questions.q: In essential fructosuria, there is reduced or complete absence of:
questions.e: Essential fructosuria = fructokinase deficiency, so fructose is never phosphorylated and simply spills into urine unchanged (harmless, unlike Hereditary Fructose Intolerance, which is aldolase B/F1P-aldolase deficiency).

questions.q: The main transporter of fructose in the intestinal cells is:
questions.e: GLUT5 is the fructose-specific transporter on the apical membrane of intestinal enterocytes; GLUT2 then moves fructose out across the basolateral membrane (and is the main liver fructose transporter).

questions.q: An enzyme used in both glycolysis and gluconeogenesis is:
questions.e: 3-phosphoglycerate kinase catalyzes a freely reversible reaction, so it's shared by both pathways; the other options are each committed/irreversible and specific to only one direction (glucose-6-phosphatase and PFK-1/hexokinase/pyruvate kinase are each exclusive to one pathway).

questions.q: Which of the following influences feedback inhibition?
questions.e: Feedback inhibition is driven by the pathway's own end-PRODUCT accumulating and shutting down an earlier (usually the first committed) enzyme in that same pathway.

questions.q: The conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate:
o: Is the second priming step in glycolysis
questions.e: Hexokinase/glucokinase (not pyruvate kinase) catalyzes this first priming step, and like most kinases it requires Mg²⁺ to coordinate the ATP phosphates during phosphoryl transfer.

questions.q: The rate-limiting step of glycolysis is:
questions.e: Step 3 is the PFK-1 reaction (F6P → F1,6BP) — the committed, rate-limiting, allosterically regulated step of glycolysis.

questions.q: An enzyme and a coenzyme together is called:
questions.e: Apoenzyme (protein) + coenzyme = holoenzyme, the fully active complex — this is essentially the same relationship tested in Q116, just from the other direction.

questions.q: The specificity of enzymes is a result of:
questions.e: Specificity comes from the precise complementary fit between active site and substrate — shape plus the matching arrangement of charged/polar groups. Among these single-word options, charges is the best fit (though in fuller terms it's really 'shape and charge complementarity').

questions.q: An activated enzyme made of a polypeptide chain and a cofactor is:
questions.e: Apoenzyme (protein) + cofactor = holoenzyme, the complete catalytically active form.

questions.q: Who proposed the 'lock and key' model to study enzyme-substrate interaction?
questions.e: Emil Fischer proposed the lock-and-key model in 1894/1898, picturing the enzyme's active site as a rigid, pre-shaped mould.

questions.q: Competitive inhibitors stop an enzyme from working by:
o: Changing the shape of the enzyme
Blocking the active site of the enzyme
Combining with the product of the reaction
questions.e: Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate closely enough to occupy (block) the active site, competing directly with the real substrate for that same site.

questions.q: The enzyme minus its coenzyme is referred to as the:
questions.e: Remove the coenzyme/cofactor from a holoenzyme and you're left with the apoenzyme (the protein-only, inactive part).

questions.q: An inhibitor that changes the overall shape and chemistry of an enzyme is known as a(n):
questions.e: Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere on the enzyme (not the active site) and distort its overall conformation, indirectly disabling catalysis.

questions.q: An enzyme is generally named by adding ___ to the end of the name of the ___:
o: '-ase', cell in which it is found
questions.e: E.g. lactase (acts on lactose), sucrase (acts on sucrose) — the substrate's name plus the suffix '-ase'.

questions.q: Enzymes function as:
questions.e: Enzymes are proteins (organic molecules) that catalyze reactions — organic catalysts.

questions.q: The first step in any enzyme-catalysed reaction is the formation of a specific association between the molecules called an:
questions.e: Enzyme and substrate first come together as the enzyme-substrate (ES) complex before the reaction proceeds.

questions.q: Which one inactivates an enzyme by indirectly changing the shape of the active site of an enzyme?
questions.e: Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and distort the enzyme's overall shape, which indirectly disrupts the active site too.

questions.q: Enzymes are highly specific for a given substrate due to the shape of their:
questions.e: The precise 3D shape (and charge pattern) of the active site is what makes each enzyme substrate-specific.

questions.q: The 'lock and key hypothesis' attempts to explain the mechanism of:
questions.e: It's a model for why each enzyme works on only its own specific substrate(s).

questions.q: What is a cofactor?
questions.e: Cofactors span both inorganic metal ions (activators) and organic molecules (coenzymes).

questions.q: Which antibiotic blocks the active site of an enzyme that many bacteria use to make cell walls?
questions.e: Penicillin blocks the transpeptidase enzyme that cross-links peptidoglycan in bacterial cell walls. (Cephalosporins work similarly, but penicillin is the classic textbook answer here.)

questions.q: Which of the following enzymes would digest a fat?
questions.e: Lipase hydrolyzes fats (triglycerides) into fatty acids and glycerol/monoacylglycerol.

questions.q: A certain enzyme will hydrolyze egg white but not starch. Which statement best explains this observation?
o: Starch molecules are too large to be hydrolyzed
Enzyme molecules are specific in their actions
Egg white acts as a coenzyme for hydrolysis
Starch is composed of amino acids
questions.e: Working on protein (egg white) but not carbohydrate (starch) is a textbook demonstration of enzyme substrate specificity.

questions.q: When a molecule binds to an area of an enzyme that is not the active site, and changes the shape of the enzyme so it no longer works, this is called:
questions.e: Binding away from the active site and disabling the enzyme via a shape change is the definition of non-competitive (allosteric) inhibition.

questions.q: The enzyme ___ catalyses an anaplerotic reaction:
questions.e: Pyruvate carboxylase (pyruvate → oxaloacetate) is the classic anaplerotic reaction, replenishing TCA cycle intermediates. ('Malate carboxykinase' and 'malate synthetase' aren't standard enzyme names — likely mean PEP carboxykinase and malate synthase respectively, neither of which is anaplerotic in the mammalian TCA sense.)

questions.q: The step at which substrate-level phosphorylation occurs is catalysed by which enzyme?
questions.e: Succinyl-CoA synthetase (synthase) directly generates GTP/ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation as succinyl-CoA is converted to succinate — the TCA cycle's only substrate-level phosphorylation step.

questions.q: The TCA cycle is:
questions.e: Amphibolic — it serves both catabolic (energy-releasing) and anabolic (precursor-supplying) roles.

questions.q: The TCA cycle is NOT inhibited by:
questions.e: Fluoride inhibits enolase — a glycolytic enzyme, not a TCA cycle enzyme — so it doesn't directly inhibit the TCA cycle itself. Fluoroacetyl-CoA (via fluorocitrate) blocks aconitase, and PDH deficiency starves the cycle of acetyl-CoA, so both of those genuinely impair it.

questions.q: The rate-limiting enzyme for the Pentose Phosphate Pathway is:
questions.e: G6PD catalyses the first, committed step of the PPP and is its main regulatory/rate-limiting enzyme — its deficiency (G6PD deficiency) is also a well-known cause of haemolytic anaemia.

questions.q:
Assertion: Metabolism in living organisms is very important
Reason: metabolism is organized into several discrete pathways.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both statements are true, but organization into pathways doesn't explain WHY metabolism is important — that's about sustaining life processes.

questions.q:
Assertion: Enzymes are known as biological catalysts
Reason: enzymes speed up biological reactions.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true, and speeding up reactions without being consumed is literally the definition of a catalyst — correct explanation.

questions.q:
Assertion: Hexokinase is an isomerase
Reason: hexokinase is involved in the transfer of a functional group from one molecule to another.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Hexokinase is a transferase/kinase (EC 2.7.1.1), not an isomerase — assertion false. The reason correctly describes what a transferase/kinase does (transfers the phosphate group) — reason true.

questions.q:
Assertion: All enzymes are immortal
Reason: all enzymes have half-lives.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion false (enzymes degrade over time, they aren't immortal). Reason true — having a half-life is exactly why they're not immortal.

questions.q:
Assertion: The cells in the eye do not solely depend on glycolysis for energy supply
Reason: the cells in the eye have mitochondria which serve as an alternative source of energy.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both statements are true, and the reason is the explanation. The eye is not one tissue: the retina is among the most metabolically active tissues in the body, and the inner segments of its photoreceptors are packed with mitochondria running oxidative phosphorylation. The retinal pigment epithelium, corneal endothelium and ciliary epithelium are mitochondria-rich too. Having mitochondria is precisely why these cells are not restricted to glycolysis — so the reason correctly explains the assertion. (The one exception is the LENS: its mature fibre cells lose their mitochondria to stay transparent, and the avascular lens does rely on anaerobic glycolysis. That special case does not apply to ‘cells in the eye’ in general.)

questions.q:
Assertion: Fructolysis occurs mainly in the liver
Reason: fructolysis is mainly directed towards glycogen replenishment.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both statements are commonly taught as true, with liver fructose metabolism feeding glycogen stores — though note the deeper reason liver dominates fructolysis is really its unique enzyme complement (fructokinase, GLUT2, aldolase B).

questions.q:
Assertion: Lactose intolerance results in bloating of the stomach after ingestion of lactose
Reason: lactose intolerance results from a lack of lactase.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — without lactase, undigested lactose ferments in the gut, producing gas and bloating; a correct explanation.

questions.q:
Assertion: The Krebs cycle derives its acetyl units from only carbohydrates
Reason: the Krebs cycle is solely carbohydrate dependent.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both false — acetyl-CoA feeding the cycle can come from carbohydrates, fats, and proteins; the TCA cycle is amphibolic, not carbohydrate-exclusive.

questions.q:
Assertion: Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Deficiency results in metabolic acidosis
Reason: the metabolic acidosis is a result of the build-up of pyruvic acid.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both are true, and the reason explains the assertion. In pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle, so it accumulates and is shunted to lactate and alanine — producing the metabolic (lactic) acidosis. The pyruvate build-up is the direct upstream cause, and pyruvic acid (pKₐ ≈ 2.5) is itself fully dissociated at body pH. This is why PDH deficiency characteristically shows a NORMAL lactate:pyruvate ratio — both rise together — unlike respiratory-chain defects, where lactate rises far more than pyruvate and the ratio is high.

questions.q:
Assertion: The isocitrate dehydrogenase reaction of the TCA cycle produces the first reducing equivalent of the pathway
Reason: the isocitrate dehydrogenase reaction produces NADPH.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion true (it is indeed the first NADH-producing step). Reason false — the mitochondrial TCA-cycle isocitrate dehydrogenase produces NADH, not NADPH.

questions.q:
Assertion: The Krebs cycle is an amphibolic pathway
Reason: the Krebs cycle serves in both catabolic and anabolic pathways.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — that dual catabolic/anabolic role is exactly the definition of 'amphibolic'.

questions.q:
Assertion: Fluoride is used as an additive in blood fructose checks
Reason: it is an inhibitor in fructolysis.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both false as written — fluoride-oxalate tubes are used to preserve blood GLUCOSE (not fructose) samples, and fluoride works by inhibiting enolase, a glycolysis enzyme, not a fructolysis enzyme (fructokinase, aldolase B, triokinase). This looks like a typo for 'glucose check' in the original question.

questions.q:
Assertion: Gluconeogenesis mainly occurs in the kidney
Reason: gluconeogenesis helps release glucose for use by cells.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion false — the liver is the main site of gluconeogenesis (the kidney contributes more only during prolonged fasting). The reason is essentially true: gluconeogenesis exists to supply glucose that other tissues can take up and use.

questions.q:
Assertion: Severe alcoholism can affect α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
Reason: α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase requires thiamine pyrophosphate as a cofactor.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true (note: the original question says 'thymine pyrophosphate', which looks like a typo for 'thiamine pyrophosphate' — thymine is a DNA base, not a cofactor). Chronic alcoholism causes thiamine deficiency, which impairs the TPP-dependent α-KGDH — a correct explanation.

questions.q:
Dihydrolipoamide acetyltransferase (E2) uses cofactor(s):
I. Thiamine Pyrophosphate (TPP)
II. Lipoamide
III. CoASH
IV. FAD
V. NAD
o: i, ii, iii and v only
questions.e: E2 uses its lipoamide arm to accept the acetyl group and transfer it to CoASH — items ii and iii, option C.

questions.q:
Thiamine deficiency:
I. Impairs neurological function
II. Decreases the activity of pyruvate dehydrogenase
III. Decreases the activity of α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
IV. Decreases the activity of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
V. Decreases ATP production and increases pyruvate levels
o: i, ii, iii and v only
questions.e: Thiamine (as TPP) is needed by PDH and α-KGDH, not by G6PD (which is NADP⁺-dependent, unrelated to TPP) — so iv is excluded. i, ii, iii, v are all true → option B.

questions.q: In the seminal vesicles, glucose is converted to:
questions.e: Seminal vesicles synthesize fructose (from glucose) as the main energy fuel for sperm in seminal fluid.

questions.q: The end product of fructolysis in the muscles is:
questions.e: Muscle does not express fructokinase — that enzyme is essentially confined to liver, kidney and intestine. In muscle, fructose is phosphorylated by HEXOKINASE to fructose-6-phosphate, which then joins glycolysis at the phosphofructokinase step. (Fructose-1-phosphate, which the paper’s key gave, is the LIVER product, and this same paper’s Passco Q55 states the muscle route correctly.)

questions.q: Which of the following is TRUE about enzymes?
questions.e: Enzymes bind substrate (not product), not all need cofactors, and they're regenerated unchanged after catalysis — but they CAN be denatured by heat, pH, etc.

questions.q: The TCA cycle:
o: Uses 2 molecules of acetyl-CoA per turn of the cycle
Is coupled with the release of NADPH
questions.e: Corrected: the TCA cycle uses only ONE acetyl-CoA per turn, is net energy-YIELDING (not consuming), and produces NADH (not NADPH). It does produce high-energy compounds: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP/ATP per turn.

questions.q: Which TCA intermediate is NOT used up by other synthetic pathways?
questions.e: Citrate feeds fatty-acid synthesis, succinyl-CoA feeds heme synthesis, oxaloacetate feeds gluconeogenesis/amino acids — malate is mainly retained within the cycle/shuttle systems.

questions.q: The TCA cycle is a/an ___ pathway:
questions.e: Amphibolic: it serves both catabolic (energy release) and anabolic (biosynthetic precursor supply) roles.

questions.q: The TCA cycle is NOT inhibited by:
questions.e: Fluoride inhibits enolase — a glycolytic enzyme, not a TCA cycle enzyme. Fluoroacetate (via fluorocitrate) blocks aconitase, and PDH deficiency starves the cycle of acetyl-CoA.

questions.q: Comparing the Glyoxylate cycle to the TCA cycle, it bypasses the ___ of the TCA cycle:
questions.e: Isocitrate lyase cleaves isocitrate straight to succinate + glyoxylate, skipping the two oxidative decarboxylation steps (isocitrate DH & α-KGDH) and their CO₂ loss.

questions.q: Which statement(s) about the blue top (sodium citrate) tube is/are TRUE?
questions.e: Blue top citrate tubes are for coagulation/PT studies (ii ✓), contain ~3.2–3.8% trisodium citrate (iii ✓), and citrate chelates calcium = clotting factor IV (iv ✓). It is NOT suited for trace-element/toxicology work (i is false — those need special metal-free tubes).

questions.q: Which statement(s) about the green top/heparin tube is/are TRUE?
questions.e: Heparin tubes are used for chromosome/cytogenetic studies (i ✓) and are anticoagulant tubes (ii ✓); heparinized plasma is also widely used for rapid/STAT chemistry panels including glucose (iv ✓). Heparin tubes have NO clot activator coating (iii is false — that's the opposite of an anticoagulant tube's purpose).

questions.q: HCl has specific gravity 1.5 and purity 78% (MW = 36.5 g/mol). What volume is needed to prepare a 1M solution?
questions.e: Stock molarity = (1.5 × 1000 × 0.78) / 36.5 ≈ 32.05 M. To get 1 mol in solution: V = 1000 mL × 1M / 32.05M ≈ 31.2 mL → 31 mL.

questions.q: Glycolysis is classified (metabolically) as:
questions.e: Glycolysis breaks glucose down — a catabolic pathway.

questions.q: Gluconeogenesis is classified as:
questions.e: Gluconeogenesis synthesizes new glucose — anabolic.

questions.q: The Citric acid cycle is organized as a:
questions.e: Oxaloacetate is regenerated each turn — a true cycle.

questions.q: Gluconeogenesis is organized as a:
questions.e: Gluconeogenesis proceeds stepwise from pyruvate to glucose — linear.

questions.q: High concentration of glucose-6-phosphate is inhibitory to:
questions.e: G6P (the immediate product of the hexokinase reaction) feeds back to inhibit hexokinase itself — classic product inhibition.

questions.q: Which of the following is produced by the combination of apoenzyme and coenzyme?
questions.e: Apoenzyme (protein part) + coenzyme/cofactor = holoenzyme, the complete, catalytically active enzyme.

questions.q: The first step in the payoff phase of glycolysis is:
o: Irreversible conversion of DHAP to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate
Reversible conversion of DHAP to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate
questions.e: The payoff phase begins with GAPDH oxidising (and phosphorylating) glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate into 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, generating the first NADH of glycolysis.

questions.q: Galactitol is formed from galactose by the enzyme:
questions.e: Aldose reductase reduces excess galactose to galactitol (using NADPH); galactitol build-up in the lens is what drives cataract formation in galactosemia/galactokinase deficiency.

questions.q: The coenzyme is:
questions.e: Many coenzymes are vitamin-derived (e.g. NAD⁺/NADP⁺ from niacin, FAD from riboflavin, TPP from thiamine, CoA from pantothenic acid) — coenzymes are organic, not inorganic, and not proteins themselves.

questions.q: Which of the following is/are types of reversible inhibition?
questions.e: Competitive (and non-competitive/uncompetitive) inhibition is reversible; covalent modification is the hallmark of irreversible inhibition. 'Hydrogen' and 'oxidative' inhibition aren't standard inhibition categories.

questions.q: Inorganic fluoride inhibits enolase. In an anaerobic system metabolizing glucose, which compound would increase in concentration after fluoride is added?
questions.e: Enolase converts 2-phosphoglycerate → PEP. Block enolase, and its substrate — 2-phosphoglycerate — backs up and accumulates, while everything downstream (PEP, pyruvate) falls.

questions.q: Cleavage of Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate yields:
questions.e: Aldolase splits F1,6BP into DHAP (a ketose) and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (an aldose) — one of each.

questions.q: Which of the following is/are TRUE about the structure of Enzymes?
o: Most enzymes are smaller than their substrate
Active site usually has 10-15 amino acids
Are usually primary structures of proteins
Most enzymes have the same size as their substrate
questions.e: Enzymes are proteins with tertiary/quaternary structure (not just primary), are typically much LARGER than their substrates, and can be denatured by heat — the only true statement here.

questions.q: Enzyme complex involved in alcoholic fermentation is:
questions.e: Zymase is the multi-enzyme complex (in yeast) that converts sugars into ethanol and CO₂ during alcoholic fermentation.

questions.q: In comparison with the resting state, actively contracting human muscle tissue has a:
o: Lower rate of consumption of oxygen
Lower ratio of NADH to NAD⁺
questions.e: Corrected: contracting muscle ramps up anaerobic glycolysis, producing MORE lactate — the classic true statement here. It actually consumes more oxygen and more glucose (not less), and ATP is being used up (not sitting at a higher concentration), with a HIGHER (not lower) NADH:NAD⁺ ratio from the extra glycolytic flux.

questions.q: Koshland in 1959 proposed the:
questions.e: Koshland's induced-fit model (1959) proposed that the active site's shape adjusts to better fit the substrate upon binding.

questions.q: In the human body, the optimum temperature for enzymatic activities is:
questions.e: 37°C — normal human body temperature — is the optimum for most human enzymes.

questions.q: The enzymes are sensitive to:
questions.e: Both pH and temperature affect enzyme shape/charge and therefore activity — extremes of either can denature the enzyme.

questions.q: The 'lock and key' model of enzyme action illustrates that a particular enzyme molecule:
o: May be destroyed and resynthesized several times
Interacts with a specific type of substrate molecule
Reacts at identical rates under all conditions
questions.e: The model's core point is specificity — a given enzyme's active site shape fits only a particular substrate, like a specific key fits a specific lock.

questions.q: Non-protein components of enzymes are known as:
questions.e: 'Cofactor' is the umbrella term for any non-protein helper an enzyme needs; coenzymes (organic) and metal activators (inorganic) are simply the two main subtypes of cofactor.

questions.q: A catalyst is a chemical involved in, but not ___ by, a chemical reaction:
questions.e: Catalysts (including enzymes) speed up reactions without being permanently altered or consumed themselves.

questions.q: It suggests that the binding of substrate to the enzyme alters the structure of the enzyme, placing some strain on the substrate and further facilitating the reaction:
questions.e: This dynamic, shape-adjusting description is exactly the induced-fit model (Koshland), as opposed to the rigid lock-and-key model.

questions.q: The function of competitive inhibitors is defined by their ability to interact or bind to:
o: The active site of an enzyme
questions.e: Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate and compete directly for the active site.

questions.q: The enzymes are classified into:
questions.e: The classic IUBMB scheme has six main EC classes (oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases) — a 7th, translocases, was added more recently, but 'six' is the standard teaching answer.

questions.q: The name 'enzyme' was suggested in 1878 by the German physiologist:
questions.e: Wilhelm Kühne coined the term 'enzyme' (from Greek, 'in yeast') in 1878.

questions.q: An enzyme that hydrolyzes protein will not act upon starch. This fact indicates that enzymes are:
questions.e: Only working on one type of substrate (protein, not starch) demonstrates substrate specificity.

questions.q: Mg²⁺ is an inorganic activator for the enzyme:
questions.e: Many phosphatases (and kinases) rely on Mg²⁺ to help coordinate phosphate groups during catalysis. (Carbonic anhydrase needs Zn²⁺ instead — see the next question.)

questions.q: DDT and Parathion are inhibitors of key enzymes in the:
questions.e: Both are acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, disrupting nerve signal termination in the nervous system — the basis of their toxicity as pesticides/nerve agents.

questions.q: In the Lock and Key model of enzyme action, the part of the enzyme that recognizes the substrate is known as the:
questions.e: The active site is the specific region shaped to recognize and bind the substrate.

questions.q: At about 0°C, most enzymes are:
questions.e: Near-freezing temperatures dramatically slow molecular motion, making enzymes effectively inactive — though (unlike heat denaturation) they're usually not permanently destroyed and can become active again on warming.

questions.q: What is a coenzyme?
questions.e: Coenzymes are specifically organic cofactors (often vitamin-derived) — inorganic ion cofactors are called activators instead.

questions.q: Which enzyme represents an enzyme functioning in this reaction?
questions.e: ⚠️ This question depends entirely on a reaction diagram that wasn't captured in the extracted text — there's no way to determine the correct letter without seeing it. Please check the original slide/handout for the diagram and pick the labelled component that appears unchanged before and after the reaction (that's the enzyme).

questions.q: The following are true about the tricarboxylic acid cycle EXCEPT:
questions.e: The TCA cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, NOT the cytosol — that's the false (exception) statement. It genuinely does supply biosynthetic precursors, GTP (succinyl-CoA synthetase), and (via oxidative phosphorylation) ATP.

questions.q: Starting molecule for the Krebs cycle:
questions.e: Each turn begins when acetyl-CoA condenses with oxaloacetate (citrate synthase) to form citrate. Oxaloacetate is regenerated/recycled rather than being the fresh 'starting' input — acetyl-CoA is the new carbon source that kicks off each turn.

questions.q: The TCA cycle:
o: Uses 2 molecules of pyruvate per turn of the cycle
Is coupled with the release of NADPH
Produces energy in the form of ADP
questions.e: Corrected: the cycle doesn't use pyruvate directly (it uses 1 acetyl-CoA/turn), is net energy-YIELDING (not consuming), releases NADH (not NADPH), and produces ATP/GTP (ADP is what's consumed to make ATP, not a product). Only 'produces high-energy compounds' (3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP per turn) is true.

questions.q: This compound is produced in the oxidative phase of the Pentose Phosphate Pathway:
questions.e: 6-Phosphogluconolactone is formed by glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, the very first (oxidative-phase) reaction of the PPP. The other three are all non-oxidative-phase intermediates.

questions.q:
Assertion: Enzymes are crucial to metabolism
Reason: enzymes drive desirable reactions that cannot occur on their own (at a biologically useful rate).
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true, and this is exactly why enzymes are crucial — they make otherwise-too-slow reactions happen fast enough for life.

questions.q:
Assertion: The active site is directly involved in catalysis
Reason: the active site contains between 8 to 10 amino acid residues.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion true. The specific '8–10 residues' figure is not an accepted general rule (active sites are typically described as having only a few key catalytic residues) — reason is false.

questions.q:
Assertion: Holoenzyme is called a functional enzyme
Reason: holoenzyme is made up of an apoenzyme and a coenzyme.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — the holoenzyme (apoenzyme + cofactor) is the complete, catalytically active form, which is exactly why it's 'functional'.

questions.q:
Assertion: Papain can be used as a therapeutic agent
Reason: papain has anti-cancer properties.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion true (papain is used clinically, e.g. wound debridement, digestive aid). Its established therapeutic basis is its proteolytic activity, not anti-cancer effects — reason is false/unsubstantiated as the main basis.

questions.q:
Assertion: The phosphofructokinase reaction in glycolysis is the rate-limiting step
Reason: the phosphofructokinase reaction is not regulated.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion true (PFK-1 is the committed/rate-limiting step). Reason false — PFK-1 is in fact heavily regulated (by ATP, AMP, citrate, F2,6BP).

questions.q:
Assertion: Fructose absorption does not depend on sodium concentration in blood
Reason: fructose absorption is insulin independent.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true (fructose uses facilitated diffusion via GLUT5, unlike Na⁺-dependent glucose transport, and doesn't need insulin) — but insulin-independence doesn't explain sodium-independence; they're separate properties.

questions.q:
Assertion: Galactose cannot be produced in the cell
Reason: galactose is only obtained from dietary sources.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both false — the body can make galactose endogenously from glucose via UDP-glucose 4-epimerase, even without dietary galactose.

questions.q:
Assertion: In the Krebs cycle, aconitase isomerizes citrate to isocitrate
Reason: aconitase is an isomerase.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — aconitase catalyzes the isomerization of citrate to isocitrate (via cis-aconitate), consistent with its isomerase classification.

questions.q:
Assertion: Thiamine deficiency leads to high levels of pyruvate in the blood
Reason: high levels of pyruvate lead to decreased ATP production.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both statements are true, but the causal logic runs backwards for an explanation — it's the thiamine (TPP) deficiency impairing PDH that causes pyruvate to build up, not the other way around.

questions.q:
Assertion: The α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase reaction of the TCA cycle is the 3rd oxidative decarboxylation step of the pathway
Reason: it is the 5th step of the pathway.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion true when counting pyruvate dehydrogenase (pyruvate→acetyl-CoA) as the 1st oxidative decarboxylation, isocitrate DH as the 2nd, and α-KGDH as the 3rd. Reason false — within the 8-step TCA cycle itself, α-KGDH is step 4, not step 5 (corrected from the commonly circulated 'E' answer).

questions.q:
Assertion: The Lineweaver-Burk plot makes it easier to calculate Km and Vmax of a reaction
Reason: the Lineweaver-Burk plot gives a straight line.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — plotting 1/v vs 1/[S] linearises the Michaelis-Menten curve, and reading the slope/intercepts of that straight line is exactly how Km and Vmax are extracted.

questions.q:
Assertion: Essential fructosuria results in fructose appearing in the urine
Reason: it is an autosomal recessive disorder.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — fructokinase deficiency (essential fructosuria) is indeed autosomal recessive, and unmetabolized fructose does spill into urine. But the inheritance pattern doesn't explain WHY fructose ends up in urine — that's due to the enzyme deficiency itself, not how the condition is inherited.

questions.q:
Assertion: Fats are preferred over glycogen as a source of energy
Reason: fat can be rapidly metabolized.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both false — glycogen/glucose is actually mobilized and metabolized FASTER (better for quick energy needs), while fat oxidation (β-oxidation) is comparatively slow to ramp up, even though it yields more energy per gram over the long haul.

questions.q:
Dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (E3) uses cofactor(s):
I. Thiamine Pyrophosphate (TPP)
II. Lipoamide
III. CoASH
IV. FAD
V. NAD
o: i, ii, iii and v only
questions.e: E3 contains FAD, which is re-oxidized by passing electrons to NAD⁺ — items iv and v, option A.

questions.q:
α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is:
I. Inhibited by high levels of succinyl-CoA
II. Activated by Ca²⁺ ions
III. Inhibited by high levels of NADH
IV. Not involved in regulation of the TCA cycle
V. Inhibited by high levels of ATP
o: i, ii, iii and v only
questions.e: α-KGDH IS a regulated, key control point (iv is false and excluded). It's product-inhibited by succinyl-CoA and NADH, activated by Ca²⁺, and inhibited by high energy charge (ATP) — i, ii, iii, v → option B.

questions.q: Whenever the cell's ATP supply is depleted, which enzyme's activity is increased?
questions.e: Low ATP (high AMP/ADP) allosterically activates PFK-1, the committed, rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis.

questions.q: The enzyme involved in the first step of fructolysis in the liver is:
questions.e: In the liver, fructokinase phosphorylates fructose to fructose-1-phosphate as the first committed step.

questions.q: Enzymes belonging to EC class 5 are:
questions.e: EC 5 = Isomerases (EC1=oxidoreductases, EC2=transferases, EC3=hydrolases, EC4=lyases, EC6=ligases).

questions.q: The pyruvate dehydrogenase enzyme complex is composed of:
questions.e: E1 (decarboxylase), E2 (acetyltransferase), E3 (dehydrogenase) — 3 core enzymes; cofactors: TPP, lipoamide, CoASH, FAD, NAD⁺ — 5 cofactors.

questions.q: What cofactor(s) are required by the pyruvate dehydrogenase (E1) component?
questions.e: The E1 (decarboxylase) subunit specifically uses TPP; lipoamide belongs to E2, and FAD/NAD to E3.

questions.q: The enzyme ___ catalyses an anaplerotic reaction:
questions.e: Note: the classic mammalian anaplerotic enzyme is actually pyruvate carboxylase (pyruvate→OAA); PEP carboxylase performs an analogous carboxylation and is the closest match among these options.

questions.q: The Glyoxylate cycle:
o: Is a source for carbohydrate synthesis in some yeast
Uses one acetyl-CoA per turn of the cycle
questions.e: The glyoxylate cycle lets plants, some fungi/yeast and bacteria convert fatty-acid-derived acetyl-CoA into carbohydrate. It uses TWO acetyl-CoA per turn and does NOT occur in mammals (they lack malate synthase/isocitrate lyase).

questions.q: The Glyoxylate cycle occurs in the ___ of some bacteria:
questions.e: Classically the glyoxysome (a specialised peroxisome) houses this cycle in plants/fungi; note that true bacteria (no organelles) generally run these reactions in the cytosol, so this is a point worth clarifying with your lecturer.

questions.q: The by-passing enzymes in the Glyoxylate cycle are:
questions.e: Malate synthase and isocitrate lyase are the two unique enzymes that bypass the CO₂-releasing steps of the TCA cycle.

questions.q: Which statement(s) about the gold top/gel (SST) tube is/are TRUE?
questions.e: Gold/gel tubes have silica clot activator (i ✓) and a gel barrier that separates serum from cells on spinning (iii ✓), and are used for biochemical/chemistry tests (iv ✓). They do NOT contain EDTA (ii is false — that's the lavender tube).

questions.q: Which of the following is a TRUE statement?
o: Variable pipettes transfer small volumes of liquid accurately
Glass pipettes are highly precise (less than 0.5% error)
Glass pipettes come with their own pipette tips
Pipette fillers are used to fill micropipettes with liquid
questions.e: Class A glass volumetric pipettes have a well-known tolerance of under 0.5% — a standard fact in practical classes. Glass pipettes don't use disposable tips, and bulb/pump fillers are used with glass (not micro-) pipettes.

questions.q: CuSO₄·5H₂O stock (4.0%) is diluted with DF = 6.5 (→X1) and DF = 10 (→X2), 9 mL total each (FW = 250 g/mol). What is the molar concentration of X1?
Glycogenesis is classified as:
questions.e: Glycogenesis builds glycogen from glucose — an anabolic (synthetic) pathway.

questions.q: Galactose metabolism is classified as:
questions.e: The Leloir pathway converts galactose into glucose-1-phosphate for use/breakdown — catabolic.

questions.q: Fatty acid synthesis is organized as a:
questions.e: The same enzyme complex repeatedly adds 2-carbon units, elongating the chain each round — a spiral pathway.

questions.q: Cofactors that are tightly bound to an enzyme are known as:
questions.e: A cofactor that is permanently/tightly bound (rather than loosely associating and dissociating) is specifically called a prosthetic group; a loosely-bound organic cofactor is usually just called a coenzyme.

questions.q: Glycolysis:
o: Produces 4 ATPs at the end of the reaction
Occurs in the mitochondrion of the cell
questions.e: The payoff phase generates 4 ATP in total (2 per triose × 2 trioses); after subtracting the 2 ATP invested earlier in the preparatory phase, the NET yield is 2 ATP — but the gross amount produced 'at the end' (payoff phase) is 4.

questions.q: Cleavage of fructose-1-phosphate in fructolysis yields:
questions.e: Aldolase B splits fructose-1-phosphate into DHAP and free glyceraldehyde. DHAP can enter glycolysis directly (via isomerisation); the glyceraldehyde must first be phosphorylated by triokinase to become G3P.

questions.q: An enzyme catalyzing rearrangement of atomic groupings without altering molecular weight or number of atoms is:
questions.e: That's exactly the definition of an isomerase — it rearranges atoms within the same molecule without adding, removing, or changing the total atom count.

questions.q: Glycolysis in the erythrocyte produces pyruvate that is further metabolized to:
questions.e: Red blood cells have no mitochondria, so pyruvate can't enter the TCA cycle — it's reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, regenerating NAD⁺ for glycolysis to continue.

questions.q: An enzyme that joins the ends of two strands of nucleic acid is:
questions.e: DNA/RNA ligase seals nicks by joining the 3'-OH end of one strand to the 5'-phosphate end of another.

questions.q: Enzymes belonging to EC class 1 are the:
questions.e: EC 1 = Oxidoreductases (EC2=transferases, EC3=hydrolases, EC4=lyases, EC5=isomerases, EC6=ligases).

questions.q: The substrate used in the last step of glycolysis is:
questions.e: The last step is pyruvate kinase converting PEP → pyruvate, so PEP is the substrate consumed in that final reaction.

questions.q: In galactokinase deficiency there is accumulation of:
questions.e: Without galactokinase, galactose can't be phosphorylated, so it accumulates and gets shunted by aldose reductase into galactitol — the compound responsible for cataract formation in this condition.

questions.q: Dihydroxyacetone phosphate is rapidly and reversibly converted to:
questions.e: Triose phosphate isomerase reversibly interconverts DHAP and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, allowing both halves of the split hexose to continue through glycolysis.

questions.q: In humans, gluconeogenesis:
o: Is activated by the hormone insulin
Can result in the conversion of protein into blood glucose
Helps to reduce blood glucose after a carbohydrate-rich meal
questions.e: Glucogenic amino acids from protein breakdown (e.g. alanine, aspartate) can be converted via gluconeogenesis into glucose. Insulin actually suppresses (not activates) gluconeogenesis, and it uses PEPCK/pyruvate carboxylase, not hexokinase.

questions.q: The catalytic activity of an enzyme is restricted to its small portion called:
questions.e: Catalysis happens specifically at the active site — the small pocket/region that binds substrate and carries out the reaction.

questions.q: Enzymes are largely ___ in their chemical nature:
questions.e: With the exception of ribozymes (catalytic RNA), enzymes are proteins.

questions.q: Optimum pH value for pepsin is:
questions.e: Pepsin works in the highly acidic stomach environment, with an optimum pH around 1.5–2 — closest to 1.4 among these options.

questions.q: Enzyme B requires Zn²⁺ to catalyze the conversion of substrate X. The zinc is best identified as a(n):
questions.e: Metal ions required for catalysis are classed as (metal) activators/cofactors — 'coenzyme' specifically refers to organic cofactors, so activator is the better fit for a metal ion like Zn²⁺.

questions.q: In the reaction that prevents accumulation of hydrogen peroxide within cells, catalase functions as an:
o: Enzyme in the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide
Enzyme in the synthesis of hydrogen peroxide
Emulsifier in the digestion of hydrogen peroxide
Indicator in the detection of hydrogen peroxide
questions.e: Catalase rapidly breaks down toxic H₂O₂ into water and oxygen, protecting cells from oxidative damage.

questions.q: A student tests the efficiency of a certain enzyme. Which would probably NOT result in a change in the enzyme's efficiency?
o: Adding an acidic solution to the setup
Adding more substrate but not enzyme
All A, B, & C change the enzyme's efficiency
questions.e: pH and temperature changes directly alter the enzyme's own conformation/activity. Adding more substrate (without more enzyme) just changes the rate of product formation up to saturation — it doesn't change how efficient each enzyme molecule is.

questions.q: They are non-protein organic molecules bound to enzymes near the active site:
questions.e: Coenzymes are the organic (often vitamin-derived) non-protein cofactors that assist catalysis near the active site.

questions.q: If an enzyme solution is saturated with substrate, the most effective way to obtain an even faster yield of products would be:
questions.e: Once substrate is saturating, every enzyme molecule is already working at Vmax — adding more substrate won't help, but adding more enzyme molecules will increase the total rate.

questions.q: Which one is NOT an attribute of an enzyme?
questions.e: Enzymes are NOT consumed — they're reused again and again, unlike substrates. That's what makes 'consumed in reaction' the false/odd-one-out attribute.

questions.q: Non-protein part of a holoenzyme is:
questions.e: The tightly-bound non-protein portion of a holoenzyme is its prosthetic group (a type of cofactor); the apoenzyme is the protein part.

questions.q: Proteinaceous part of a holoenzyme is:
questions.e: The protein component of a holoenzyme is the apoenzyme; the non-protein part is the cofactor/prosthetic group.

questions.q: The site where the enzyme-catalyzed reaction takes place is called:
questions.e: Catalysis occurs at the active site.

questions.q: Zn²⁺ is an inorganic activator for the enzyme:
questions.e: Carbonic anhydrase is a classic zinc metalloenzyme — Zn²⁺ sits in its active site and is essential for catalysing CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺.

questions.q: At high temperature the rate of enzyme action decreases because the increased heat:
o: Changes the pH of the system
Alters the active site of the enzyme
Neutralizes acids and bases in the system
questions.e: Excess heat disrupts the weak bonds holding the enzyme's 3D shape together, distorting (denaturing) the active site so substrate no longer fits well.

questions.q: Which model says the active site moulds itself around the substrate as binding occurs?
questions.e: The induced fit model (Koshland, 1959) holds that the active site is flexible: substrate binding moulds it into the complementary shape, unlike the rigid pre-formed site of the lock and key model.

questions.q: Vitamins are essential to the survival of organisms because vitamins usually function as:
questions.e: Many vitamins (B-vitamins especially) are precursors to essential coenzymes — e.g. niacin→NAD⁺, riboflavin→FAD, thiamine→TPP.

questions.q: Which statement best expresses the information typically represented in a pH-vs-enzyme-activity graph?
o: The action of enzymes varies with pH
A pH of 7 provides the optimum environment for digestive enzymes
Gastric juice is active at a pH extending from 0 to 12
Acids have a pH greater than 7
questions.e: Different enzymes have very different pH optima — pepsin works near pH 1.5–2, trypsin near pH 8 — so any pH-versus-activity graph makes the same general point: enzyme activity varies with pH. (b) and (c) are false, and (d) is wrong by definition, since acids have a pH below 7.

questions.q: Galactose is found in:
questions.e: Honey's sugars are mainly fructose and glucose, and flower nectar is mainly sucrose/glucose/fructose — galactose isn't a notable component of either. (The original question only listed 'I. Honey' and 'II. Flowers' with no third alternative, so this has been reframed as a straightforward 4-way choice covering the same ground.) Galactose is best known from lactose (dairy) and, endogenously, from the body's own UDP-glucose 4-epimerase pathway.

questions.q: Which of the following enzymes brings pyruvate to its site of action?
questions.e: The mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (pyruvate translocase) transports cytosolic pyruvate across the inner mitochondrial membrane into the matrix, where pyruvate dehydrogenase then acts on it.

questions.q: The α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex is composed of:
questions.e: Structurally analogous to the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex: 3 catalytic enzymes (E1, E2, E3) and 5 cofactors (TPP, lipoamide, CoASH, FAD, NAD⁺).

questions.q: Malic enzyme converts:
questions.e: Malic enzyme catalyses malate + NADP⁺ → pyruvate + CO₂ + NADPH — an oxidative decarboxylation, and a major source of cytosolic NADPH for lipogenesis. The paper printed the option backwards; it reads in the correct direction here.

questions.q: Which of the glycolytic intermediates is formed in the non-oxidative phase (of the PPP)?
questions.e: The point of the non-oxidative phase is to hand carbon back to glycolysis. Transketolase and transaldolase convert the pentose phosphates into FRUCTOSE-6-PHOSPHATE and GLYCERALDEHYDE 3-PHOSPHATE — those are the glycolytic intermediates produced. Ribose 5-phosphate and xylulose 5-phosphate are pentose phosphates, not glycolytic intermediates, and the paper’s third option ("epimerase") was an enzyme rather than a metabolite.

questions.q:
Assertion: ATP has high energy bonds
Reason: ATP is formed from ADP and phosphate.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both statements are true, but simply being 'formed from ADP + Pi' doesn't explain why the phosphoanhydride bonds are high-energy (that's due to charge repulsion/resonance effects) — not a correct explanation.

questions.q:
Assertion: All enzymes are denatured by heat
Reason: all enzymes have a three-dimensional structure.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: The word 'all' makes the assertion false — thermostable enzymes (e.g. from thermophilic organisms) resist heat denaturation. The reason (3D structure) is true.

questions.q:
Assertion: Irreversible inhibitors are easily dissociated from enzymes
Reason: irreversible inhibitors bind to enzymes through non-covalent forces.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both false — irreversible inhibitors bind essentially permanently (often covalently), so they are NOT easily dissociated.

questions.q:
Assertion: In type 2 diabetes, the activity of GLUT-4 is reduced
Reason: in type 2 diabetes, there is increased insulin resistance in skeletal tissues.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — insulin resistance directly impairs insulin-stimulated GLUT-4 translocation/activity, a correct explanation.

questions.q:
Assertion: Free ATP is a potent non-competitive inhibitor in glycolysis
Reason: free ATP inhibits hexokinase in glycolysis.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion true (ATP allosterically inhibits PFK-1). Reason false — it's glucose-6-phosphate (the product), not ATP, that inhibits hexokinase.

questions.q:
Assertion: Essential fructosuria results in the inability to metabolize fructose beyond fructose-1-phosphate
Reason: essential fructosuria is caused by a deficiency of fructose-1-phosphate aldolase.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both false — that description is Hereditary Fructose Intolerance (aldolase B deficiency). Essential fructosuria is caused by fructokinase deficiency, so fructose is never even phosphorylated to F1P.

questions.q:
Assertion: The Krebs cycle is called the tricarboxylic acid cycle
Reason: the first tricarboxylic acid produced is isocitrate.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion true. Reason false — the first tricarboxylic acid formed is CITRATE (via citrate synthase); isocitrate is formed one step later by aconitase.

questions.q:
Assertion: The Krebs cycle is halted by fluoroacetate
Reason: fluoroacetate binds tightly to citrate synthase.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion true. Reason false — fluoroacetate is actually converted BY citrate synthase into fluorocitrate, and it's the fluorocitrate that then tightly inhibits aconitase, halting the cycle.

questions.q:
Assertion: The succinyl-CoA synthetase reaction is a substrate-level phosphorylation reaction
Reason: succinyl-CoA synthetase uses 5 enzymes and 3 cofactors.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Assertion true (it directly generates GTP/ATP). Reason false — that '5 enzymes, 3 cofactors' description actually belongs to the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, not succinyl-CoA synthetase (a single enzyme).

questions.q:
Assertion: Increase in alanine transaminase (ALT) in the blood is a result of liver damage
Reason: increase in ALT in the blood results from leakage from damaged hepatocytes.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — ALT is a liver-enriched cytosolic enzyme, so it normally stays inside hepatocytes; injury lets it leak into the bloodstream, which is exactly why elevated ALT signals liver damage.

questions.q:
Assertion: Galactose cannot be made in the body
Reason: galactose can only be obtained from dietary sources.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both false — the body can synthesize galactose endogenously from glucose via UDP-glucose 4-epimerase, even without any dietary galactose.

questions.q:
Assertion: Epimerase converts ribulose-5-phosphate to xylulose-5-phosphate in the hexose monophosphate shunt
Reason: epimerase is an isomerase.
o: Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion & Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE
questions.e: Both true — ribulose-5-phosphate 3-epimerase inverts the configuration at one carbon to make xylulose-5-phosphate, and epimerases are indeed a subclass of isomerases (EC 5), which is exactly why it can perform this interconversion.

questions.q:
Pyruvate Dehydrogenase (E1) uses cofactor(s):
I. Thiamine Pyrophosphate (TPP)
II. Lipoamide
III. CoASH
IV. FAD
V. NAD
o: i, ii, iii and v only
questions.e: The E1 (decarboxylase) component specifically requires only TPP (item i) — matches option D, 'i only'.

questions.q:
α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (E1 analogue) uses cofactor(s):
I. Thiamine Pyrophosphate (TPP)
II. Lipoamide
III. CoASH
IV. FAD
V. NAD
o: i, ii, iii and v only
questions.e: Structurally analogous to the PDH complex, its decarboxylase component uses TPP only — option D.
